aquifer_name: Nappe de la Plaine des Angad et de Maghnia; Nappe profonde de Jbel-Hamra
claim_tested: More than 99% of MAR's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (150 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
gis_acceptance: accepted: feature strictly inside the polygon and band
error_class_description: applied: interior cropland understated, concentration share collapses
applied_to: class only (classF unchanged: absorbed by the future projection)
evidence: The Moroccan part of this system is the Angads plain aquifer (~450-460 km2), which underlies Oujda and extends west and south of it; Oujda itself is ~15 km from the Algerian border and the plain continues a further ~30 km westward (fed laterally by the Bouhouria aquifer). Basin documentation for the Moulouya gives total Angad abstraction of ~36 Mm3/yr of which ~20 Mm3/yr is for irrigation, i.e. on the order of 3,000-5,000 ha of groundwater-irrigated land; peer-reviewed surveys of the plain report groundwater as the principal/only water source and intensive fertilised, irrigated agriculture 'in the south and around Oujda'. That places substantial groundwater-irrigated cropland over the mapped aquifer well beyond 10 km from the Algeria-Morocco border.
sources: [T1] Bouhout, S. et al. (2025). Assessment of groundwater pollution using PIG index and microbiological indicators in the Angads plain, Morocco. Scientific Reports 15. (Angads plain 460 km2; groundwater is the principal, indeed only, supply source; high agricultural activity; irrigation-water infiltration; Oujda draws 63% of drinking water from the aquifer.) https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-99956-z | [T1] Taoufiq, H. et al. (2024). Monitoring the Overall Quality of Groundwater Using a Geographic Information System in the Angads Plain (Oujda, Morocco). The Scientific World Journal. (Study area extent and agricultural setting of the Angads plain, eastern Taourirt-Oujda corridor.) https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1155/tswj/7511804 | [T2] Moulouya basin hydrological synthesis chapter (nappe des Angad: ~450 km2, recharge ~32 Mm3/yr, abstraction ~36 Mm3/yr of which 20 Mm3/yr for irrigation and 16 Mm3/yr for drinking water incl. Oujda; underground inflow from the Bouhouria aquifer). Accessed via a document-hosting mirror; original agency publication not verified. https://pdfcoffee.com/11-moulouya-def-pdf-free.html | [T1] Diagnostic de l'etat d'utilisation et de gestion de l'eau dans la ville d'Oujda (MON-3 / Plan Communal d'Oujda, 2019). (Nappe des Angads shallow aquifer and Jbel Hamra deep dolomitic aquifer both heavily exploited; ~1.5 m3/s abstracted in the Taourirt-Oujda corridor for agriculture, industry and drinking water.) https://mon-3.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/Diagnostic-de-etat-utilisation-et-gestion-de-eau-dans-la-ville-Oujda.pdf
notes: The contradiction is to the BL trigger only: it is the '100% of MAR's 1,501 ha lies within 10 km' figure that is not tenable, not the existence of border-proximate irrigation (which is real, on both sides). Applying the ordered rule to corrected numbers: not IU0/IU1 (both sides have groundwater irrigation and urban land within 100 km); not UB; BL fails on both sides (DZA is 2,276/2,359 = 96.5%, below 99%, and MAR is no longer ~100%); therefore DA. Caveat: I could not obtain a source that states irrigated hectares by distance band, so the quantitative split is inferred from the aquifer's mapped footprint (Oujda at ~15 km from the border, plain extending ~30 km further west) combined with the 20 Mm3/yr irrigation abstraction figure. The strongest single number (20 Mm3/yr for irrigation) comes from a mirrored copy of a basin report whose original publisher I could not verify, so it is recorded as Tier 2; the Tier 1 basis for the verdict is the peer-reviewed delineation of the Angads plain plus its documented irrigated-agriculture groundwater use. If the authors can check the AF074 polygon geometry directly, that would settle it quickly. Note also AF078 (Jbel Hamra deep dolomites) is exploited mainly for Oujda's municipal supply, not cropland irrigation.

claim_tested: More than 99% of RUS's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (6 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Irrigation on the Russian (Dagestan) side of the Samur is supplied by the Samur-Derbent canal, i.e. surface water diverted from the Samur River, not by groundwater. The documented groundwater development in the Russian part of the aquifer is the Samur forest wellfield in Magaramkent district, drilled to supply drinking water to the city of Derbent - municipal abstraction, not cropland irrigation.
sources: [T2] OC Media (2018). Daghestani village demands end to water extraction in 'unique forest'. (Wells drilled in the Samur Forest, Magaramkent district, to provide drinking water to Derbent.) https://oc-media.org/daghestani-village-demands-end-to-water-extraction-in-unique-forest/ | [T1] UNECE, Second Assessment of Transboundary Rivers, Lakes and Groundwaters, Part IV Chapter 4: Drainage basin of the Caspian Sea (Samur basin; Samur-Absheron and Samur-Derbent diversions are surface-water canals). https://unece.org/DAM/env/water/publications/assessment/English/H_PartIV_Chapter4_En.pdf
notes: Near-miss worth recording: substantial groundwater abstraction does occur on the Russian side within ~10-20 km of the border (Samur forest wellfield, Magaramkent district), but it is municipal supply for Derbent, so under the protocol it does not contradict a cropland claim. It may nonetheless matter for any abstraction-based robustness variant. The UNECE chapter could not be retrieved directly (403) and is cited from the search record plus general basin documentation; the substantive point - that Dagestani irrigation south of Derbent is canal-fed from the Samur - is well established. Russia's 61 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland is a very small number and I found nothing that would displace it northward along the coastal plain.

claim_tested: More than 99% of KHM's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (21 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
gis_acceptance: accepted: feature strictly inside the polygon and band
error_class_description: applied: interior cropland understated, concentration share collapses
applied_to: class only (classF unchanged: absorbed by the future projection)
evidence: Cambodia has widespread tube-well groundwater irrigation distributed across the lowlands overlying this aquifer, far more than 209 ha and not confined to a 10 km border strip: Prey Veng 9,038 tube-wells irrigating 13,557 ha, Takeo 1,253 wells / 2,753 ha, Kampong Cham 1,258 wells / 2,402 ha, Kandal 347 wells / 372 ha, plus Siem Reap (110 ha) and Battambang (22 ha) in the Tonle Sap region - roughly 12,000 tube-wells and ~9% of Cambodia's irrigated area. Prey Veng, Kampong Cham and Kandal extend tens to well over 100 km from the Vietnamese border, so the great majority of this groundwater-irrigated cropland lies beyond 10 km of that border while remaining over the mapped aquifer.
sources: [T1] Ministry of Water Resources and Meteorology / UNDP, Development of Groundwater Management Strategy in Cambodia (2020). Table 6, tube-wells and groundwater-irrigated area by province; 'Areas where groundwater irrigation is known to take place include Siem Reap, Battambang, and Kampong Chhnang in the Tonle Sap region; Kampong Cham province in the Phnom Penh region; and Prey Veng, Svay Rieng, Takeo, and Kandal in the south.' https://www.adaptation-undp.org/sites/default/files/resources/groundwater_managment_in_cambodia_-_v.24.02.202027958.pdf | [T2] Open Development Cambodia, Groundwater topic page. ('Tube wells are mostly used in Prey Veng and Svay Rieng (South-east Cambodia). Dug wells are commonly found in Kampong Thom province, as well as in central and North-east Cambodia'; ~270,000 tube wells nationally; groundwater used for late-dry-season and supplementary wet-season rice irrigation.) https://opendevelopmentcambodia.net/topics/groundwater/
notes: This is the clearest contradiction in the batch. The 209 ha assigned to Cambodia understates documented groundwater irrigation over this polygon by roughly two orders of magnitude, and the spatial pattern is the opposite of border-concentrated: the largest block (Prey Veng, 13,557 ha) is spread across a province whose north-south extent is ~100 km, and Kampong Cham and Kandal sit around Phnom Penh, 50-150 km from the Vietnamese border. Applying the ordered rule: not IU0/IU1; not UB; BL fails on both sides (VNM is 1,529/13,576 = 11%; KHM is no longer concentrated); therefore DA. Likely cause on our side: the global groundwater-irrigation layer misses smallholder shallow tube-well dry-season rice in the Cambodian lowlands, which is exactly the land use this aquifer is known for. The same failure mode probably affects other Mekong-lowland dyads in the wider dataset, so this one is worth flagging beyond the single reclassification. Provincial figures date from the 2001-2005 period and groundwater irrigation has expanded since.

aquifer_name: Umm er Radhuma-Dammam Aquifer System (Centre): Gulf
claim_tested: More than 99% of ARE's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (3 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: UN-ESCWA's Inventory chapter for the Umm er Radhuma-Dammam Aquifer System (Centre)/Gulf lists its riparians as Bahrain, Qatar and Saudi Arabia only and does not extend the unit into the UAE; the IGRAC polygon evidently clips only the far-western corner of Abu Dhabi (Sila/Ghuwaifat), a sabkha and desert strip immediately adjacent to the Saudi border where a token 28 ha of cropland within 10 km is entirely plausible.
sources: [T1] UN-ESCWA & BGR (2013). Inventory of Shared Water Resources in Western Asia, Chapter 15: Gulf Umm er Radhuma-Dammam Aquifer System (Centre). ('This section extends across three Gulf states: Bahrain, Qatar and Saudi Arabia'; riparian countries Bahrain, Qatar, Saudi Arabia.) https://waterinventory.org/sites/waterinventory.org/files/chapters/Chapter-15-Umm-er-Radhuma-Dammam-Aquifer-System-Center-web.pdf | [T1] UN-ESCWA & BGR (2013). Inventory of Shared Water Resources in Western Asia, Chapter 14: Rub' al Khali Umm er Radhuma-Dammam Aquifer System (South). (Assigns the UAE's Liwa/Al Dhafra groundwater irrigation area to the southern, not the central, system.) https://waterinventory.org/sites/waterinventory.org/files/chapters/Chapter-14-Umm-er-Radhuma-Dammam-Aquifer-System-South-web.pdf | [T1] IWMI/GW-MENA, Groundwater governance in Liwa oasis: agriculture and groundwater in Liwa, United Arab Emirates. (Documents the UAE's principal groundwater-irrigated date-palm and forage area, in Liwa.) https://gw-mena.iwmi.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2017/04/Rep.15-Groundwater-governance-in-Liwa-oasis-report_final_cover.pdf
notes: Important near-miss the authors should be aware of: the UAE does have very large groundwater-irrigated areas over Umm er Radhuma-Dammam rocks - Liwa oasis and the Al Dhafra farms - and if the IGRAC AS140 polygon were extended south/east to cover them, ARE's total would be thousands of hectares, none of it within 10 km of the Saudi border, and the dyad would not be BL. Under ESCWA's delineation those areas belong to the *South* (Rub' al Khali) system, so they are correctly excluded here, but the AS140/AS141 boundary in the IGRAC layer is the load-bearing assumption. Note also that both sides show 0 ha of urban land within 100 km, which is consistent with a remote desert border segment. I did not find any evidence of cropland in far-western Abu Dhabi beyond the 10 km band inside this polygon.

claim_tested: More than 99% of USA's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (3 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: The two authoritative treatments of this aquifer I could locate - the NM WRRI assessment of trans-international boundary aquifers in southwestern New Mexico and the peer-reviewed identification/categorization of Chihuahua-New Mexico transboundary aquifers - characterize the Hachita-Moscos/Ascension system hydrogeologically (a closed, partly drained basin of ~2,700 km2, ~1,100 km2 in Mexico, with ephemeral axial drainage to Laguna los Moscos and estimated transboundary flow of no more than ~2.5 Mm3/yr) but contain no land-use, irrigated-acreage or well-inventory data for either side.
sources: [T1] New Mexico Water Resources Research Institute, Trans-International Boundary Aquifers in Southwestern New Mexico, Executive Summary. (Hachita-Moscos basin extent; ephemeral Hachita and Wamels Draws; preliminary transboundary flow estimate.) https://nmwrri.nmsu.edu/publications/pub-documents/trans-international-boundary-aquifers-in-southwest-new-mexico/execsum.pdf | [T1] Sanchez, R. et al. (2021). Transboundary Aquifers between Baja California, Sonora and Chihuahua, Mexico, and California, Arizona and New Mexico, United States: Identification and Categorization. Water 13(20), 2878. (Ascension Aq./Hachita Moscos Basin: good aquifer potential and good water quality; northern boundary at the Continental Divide.) https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4441/13/20/2878
notes: I searched and found nothing contradicting the claim, but I also found nothing that positively characterizes irrigation on the New Mexico (Hidalgo County / Hachita valley) side, so I am reporting INSUFFICIENT rather than CONFIRMED. The claim is not implausible on its face - the US portion is sparsely settled ranching country with playas and no perennial surface water, and 30 ha is a token figure - but nothing I retrieved lets me verify the distance distribution. The Mexican side (Ascension, Chihuahua, 12,628 ha of groundwater irrigation, only 19% within 10 km) is consistent with the well-documented Ascension/Janos irrigated pivots, and that half of the classification looks sound. USGS/NM Office of the State Engineer well-permit records or USDA county irrigation statistics for Hidalgo County would resolve the US side if the authors want to close it.

claim_tested: More than 99% of MEX's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (8 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: The Redford Bolson is a narrow bolson (295 km2 in the IGRAC polygon) whose southwestern boundary is the Rio Grande itself - which is the international border - and which is hemmed in by the Chinati, Cienega, Black Hills and Bofecillos uplands; essentially the entire unit therefore lies within ~10-15 km of the border, and the farming reported in the southern part of Presidio County is floodplain truck farming (onions and vegetables) along the river.
sources: [T1] Presidio County Underground Water Conservation District Management Plan (2015), Texas Water Development Board. ('bounded along the northeast by the Chinati Mountains and along the southeast by the Cienega Mountains, the Black Hills and the Bofecillos Mountains. The southwest boundary of the Bolson in the District is the Rio Grande'; farming is the major income in the southern county, truck farming such as onions and other vegetables.) https://www.twdb.texas.gov/groundwater/docs/GCD/pcuwcd/pcuwcd_mgmt_plan2015.pdf
notes: This claim is close to geometrically self-fulfilling: a 295 km2 bolson bounded on one side by the border river cannot hold much cropland more than 10 km from the border, so BL on the Mexican side (81 ha, all within 10 km) is what the geometry predicts. The management plan does not disaggregate irrigated acreage between the Presidio and Redford portions or by water source, so the groundwater-versus-Rio-Grande split for the small acreage involved is unverified; either way the distance band is unaffected. Both sides are tiny (MEX 81 ha, USA 38 ha) and both are ~100% within 10 km, so the dyad would be BL under almost any perturbation.

claim_tested: COL has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: Agriculture in the Amazon basin is overwhelmingly rainfed - 'at present, agriculture in the region is primarily rain-fed and relies almost exclusively on green-water resources' - and no groundwater-irrigated cropland is documented in the Colombian Amazon near the Venezuelan border (Guainia/Vaupes/Amazonas departments), where settlement is sparse and riverine.
sources: [T1] Zaehle, S. et al. / Bagley, J.E. et al. (2016). A review of green- and blue-water resources and their trade-offs for future agricultural production in the Amazon Basin: what could irrigated agriculture mean for Amazonia? Hydrology and Earth System Sciences 20, 2179-2197. https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/20/2179/2016/ | [T1] FAO, Transboundary River Basin Overview - Amazon (AQUASTAT). https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/b8d766bb-e7c7-4857-9911-d09d9035cf4c/content
notes: Colombia's 84 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland over the whole 3.74 million km2 Amazonas polygon are located far from this border, which is consistent with Colombian irrigation being concentrated in the Andean and Caribbean regions, not the Amazon. Generic caveat applying to all eight S013 dyads: the polygon is enormous and a single 'Amazonas' aquifer treated as one transboundary unit means the 100 km border bands sample only remote, forested, riverine terrain. Groundwater in this region is developed for municipal supply (e.g. the OTCA hydrogeological work at Leticia-Tabatinga), not for irrigation.

claim_tested: PER has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: No groundwater-irrigated cropland is documented in the Peruvian Amazon (Madre de Dios) within 100 km of the Bolivian border; Amazonian agriculture there is rainfed, and Peru's groundwater irrigation is confined to the Pacific coastal valleys.
sources: [T1] Bagley, J.E. et al. (2016). A review of green- and blue-water resources and their trade-offs for future agricultural production in the Amazon Basin. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences 20, 2179-2197. ('At present, agriculture in the region is primarily rain-fed and relies almost exclusively on green-water resources.') https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/20/2179/2016/ | [T1] FAO, Transboundary River Basin Overview - Amazon (AQUASTAT). https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/b8d766bb-e7c7-4857-9911-d09d9035cf4c/content
notes: Peru shows exactly zero irrigated cropland of any kind over this polygon in our data, which is consistent with the literature: Peruvian irrigation, including all of its groundwater irrigation, is on the Pacific slope, hundreds of kilometres west of the Amazonas polygon. Bolivia's 22 ha within 100 km on the other side is the only irrigation in the dyad and is what makes this UB rather than IU1.

claim_tested: BRA has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: No groundwater-irrigated cropland is documented on the Brazilian side within 100 km of the Peruvian border (western Amazonas and Acre states); agriculture there is rainfed smallholder and pasture, and Brazil's irrigated agriculture - including centre pivots - lies in the southern and eastern Amazon frontier and the Cerrado, far outside this band.
sources: [T1] Bagley, J.E. et al. (2016). A review of green- and blue-water resources and their trade-offs for future agricultural production in the Amazon Basin. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences 20, 2179-2197. https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/20/2179/2016/ | [T1] FAO, Transboundary River Basin Overview - Amazon (AQUASTAT). https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/b8d766bb-e7c7-4857-9911-d09d9035cf4c/content
notes: Brazil records 0 ha of groundwater irrigation and only 3 ha of irrigation of any kind over this polygon, against 186,961 ha of urban land within 100 km - the urban figure is driven by Amazonian river towns (and, at this scale, by the polygon's reach). Nothing found contradicts the cropland claim. The Brazilian Amazon does use groundwater heavily for municipal supply (e.g. the Alter do Chao aquifer), which is not cropland irrigation.

claim_tested: BRA has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: No groundwater-irrigated cropland is documented on the Brazilian side within 100 km of the Colombian border; the tri-border area around Tabatinga-Leticia is forested and riverine, its agriculture rainfed, and the documented groundwater development there is for urban drinking-water supply, not irrigation.
sources: [T1] OTCA / Amazon Basin Project, Hydrogeological, vulnerability and risk assessment for the development of policies for the protection and sustainable use of groundwater in the transboundary region of Leticia and Tabatinga. (Groundwater in the tri-border area is developed for urban supply.) https://aguasamazonicas.otca.org/intervencion/hydrogeological-vulnerability-and-risk-assessment-for-the-development-of-groundwater-protection-and-use-policies-for-the-transboundary-region-of-leticia-and-tabatinga/?lang=en | [T1] Bagley, J.E. et al. (2016). A review of green- and blue-water resources and their trade-offs for future agricultural production in the Amazon Basin. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences 20, 2179-2197. https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/20/2179/2016/
notes: This is the dyad where the Leticia-Tabatinga groundwater work is most directly relevant, and it is unambiguously about protecting urban water supply wells, not irrigation - a near-miss under the protocol's water-use test rather than a contradiction. Both sides' urban figures (BRA 186,961 ha, COL 128,590 ha within 100 km) are what drives the UB classification.

claim_tested: COL has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: No groundwater-irrigated cropland is documented in the Colombian Amazon (Amazonas department, around Leticia) within 100 km of the Peruvian border; agriculture is rainfed smallholder cultivation and the local groundwater development at Leticia is for municipal supply.
sources: [T1] OTCA / Amazon Basin Project, Hydrogeological, vulnerability and risk assessment ... transboundary region of Leticia and Tabatinga. https://aguasamazonicas.otca.org/intervencion/hydrogeological-vulnerability-and-risk-assessment-for-the-development-of-groundwater-protection-and-use-policies-for-the-transboundary-region-of-leticia-and-tabatinga/?lang=en | [T1] Bagley, J.E. et al. (2016). A review of green- and blue-water resources and their trade-offs for future agricultural production in the Amazon Basin. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences 20, 2179-2197. https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/20/2179/2016/
notes: Colombia's 84 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland over the polygon are not near this border segment. Peru contributes zero irrigation of any kind, so the dyad is UB on the strength of urban land on both sides.

claim_tested: BRA has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: No groundwater-irrigated cropland is documented on the Brazilian side within 100 km of the Bolivian border over this polygon (Acre and southern Amazonas); land use there is forest, pasture and rainfed cropping.
sources: [T1] Bagley, J.E. et al. (2016). A review of green- and blue-water resources and their trade-offs for future agricultural production in the Amazon Basin. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences 20, 2179-2197. https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/20/2179/2016/ | [T1] FAO, Transboundary River Basin Overview - Amazon (AQUASTAT). https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/b8d766bb-e7c7-4857-9911-d09d9035cf4c/content
notes: Weakest of the eight Amazonas cases in principle, because the Bolivia-Brazil border segment runs closest to the expanding southern Amazon agricultural frontier (Rondonia). Irrigated agriculture on that frontier is however still small and predominantly surface-water or supplementary; I found no evidence of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of this border segment. Worth a second look if the authors have access to Brazilian IBGE municipal irrigation statistics for Rondonia and Acre.

claim_tested: ECU has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: No groundwater-irrigated cropland is documented in the Ecuadorian Amazon (Orellana, Pastaza, Morona Santiago, Zamora Chinchipe) within 100 km of the Peruvian border; Ecuador's Amazonian agriculture is rainfed and its irrigation is concentrated in the Sierra and coastal provinces.
sources: [T1] Bagley, J.E. et al. (2016). A review of green- and blue-water resources and their trade-offs for future agricultural production in the Amazon Basin. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences 20, 2179-2197. https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/20/2179/2016/ | [T1] FAO, Transboundary River Basin Overview - Amazon (AQUASTAT). https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/b8d766bb-e7c7-4857-9911-d09d9035cf4c/content
notes: Both sides record zero irrigated cropland of any kind over this polygon; the dyad is UB purely on urban land (ECU 84,220 ha, PER 59,026 ha within 100 km). Nothing found contradicts the claim. The dominant water-related activity in the Ecuadorian Amazon is oil-sector abstraction and produced water, not irrigation.

claim_tested: COL has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: No groundwater-irrigated cropland is documented in the Colombian Amazon (Putumayo) within 100 km of the Ecuadorian border; agriculture in the Putumayo piedmont is rainfed, and Colombia's groundwater irrigation is concentrated in the Caribbean, Cauca and upper Magdalena regions.
sources: [T1] Bagley, J.E. et al. (2016). A review of green- and blue-water resources and their trade-offs for future agricultural production in the Amazon Basin. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences 20, 2179-2197. https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/20/2179/2016/ | [T1] FAO, Transboundary River Basin Overview - Amazon (AQUASTAT). https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/b8d766bb-e7c7-4857-9911-d09d9035cf4c/content
notes: This border segment sits at the Andean piedmont, the part of the Amazonas polygon where agricultural intensification is most advanced, so it is the S013 dyad most exposed to future change. Current evidence still shows rainfed systems; Colombia's 84 ha of groundwater irrigation over the polygon are recorded as being outside the 100 km band.

claim_tested: BDI has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: Burundi's irrigation assessment states explicitly that 'there is no significant use of groundwater for irrigation'; 99% of Burundi's irrigated fields are in the Imbo, Moso and Bugesera plains and the marshes, supplied by rivers, streams and (near Nyanza-Lac) lake water pumped from Lake Tanganyika, and the country's groundwater - almost entirely from springs - is used for domestic supply.
sources: [T1] FutureWater / IFAD, Assessment of the Irrigation Potential in Burundi, Eastern DRC, Kenya, Rwanda, South Sudan, Tanzania and Uganda - Appendix Burundi. ('There is no significant use of groundwater for irrigation'; 99% of irrigated fields in the Imbo, Moso, Bugesera plains and marshes; area equipped for irrigation 23,000 ha in 2005.) https://www.futurewater.eu/irripot/Appendix_Burundi_V11.pdf | [T1] British Geological Survey, Africa Groundwater Atlas: Hydrogeology of Burundi. ('Most domestic water supplies in Burundi rely on groundwater, almost all from springs' - ~22,000 springs versus fewer than 30 boreholes in 2010.) https://earthwise.bgs.ac.uk/index.php/Hydrogeology_of_Burundi
notes: The Imbo plain along Lake Tanganyika, immediately west of Bujumbura and within 100 km of the DRC border, is genuinely irrigated - but from the Rusizi river and its distributaries and from lake pumping, i.e. surface water, so it does not contradict a groundwater claim. That is the near-miss to record. Our data are consistent with this: Burundi shows 405 ha of irrigated cropland but 0 ha groundwater-irrigated. The high urban figure (1,449,950 ha within 100 km) reflects Bujumbura and the dense Burundian settlement belt.

claim_tested: BDI has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: Same Tier 1 finding as for the BDI-COD dyad: Burundi has no significant groundwater irrigation, its 23,000 ha equipped area (of which ~5,000 ha actually irrigated) being surface-water schemes in the Imbo, Moso and Bugesera plains and marshes, and its groundwater use is spring-based domestic supply.
sources: [T1] FutureWater / IFAD, Assessment of the Irrigation Potential in Burundi ... - Appendix Burundi. ('There is no significant use of groundwater for irrigation'; 'No data are available on groundwater usage'; only one drilling company in country with little equipment.) https://www.futurewater.eu/irripot/Appendix_Burundi_V11.pdf | [T1] British Geological Survey, Africa Groundwater Atlas: Hydrogeology of Burundi. https://earthwise.bgs.ac.uk/index.php/Hydrogeology_of_Burundi
notes: The Burundi-Tanzania border runs through the Moso plain and the Malagarasi headwaters, where the Moso irrigation schemes sit; those are surface-water schemes, so again a near-miss rather than a contradiction. Tanzania's side contributes just 1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km, and the Kigoma-region irrigation that does exist is river-fed traditional and improved schemes.

claim_tested: COD has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: Neither the DRC side (Uvira, Fizi, Kalemie in South Kivu and Tanganyika province) nor the Tanzanian side (Kigoma, Katavi, Rukwa) has documented groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of this border; irrigation in the eastern DRC around Lake Tanganyika is confined to the Ruzizi plain and is river-fed, and the regional irrigation assessment finds no significant groundwater irrigation anywhere in the Lake Tanganyika riparian zone.
sources: [T1] FutureWater / IFAD, Assessment of the Irrigation Potential in Burundi, Eastern DRC, Kenya, Rwanda, South Sudan, Tanzania and Uganda. https://www.futurewater.eu/irripot/Appendix_Burundi_V11.pdf | [T1] United Republic of Tanzania, Ministry of Water, Lake Tanganyika Basin Fact Sheet. (Basin water resources and use in the Tanzanian portion.) https://www.maji.go.tz/uploads/publications/sw1583410571-Lake%20Tanganyika%20Basin%20Fact%20Sheet.pdf
notes: The DRC-Tanzania border here is the lake itself, so the 100 km bands cover the Congolese lakeshore escarpment and the Tanzanian Kigoma/Katavi hinterland - both areas of rainfed cassava, maize and oil palm with negligible irrigation of any kind (our data give COD 1 ha and TZA 40 ha of irrigation in total). Confidence is medium rather than high because DRC land- and water-use statistics are poor; the FutureWater assessment's eastern-DRC coverage is the best source I found and it reports no groundwater irrigation.

claim_tested: Both KAZ and RUS have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Irrigation in the Irtysh basin on both the Kazakh (Pavlodar, East Kazakhstan, Kostanay) and Russian (Omsk, Tyumen, Novosibirsk) sides is dominated by surface-water diversion from the Irtysh and its canals, with groundwater used for scattered small-scale irrigation, stock watering and rural supply distributed across the West Siberian plain rather than concentrated in a border strip - which is what the DA claim asserts.
sources: [T1] Eurasian Development Bank, The Irtysh River Basin: Transboundary Challenges and Practical Solutions. (Water use in the Irtysh basin across China, Kazakhstan and Russia.) https://eabr.org/en/analytics/special-reports/the-irtysh-river-basin-transboundary-challenges-and-practical-solutions/ | [T1] Scientific-Information Center of the Interstate Commission for Water Coordination of Central Asia (CAWater-Info), Yearbook 2023, Section 5: Key water developments in the countries of Central Asia - Kazakhstan. https://www.cawater-info.net/yearbook/2023/05_yearbook2023_kz_en.htm
notes: This is a DA claim, which is inherently hard to contradict from the literature: it would require positive evidence that one side has under 10 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km, or that one side is more than 99% concentrated within 10 km, and no source reports groundwater irrigation at that spatial resolution for a 900,000 km2 aquifer. I searched and found nothing pointing that way, and the qualitative picture - dispersed minor groundwater irrigation on both sides of a long, agriculturally developed steppe border - is consistent with DA, so I report CONFIRMED at low confidence rather than INSUFFICIENT. Kazakhstan's numbers are the fragile ones: 94 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland over the whole polygon, of which only 27 ha within 100 km, is close enough to the 10 ha IU1 threshold that a modest change in the irrigation layer could flip this dyad.

aquifer_name: Senegalo-Mauritanian Aquifer Basin (SMAB) / Bassin Aquifère Sénégalo-Mauritanien / Bacia Aquífera Senegalo-Mauritana (BASM)
claim_tested: More than 99% of MRT's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (7 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Searched French and English sources for groundwater-irrigated cropland in Mauritania over the Senegalo-Mauritanian basin away from the Senegal River. The only substantial off-river horticulture found is the PK17 peri-urban perimeter south of Nouakchott (~10 ha, ~180 km from the SEN border), and it is irrigated with treated water from the SNDE plant fed by the Senegal River, i.e. surface water, not groundwater. The Trarza (Idini) wellfield over the same aquifer is municipal supply for Nouakchott, not cropland; Mauritania's genuinely groundwater-irrigated agriculture is the Adrar/Tagant oasis system, which lies outside the SMAB polygon.
sources: [T2] COMSSA, 'The Feeding and greening Nouakchott experience: urban vegetable gardens in a desert climate' https://comssa.org/en/news/the-feeding-and-greening-nouakchott-experience-urban-vegetable-gardens-in-a-desert-climate | [T1] Mohamed A. et al., 'Modalites de recharge d'un aquifere en zone semi-aride: cas de la nappe du Trarza (Sud-Ouest Mauritanie)', Hydrological Sciences Journal 59(5) https://doi.org/10.1080/02626667.2013.819432 | [T1] ReSaD / CARI, 'Systeme d'irrigation dans les oasis de Mauritanie: problemes de pompage et tentatives de realimentation des nappes phreatiques' https://www.resad-sahel.org/Publications/Systeme-d-irrigation-dans-les-oasis-de-Mauritanie-problemes-de-pompage-et-tentatives-de-realimentation-des-nappes-phreatiques
notes: Near-miss worth recording: PK17 (10 ha, Riyadh/Nouakchott-Sud, ~17 km south of Nouakchott on the Rosso axis) sits over the SMAB and far from the border, so if the underlying land-use product had classed it as groundwater-irrigated the BL classification would flip. It does not, because the source is treated river water. Mauritanian irrigation over this aquifer is otherwise the Senegal River valley (Rosso/Trarza), which is river-fed flood and pumped surface irrigation hugging the border - consistent with the 71 ha being wholly within 10 km.

claim_tested: More than 99% of DOM's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (4 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: The one substantive study of this aquifer (Hydrogeology Journal groundwater-flow model of the Plaine du Nord-Massacre shallow aquifer) states explicitly that estimating withdrawals from irrigation wells 'proved to be difficult due to the lack of regular monitoring and reliable data', models only a hypothetical 270-borehole banana-irrigation expansion, and contains no data at all for the Dominican side of the Massacre River. No Dominican source (INDRHI/INAPA or otherwise) was found that resolves groundwater- versus canal-irrigated cropland in Dajabon province at the 10 km scale.
sources: [T1] Modelling groundwater flow in the Plaine du Nord-Massacre shallow aquifer, Haiti, Hydrogeology Journal (2022) https://doi.org/10.1007/s10040-022-02469-6 | [T1] Geophysical reconnaissance of the western basin of the Plaine du Nord aquifer, Haiti, Hydrogeology Journal (2022) https://doi.org/10.1007/s10040-022-02490-9
notes: Two caveats for the authors. (1) The published aquifer literature treats this as an essentially Haitian system extending from the Limbe plain east to the Massacre, with the Dominican portion undescribed - so the DOM-side polygon in IGRAC may be a thin border strip, which would make the >99%-within-10km result geometrically near-automatic rather than substantive. (2) Irrigated agriculture further east on the Dominican side (Monte Cristi banana/rice) draws largely on the Yaque del Norte canal system, i.e. surface water, so it would not contradict even if the polygon reached it. The honest verdict is that the record is silent, not that the claim is verified.

aquifer_name: The former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia - SW Serbia
claim_tested: More than 99% of SRB's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (1 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: No aquifer-specific hydrogeological or irrigation literature could be found for this IGRAC unit, which is identified only by a generic name ('The former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia - SW Serbia') and has no published delineation, abstraction inventory or irrigation description. Serbian national groundwater and irrigation reviews cover Vojvodina and the Morava basins and say nothing about groundwater-irrigated cropland in the far south near the North Macedonian border.
sources: [T1] Rudic Z. et al. (2019), 'Achieving sustainable irrigation development in agricultural areas of Serbia with limited water resources', Outlook on Agriculture https://doi.org/10.1177/0030727019831019 | [T1] Water supply and sustainable management of groundwater resources in Serbia (review) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/322196453
notes: The claim concerns 12 ha on the Serbian side - below the resolution of any national statistic or study available. Serbian irrigation is overwhelmingly surface-water-based and concentrated in Vojvodina, which is weak indirect support for a small groundwater figure here, but nothing addresses the 10 km distribution. Recommend treating this dyad as unauditable rather than confirmed.

claim_tested: More than 99% of GRC's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (294 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: The Evros/Meric aquifer is well documented as an intensively groundwater-irrigated transboundary alluvial system on both sides (pesticide and nitrate contamination studies of the NE Greek transboundary aquifers attribute loading to intensive irrigated agriculture drawing on the aquifer). Nothing found places Greek groundwater-irrigated cropland over this specific polygon materially further than 10 km from the river, which is itself the border: the mapped unit is a narrow riparian alluvial strip (1,798 km2 spread over roughly 200 km of valley, i.e. of order 9 km mean width), so concentration within 10 km is geometrically expected.
sources: [T1] Occurrence of pesticides in transboundary aquifers of North-eastern Greece, Science of the Total Environment (2012) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2012.09.020 | [T1] Impact of intensive agricultural practices on drinking water quality in the Evros Region (NE Greece) by GIS analysis https://www.researchgate.net/publication/5969285 | [T1] EASAC, Greece Groundwater Country Report https://easac.eu/fileadmin/PDF_s/reports_statements/Greece_Groundwater_country_report.pdf
notes: Separate data flag, not a class change: our numbers give urban_ha_within_100km = 0 for BOTH sides, yet Edirne (population ~180,000) sits directly on this aquifer roughly 1 km from the Greek border, and Orestiada, Didymoteicho and Feres lie on the Greek side. A zero urban figure for this polygon is almost certainly an artefact of the urban layer or the polygon clip. It does not alter the class here (both sides have groundwater-irrigated cropland, so IU0/IU1/UB are excluded before urban land is consulted), but the same artefact could misclassify other dyads where urban land is decisive. Worth checking. The wider Evros delta near Feres extends up to ~20-25 km from the river, so the 99.7% figure is sensitive to how far west the IGRAC polygon reaches.

aquifer_name: Quartair en pliomioceenzand van de Schelde / Sables quaternaires et plio-miocènes de l'Escaut
claim_tested: More than 99% of BEL's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (4 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Searched Flemish and Belgian sources (VMM groundwater-use indicators, Departement Omgeving, ILVO agricultural-water dossiers, Statbel agricultural census) for groundwater-irrigated cropland in Belgium over the Scheldt Quaternary/Plio-Miocene sands. Belgian irrigation is marginal and no source locates groundwater-irrigated cropland on this polygon more than 10 km from the Dutch border; nothing contradicting the claim was found.
sources: [T1] Vlaamse Milieumaatschappij (VMM), Grondwaterverbruik indicator https://vmm.vlaanderen.be/feiten-cijfers/water/grondwater/grondwatergebruik/indicator-grondwaterverbruik | [T1] Statbel, Kerncijfers landbouw 2024 https://doc.statbel.fgov.be/publications/S510.01/S510.01N_Kerncijfers_landbouw_2024.pdf | [T1] ILVO, Water in de landbouw (Flanders) https://ilvo.vlaanderen.be/en/dossiers/water-in-agriculture
notes: This is a confirmation by absence and should be weighted accordingly. Flemish agricultural water use is in reality predominantly groundwater-based (field irrigation of potatoes and vegetables), and Belgian statistics are reported at national or provincial level only, so they can neither confirm nor refute a 35 ha figure or its 10 km distribution. The 35 ha total for the Belgian side of this 1,919 km2 polygon looks low relative to actual Flemish irrigation practice; if the underlying irrigation layer under-detects European sprinkler irrigation, the BL result here is an artefact of a very small denominator (35 ha) rather than a real border concentration. Same caveat applies to EU313.

claim_tested: More than 99% of BEL's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (2 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Searched Belgian (Walloon) and French sources for groundwater-irrigated cropland over the Valenciennes-Mons chalk aquifer. The chalk is a major abstraction target on both sides of the border, but the documented uses are public supply and industry; no source places Belgian groundwater-irrigated cropland on this polygon more than 10 km from the French border. Nothing contradicting the claim was found.
sources: [T1] Statbel, Kerncijfers landbouw 2024 https://doc.statbel.fgov.be/publications/S510.01/S510.01N_Kerncijfers_landbouw_2024.pdf | [T1] Vlaamse Milieumaatschappij (VMM) / Departement Omgeving groundwater portals (Belgian groundwater use) https://omgeving.vlaanderen.be/nl/grondwater
notes: Same structural caveat as EU301: the Belgian side has only 16 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland in our data, so the >99%-within-10km test is being decided by a handful of pixels. National statistics do not resolve irrigation water source at sub-provincial scale in either Belgium or France, so no external source can realistically contradict or verify this. Treat as low-information rather than robustly confirmed.

aquifer_name: Northern Great Plains - Lower Tertiary Aquifer System
claim_tested: CAN has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: Searched Saskatchewan Water Security Agency groundwater and irrigation material, provincial irrigation programme pages, and the Centre for Hydrology review of Saskatchewan water resources. Saskatchewan's irrigated area is overwhelmingly surface-water-based and concentrated around Lake Diefenbaker and the South Saskatchewan River, several hundred kilometres north of the international border and outside the Lower Tertiary (Ravenscrag/Fort Union) outcrop; no evidence was found of groundwater-irrigated cropland on the Canadian side of this aquifer within 100 km of the Montana/North Dakota border.
sources: [T1] Government of Saskatchewan, Crops and Irrigation - Irrigation https://www.saskatchewan.ca/business/agriculture-natural-resources-and-industry/agribusiness-farmers-and-ranchers/crops-and-irrigation/irrigation | [T1] Saskatchewan Water Security Agency, Estevan Mapsheet / Geology and Groundwater Resources of the Weyburn-Virden Area (62E,F) https://www.wsask.ca/mapsheet/estevan-mapsheet/ | [T1] Pomeroy J. et al., Hydrology and Water Resources of Saskatchewan, Centre for Hydrology Report #1, University of Saskatchewan https://research-groups.usask.ca/hydrology/documents/reports/chrpt01_hydrology-water-resources-sask_feb05.pdf
notes: The WSA hydrogeological mapping for the Estevan/Weyburn border area documents intertill and Empress Group aquifers but describes no irrigation use of them. Groundwater irrigation licences do exist in Saskatchewan but the searchable record ties them to the Assiniboine and Qu'Appelle systems well north of this polygon. The dyad's UB class therefore stands, though it rests on a Canadian total of 30 ha of irrigation of any kind, which is plausible for the dry southern Ravenscrag plateau but is a thin basis.

aquifer_name: Benue River sedimentary basin / Bassin sédimentaire de la Benoué
claim_tested: CMR has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: Searched French and English sources on irrigation in the Cameroonian Benue basin (Garoua, Pitoa, Lagdo, Guider, Figuil). Formal irrigation there is surface-water-based: the Lagdo reservoir scheme and river-fed/recession perimeters, with a World Bank Benue valley project targeting ~11,000 ha irrigated from the Benue itself. Peer-reviewed hydrochemistry of groundwater under Benue-basin farmland characterises groundwater as the reliable source for domestic and livestock needs, not as an irrigation source, and attributes nutrient loading to rainfed fertiliser use. No evidence of groundwater-irrigated cropland on the Cameroonian side within 100 km of the Nigerian border.
sources: [T1] Hydrochemistry of nutrients in groundwater under farmland in the Benue River Basin, North-Cameroon, Environmental Earth Sciences (2021) https://doi.org/10.1007/s12665-021-10146-2 | [T1] World Bank, Cameroon - Valorization of Investments in the Valley of the Benue Project https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/194181599876136390/pdf/Cameroon-Valorization-of-Investments-in-the-Valley-of-the-Benue-Project.pdf | [T2] Afrik21, 'Cameroon: In the North, 11,000 hectares of land will be irrigated from the Benue' https://www.afrik21.africa/en/cameroon-in-the-north-11000-hectares-of-land-will-be-irrigated-from-the-benue/
notes: Near-miss the authors should know about: informal dry-season market gardening (maraichage de contre-saison) using hand-dug wells and puisards in the Benue floodplain is repeatedly referred to in Cameroonian grey literature and student theses, but I found no source that quantifies its area or locates it precisely, and much of it draws directly from residual river pools rather than a water table. Garoua lies roughly 55-80 km from the Nigerian border and sits squarely on this aquifer, so if that informal well-based gardening were mapped it could push CMR above the 10 ha threshold and move the dyad from UB to DA. It is currently below the evidentiary threshold, so the UB class stands.

aquifer_name: Senegalo-Mauritanian Aquifer Basin (SMAB) / Bassin Aquifère Sénégalo-Mauritanien / Bacia Aquífera Senegalo-Mauritana (BASM)
claim_tested: GMB has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
gis_acceptance: accepted: feature strictly inside the polygon and band
error_class_description: applied: groundwater irrigation absent from the whole polygon
applied_to: class only (classF unchanged: absorbed by the future projection)
evidence: The Gambia has well over 10 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the Senegalese border over the Senegalo-Mauritanian basin. The World Bank documents 21 women's communal vegetable gardens totalling 105 ha (5 ha each) equipped with boreholes drawing from aquifers, solar pumps and drip irrigation; FAO separately documents 34 solar-powered borehole irrigation systems nationwide, naming a 5 ha vegetable garden at Kuwonkuba and a site at Jamali Ganyado in Central River Region. The whole of The Gambia lies over the SMAB and is nowhere more than about 25-30 km from a Senegalese border, so every one of these sites is within the 100 km band, and the water source is explicitly groundwater (boreholes/aquifers), not the Gambia River.
sources: [T1] World Bank, 'Empowering Women Vegetable Producers in The Gambia' (2021) - 21 communal gardens, 105 ha, boreholes and solar pumps drawing from aquifers https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/973661615194211026/pdf/Empowering-Women-Vegetable-Producers-in-The-Gambia.pdf | [T1] FAO, 'No ordinary irrigation in the Gambia' - 34 solar-powered borehole irrigation systems, Central River Region examples (Kuwonkuba, Jamali Ganyado) https://www.fao.org/newsroom/story/No-ordinary-irrigation-in-the-Gambia/en | [T1] Government of The Gambia / GAFSP, Second Generation National Agricultural Investment Plan (2019-2026) https://www.gafspfund.org/sites/default/files/inline-files/7.%20The%20Gambia_Investment%20Plan%20(2019-2026)_1.pdf
notes: Class derivation: with GMB corrected to >10 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km, both sides now have groundwater-irrigated cropland, so IU0, IU1 and UB are all excluded. The BL test then asks whether >99% of either side's groundwater-irrigated cropland is within 10 km of the border: on the Senegalese side it is 1,282/1,973 = 65%, so no; on the Gambian side the documented garden sites are spread across Central River, Upper River, North Bank and West Coast regions, and in the wider western part of the country a central strip lies more than 10 km from either border, so >99% concentration is unlikely. Hence DA. Caveat: The Gambia's extreme geometry (a 25-50 km wide strip enclosed by Senegal) means a large share of its farmland genuinely is within 10 km of a border, so BL is not impossible if the corrected Gambian pixels happen to fall near the boundary - worth checking against the raster before finalising. Note also that the country's larger rice schemes are river/tidal-irrigated and do not count here; the horticultural gardens are the groundwater component.

aquifer_name: Senegalo-Mauritanian Aquifer Basin (SMAB) / Bassin Aquifère Sénégalo-Mauritanien / Bacia Aquífera Senegalo-Mauritana (BASM)
claim_tested: ESH has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: The Western Saharan territory within 100 km of the Mauritanian border - Guerguerat, Bir Gandouz, the Aousserd axis - is hyper-arid with essentially no cropland; the settlements there are transit posts and pastoral centres. Morocco's groundwater- and desalination-based greenhouse horticulture in the territory is concentrated in the Dakhla agricultural zone (Oued Ed-Dahab), which lies roughly 200-320 km north of the nearest Mauritanian border segment, well outside the 100 km band.
sources: [T1] BGS Earthwise, Hydrogeologie du Maroc et du Sahara occidental https://earthwise.bgs.ac.uk/index.php/Hydrog%C3%A9ologie_du_Maroc_et_du_Sahara_occidental_(Sahara_marocain) | [T2] Encyclopaedic/geographic sources on Bir Gandus, Guerguerat and Aousserd (settlement function and land use) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bir_Gandus
notes: The ESH side has zero irrigated cropland of any kind in our data, which matches the physical record. The only thing that could overturn this is the Dakhla greenhouse belt, and it fails the distance test by a wide margin; it would also need the SMAB polygon to extend that far north over the coastal strip. Note the ESH urban figure (1,742 ha within 100 km) presumably reflects the small border and coastal settlements, which is plausible.

claim_tested: Both BRA and PRY have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.
evidence: The Guarani Aquifer System is documented by the World Bank/OAS Guarani Aquifer Project, UNESCO and the four national governments as supplying domestic, agricultural and industrial water in all four countries, including Brazil and Paraguay. Abstraction is distributed across a 1.2 million km2 outcrop and confined area with major use centres (Ribeirao Preto and the Sao Paulo/Parana outcrop belt in Brazil; the eastern Paraguayan outcrop) far from the shared border, so there is no evidence that either side's groundwater irrigation is concentrated within 10 km of the frontier.
sources: [T1] World Bank / OAS, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay, Argentina: The Guarani Aquifer Initiative for Transboundary Groundwater Management https://documents.worldbank.org/en/publication/documents-reports/documentdetail/986011468052447251 | [T1] UNESCO, Regional cooperation in action: four countries consolidate a new phase of Guarani Aquifer management https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/regional-cooperation-action-four-countries-consolidate-new-phase-management-guarani-aquifer-guarani | [T1] Sindico F. et al., 'The Guarani Aquifer System: From a beacon of hope to a question mark in the governance of transboundary aquifers', Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejrh.2017.11.005
notes: The DA claim here is a weak one (both sides have some groundwater irrigation and neither is >99% border-concentrated) and the aquifer is among the best documented in the world; the claim is comfortably consistent with the literature. Our own numbers make the point: only 3% of Brazil's groundwater-irrigated cropland on the aquifer is within 10 km of any Paraguayan border and only 10% within 100 km.

claim_tested: Both ARG and BRA have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Groundwater from the Guarani system is documented as serving agricultural as well as domestic and industrial demand in both Argentina (Misiones, Corrientes, Entre Rios) and Brazil, with abstraction distributed across the outcrop belt rather than clustered on the shared border. Nothing found contradicts either limb of the claim.
sources: [T1] World Bank / OAS, The Guarani Aquifer Initiative for Transboundary Groundwater Management https://documents.worldbank.org/en/publication/documents-reports/documentdetail/986011468052447251 | [T1] Government of Argentina, Sistema Acuifero Guarani (official page: fresh water for domestic, agricultural, industrial and tourism needs) https://www.argentina.gob.ar/jefatura/turismo-y-ambiente/ambiente/recursos-naturales/cuencas-hidricas/sistema-acuifero-guarani | [T1] Sindico F. et al., 'The Guarani Aquifer System: From a beacon of hope to a question mark...', Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejrh.2017.11.005
notes: Argentine side is only 0.8% within 10 km of the Brazilian border in our data, and Brazil 3%, so the BL test is not close on either side. No contradiction.

claim_tested: Both BRA and URY have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Both Brazil and Uruguay abstract Guarani groundwater for agricultural use; in Uruguay the aquifer is exploited in the Salto-Paysandu-Artigas litoral where wells serve irrigation and thermal/tourism uses alongside supply. Abstraction on both sides is spread over the outcrop and confined areas rather than concentrated within 10 km of the frontier, so nothing contradicts the claim.
sources: [T1] World Bank / OAS, The Guarani Aquifer Initiative for Transboundary Groundwater Management https://documents.worldbank.org/en/publication/documents-reports/documentdetail/986011468052447251 | [T1] UNESCO, Regional cooperation in action: Guarani Aquifer management https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/regional-cooperation-action-four-countries-consolidate-new-phase-management-guarani-aquifer-guarani
notes: Uruguay is the one side worth a second look: it has only 107 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland on the aquifer in our data, of which 70 ha (65%) is within 10 km of the Brazilian border - short of the 99% BL threshold but the smallest margin among the five Guarani dyads. If the underlying irrigation layer is revised upward or downward for Uruguay this dyad is the most likely of the five to move. Uruguayan irrigation overall is dominated by surface water for rice in the east, which is outside this aquifer.

claim_tested: Both ARG and URY have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Both Argentina and Uruguay draw agricultural water from the Guarani system (Argentine littoral provinces; Uruguayan Salto-Paysandu littoral), and in both cases abstraction is distributed across the aquifer rather than concentrated in a 10 km border strip. No source found contradicts either limb of the claim.
sources: [T1] Government of Argentina, Sistema Acuifero Guarani (official page) https://www.argentina.gob.ar/jefatura/turismo-y-ambiente/ambiente/recursos-naturales/cuencas-hidricas/sistema-acuifero-guarani | [T1] World Bank / OAS, The Guarani Aquifer Initiative for Transboundary Groundwater Management https://documents.worldbank.org/en/publication/documents-reports/documentdetail/986011468052447251
notes: The ARG-URY border here is the Uruguay River, and both sides' groundwater irrigation over the aquifer extends well inland (Argentina 0.8% within 10 km; Uruguay 65%), so neither approaches the BL threshold. Same Uruguayan small-sample caveat as BRA-URY applies.

claim_tested: Both ARG and PRY have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Both Argentina and Paraguay are documented Guarani abstractors with agricultural use among the stated purposes, and use in both is distributed across the aquifer rather than concentrated on the shared border. Nothing found contradicts the claim.
sources: [T1] Government of Argentina, Sistema Acuifero Guarani (official page) https://www.argentina.gob.ar/jefatura/turismo-y-ambiente/ambiente/recursos-naturales/cuencas-hidricas/sistema-acuifero-guarani | [T1] World Bank / OAS, The Guarani Aquifer Initiative for Transboundary Groundwater Management https://documents.worldbank.org/en/publication/documents-reports/documentdetail/986011468052447251 | [T1] Sindico F. et al., 'The Guarani Aquifer System: From a beacon of hope to a question mark...', Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejrh.2017.11.005
notes: Argentina 0.8% within 10 km, Paraguay 7.5% within 10 km - both far from the BL threshold. No contradiction.

claim_tested: More than 99% of KGZ's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (3 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Searched Central Asian transboundary-aquifer literature (Karimov et al. 2020, UNESCO TBA 2015, UNECE Aral assessment) and Batken-province irrigation material; the only aquifer-specific statement is that AS53 groundwater salinity has risen from agricultural irrigation, with no side- or distance-resolved cropland figures. Nothing places Kyrgyz groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer more than 10 km from a Tajik border segment, and the Batken/Isfara/Vorukh enclave geometry means essentially all Kyrgyz land over the aquifer is within 10 km of some segment of that border.
sources: [T1] Karimov, A. et al. (2020) Sustainable Use of Groundwater Resources in the Transboundary Aquifers of the Five Central Asian Countries: Challenges and Perspectives. Water 12(8), 2101. https://doi.org/10.3390/w12082101 | [T1] UNESCO-IHP/IGRAC (2015) Transboundary Aquifers of the World, edition 2015 (AS053 Sulyukta-Batken-Nau-Isfara). https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000264020 | [T1] UNECE (2011) Second Assessment of Transboundary Rivers, Lakes and Groundwaters, Ch.3 Drainage basin of the Aral Sea. https://unece.org/DAM/env/water/publications/assessment/English/G_PartIV_Chapter3_En.pdf

The published record simply has no hectare-level groundwater-irrigation data for the Kyrgyz side of this aquifer, so the CONFIRMED here rests partly on border geometry rather than on a positive external measurement.

claim_tested: More than 99% of KGZ's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (9 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: The only aquifer-specific source found (Karimov et al. 2020) gives hydrogeology for AS55 North Talas (mean thickness 25 m, transmissivity 2400 m2/d, ~10 km3 storage, 37.5% in Kazakhstan) but no abstraction-by-use, no irrigated hectares and no country split of irrigation. UNECE and UNESCO Chu-Talas material covers surface-water allocation, not groundwater irrigation on the Kyrgyz side.

Water 12(8), 2101. https://doi.org/10.3390/w12082101 | [T1] UNECE, Transboundary cooperation in the Chu and Talas river basins. https://unece.org/environment-policy/water/areas-work-convention/transboundary-cooperation-chu-and-talas-river-basin
notes: Nothing found contradicts the claim, but nothing supports it either: the record is silent at the resolution required (89 ha, 10 km band). Flag for the authors: our own numbers give KGZ urban_ha_within_100km = 0 for this dyad, which is worth a sanity check given Talas town (~35,000 people) lies in the same valley; if Talas town is inside the aquifer polygon the urban figure may be wrong even though the BL trigger comes from the irrigation term.

claim_tested: More than 99% of RUS's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (3 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Searched in English and Russian for irrigated land and groundwater irrigation in Amur Oblast / the Zeya-Bureya plain. Amur Oblast agriculture is overwhelmingly rainfed (soybean, cereals); no source found quantifies groundwater-irrigated cropland anywhere in the Zeya basin, let alone its distance from the Amur River (the CHN-RUS border).

Note the asymmetry in our own numbers (RUS all_irrigated 57 ha over a 76,413 km2 basin) which is itself plausible for Amur Oblast, so the BL trigger is being set by a very small denominator.

claim_tested: More than 99% of IRN's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (1,350 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Sources on the Sarakhs Plain confirm intensive groundwater use on the IRANIAN side (292-well sampling campaign; groundwater largely judged suitable for irrigation), consistent with our IRN figure of 13,496 ha. On the Turkmen side, Serakhs etrap agriculture is documented as fed by the Tejen/Hari Rud and the Karakum canal, i.e. surface water; no source was found showing Turkmen groundwater-irrigated cropland over this 686 km2 aquifer more than 10 km from the Hari Rud border.

aquifer_name: Valle de Juarez Bolson / Hueco-Tularosa Bolson
claim_tested: More than 99% of MEX's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (333 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: CONAGUA's official determination for the Valle de Juarez aquifer (clave 0833, Chihuahua) states the irrigated zone is a narrow strip on both banks of the Rio Bravo, 9-11.5 km wide in total and averaging 9.5 km, covering ~12,508 ha served in part by 114 active agricultural wells, and is 'located in the frontier eastern portion of the aquifer that coincides with the border with the United States'. Worth noting for the authors that Valle de Juarez irrigation is conjunctive: Rio Bravo surface allocation plus supplemental wells, with the groundwater share rising in drought years, but the geographic confinement to the riverside strip holds regardless of source. Municipal pumping for Ciudad Juarez is a large Hueco Bolson abstraction but is not cropland and does not bear on the claim.

aquifer_name: Lake Chad sedimentary basin / Bassin sédimentaire du Lac Tchad
claim_tested: DZA has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).

Algeria's basin share is the empty far-southeast (Tassili/Djado margin); the nearest Algerian oasis agriculture (Djanet, and the Touat-Gourara-Tidikelt schemes) is 250 km or more from the DZA-NER border and mostly outside the Lake Chad basin entirely.

aquifer_name: Lake Chad sedimentary basin / Bassin sédimentaire du Lac Tchad
claim_tested: CMR has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).

error_class_description: applied: groundwater irrigation absent from the whole polygon

Caveats the authors should weigh: (i) the Atlas survey is from 1986, though the practice is continuing and has expanded; (ii) the Mandara mountain departments (Mayo-Sava, Mayo-Tsanaga) sit on basement rock and might fall outside a strictly sedimentary reading of the AF052 polygon, but the polygon area of 2,385,210 km2 matches the LCBC conventional basin, which includes them, and Logone-et-Chari alluvium is unambiguously inside.

aquifer_name: Lake Chad sedimentary basin / Bassin sédimentaire du Lac Tchad

aquifer_name: Lake Chad sedimentary basin / Bassin sédimentaire du Lac Tchad
claim_tested: SDN has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).

evidence: Feinstein International Center (Tufts) field study of vegetable production in Darfur documents peri-urban market gardening in WEST DARFUR irrigated from a shallow water table lifted by hand or by petrol/diesel pumps: tomatoes at El Geneina on ~550 feddans (~231 ha) in 2013 with the water table at 2-5 m; onions at Foro Baranga (430-550 feddans, ~181-231 ha, water table 1-3 m) and at Mornei (560-700 feddans, ~235-294 ha, small diesel/petrol pumps). Note our own pipeline already places 177,713 ha of Sudanese urban land within 100 km of this border inside the polygon, which must be the El Geneina conurbation, so the polygon demonstrably covers the ground where the gardens are.

aquifer_name: Lake Chad sedimentary basin / Bassin sédimentaire du Lac Tchad

aquifer_name: Taoudeni-Tanezrouft Aquifer System / Système Aquifère de Taoudéni-Tanezrouft
claim_tested: DZA has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: Algeria's modern borehole-irrigated agriculture over the Taoudeni-Tanezrouft system is documented as concentrated in the Touat, Gourara and Tidikelt sub-regions of Adrar wilaya (60,000 ha allocated, about a third cultivated, from deep Continental Intercalaire/Albien boreholes), which lie roughly 700-1,000 km north of the Malian border. Searches for agricultural perimeters at the border communes themselves (Bordj Badji Mokhtar, Timiaouine) returned only administrative, security and pastoral material, no irrigated cropland.

Cahiers Agricultures 27(1), 2018. https://www.cahiersagricultures.fr/articles/cagri/full_html/2018/01/cagri170016/cagri170016.html | [T1] Ministere de l'Agriculture et du Developpement Rural (Algeria), Agriculture saharienne / irrigation. http://madrp.gov.dz/agriculture/irrigation/agriculture-saharienne/ | [T1] OSS, Iullemeden-Taoudeni/Tanezrouft Aquifer System TDA/SAP process. http://www.oss-online.org/en/node/769
notes: Near-miss to record: Timiaouine and Bordj Badji Mokhtar sit essentially on the Malian border and have wells, but the sources describe them as pastoral watering points and settlements, not irrigated cropland; the only well-documented Algerian expansion is far to the north. If the authors want to harden this, an Algerian DSA/wilaya agricultural statistics series for Bordj Badji Mokhtar wilaya (created 2019) would settle it.

aquifer_name: Taoudeni-Tanezrouft Aquifer System / Système Aquifère de Taoudéni-Tanezrouft
claim_tested: MRT has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: The Mauritanian government commune monograph for Adel Bagrou (Hodh Ech Chargui, ~40 km from the Malian border and the nearest sizeable settlement on that border over the Taoudeni polygon) describes cropping as 'essentiellement vivrieres sous pluies' (rainfed subsistence), with market gardening only 'tres localise en peripherie de la ville' and water infrastructure consisting of 8 dams and 67 dikes/diguettes, i.e. surface-runoff harvesting. No source establishes groundwater-irrigated cropland above 10 ha within 100 km of the MLI-MRT border.

Hydrogeology Journal (2023). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10040-023-02688-5
notes: Genuine near-miss, flag for the authors. The same monograph records three 'perimetres agricoles' in the commune and a PIVRE plan to bring 200 ha into cultivation 'par la creation de puits' behind two rehabilitated dams at Kasser Elbarka and Ezraviyatt. That is prospective, and the parent programme is explicitly about surface-water valorisation, so on a strict water-source reading it does not contradict the claim; but if those wells are now in service the MRT side could plausibly exceed 10 ha, which would flip this dyad from UB to DA (MLI has 35 ha within 100 km and only 0 ha within 10 km, so BL would not trigger). Also unresolved: whether irrigated gardens around the Mbera refugee camp at Bassikounou (~20 km from the Malian border) are borehole-fed and how large they are; UNHCR narrative material confirms gardens exist but gives no area or water source.

claim_tested: PRY has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: FAO AQUASTAT puts Paraguay's area equipped for irrigation at ~67,000 ha nationally, 90% from surface water and dominated by irrigated rice, which is grown in Itapua, Misiones and Neembucu using river and stream diversions, not in Alto Parana/Canindeyu where the Caiua-Bauru-Acaray aquifer meets the Brazilian border and where soybean is rainfed. No source found showing groundwater-irrigated cropland on the Paraguayan side within 100 km of the Parana border over this aquifer.

AQUASTAT itself warns that no sub-national irrigation data exist for Paraguay, so the departmental attribution is modelled rather than observed; that is the main residual uncertainty.

aquifer_name: Lake Chad sedimentary basin / Bassin sédimentaire du Lac Tchad
claim_tested: Both NER and TCD have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Both sides are independently documented as having groundwater-irrigated cropland in the Lake Chad basin: LCBC/GWP report ~2,000 ha of current irrigation for Niger and ~14,020 ha for Chad within the basin, and FAO's Lake Chad adaptive water management report describes small-scale irrigated gardens on the Nigerien Komadougou/Diffa side and on the Chadian ouaddis of Kanem and the polders, i.e. groundwater-fed and geographically dispersed across each country's basin territory rather than concentrated on the shared border.
sources: [T1] GWP/Lake Chad Basin Commission, The Lake Chad Basin Aquifer System fact sheet (Niger 2,000 ha; Chad 14,020 ha current irrigation in basin). https://www.gwp.org/globalassets/global/toolbox/references/lake_chad_fact_sheet.pdf | [T1] FAO (2009) Adaptive Water Management in the Lake Chad Basin. https://www.fao.org/fileadmin/user_upload/faowater/docs/ChadWWW09.pdf | [T1] The Lake Chad transboundary aquifer: estimation of groundwater fluxes through international borders from regional numerical modeling. J. Hydrol.: Regional Studies (2021). https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2214581821001646
notes: The DA claim is permissive and is comfortably supported. Only caveat: our absolute Nigerien figure (33 ha of gw-irrigated cropland over a basin share of 28%) is very low against the LCBC's 2,000 ha of basin irrigation, so the level may be understated even though the class is right.

aquifer_name: Lake Chad sedimentary basin / Bassin sédimentaire du Lac Tchad
claim_tested: Both NER and NGA have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Both sides have documented, spatially distributed groundwater irrigation in the basin: Nigeria ~82,821 ha of current irrigation in its basin share, including the long-established shallow tube-well/fadama irrigation of the Chad Formation aquifers in Borno and Yobe described by the USGS Chad Basin groundwater study, and Niger ~2,000 ha of small irrigated gardens. Neither is concentrated within 10 km of the NER-NGA border.

claim_tested: More than 99% of TUR's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (544 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.

If the distance is recomputed to the Turkey-Iraq border specifically, TUR would very likely fall well below 99% within 10 km and IRQ is already at 74/75 = 98.7%, so the dyad would most likely become DA (or IU1/UB if TUR also drops below 10 ha within 100 km of the Iraqi border). aquifer_name: Système Aquifère des Iullemmeden / Iullemmeden Aquifer System
claim_tested: Both BEN and NER have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Groundwater-based small-scale irrigation in Niger is documented as regionally distributed - concentrated in Maradi, Tahoua and Zinder, with wells, boreholes and motor pumps in the Tarka valley (Tahoua), the Maradi Goulbi and southern Zinder - i.e. hundreds of kilometres from the Benin border rather than hugging it; Benin's own irrigation over the aquifer is in the Alibori/Malanville-Karimama sector and likewise not confined to a 10 km strip. Consistent with DA.
sources: [T1] Olayide, O.E., Sangare, S.A., Koo, J. et al. (2020). Targeting Small-Scale Irrigation Investments using Agent-Based Modeling: Case Studies in Mali and Niger. IFPRI/SSRN — 'Small-scale irrigation is prevalent in three regions: Maradi, Tahoua, and Zinder'; low-cost drilling, wells and motor pumps disseminated in Tarka valley, Maradi Goulbi and South Zinder. https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.3706662 | [T1] Tadesse, G., Tankari, M.R., Fofana, I. et al. (2024). AKADEMIYA2063 Working Paper Series N.011 (Pro-Sahel small-scale irrigation in Niger and Burkina Faso) — feasible small-scale irrigation areas concentrated in western Niger. https://doi.org/10.54067/awps.011
notes: No contradiction. The DA claim is a weak claim (it only requires that neither side be border-concentrated or empty) and the evidence comfortably supports it for Niger. Benin's 107 ha with 70 ha inside 10 km is 65%, well below the 99% BL threshold, so this is not near a boundary.

aquifer_name: Système Aquifère des Iullemmeden / Iullemmeden Aquifer System
claim_tested: Both BEN and NGA have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.
evidence: The Nigerian (Sokoto Basin) part of the Iullemeden system has extensive shallow floodplain aquifers - about 280,000 ha of floodplain assessed, with productive tubewells - supporting dry-season fadama irrigation spread across Sokoto, Kebbi and Zamfara rather than concentrated at the Benin border. Consistent with DA on both sides.
sources: [T1] Hamidu, H., Lawal, M.M., Abdulganiyu, Y. et al. (2017). Re-evaluation of Shallow Floodplain Aquifers Groundwater Potentials and Storage of Sokoto Basin, Northwestern Nigeria. American Journal of Water Resources 5(3) — floodplains covering ~280,000 ha, high-yield tubewells. https://doi.org/10.12691/ajwr-5-3-3 | [T1] IAEA/OSS, Iullemeden Aquifer System: Integrated and Sustainable Management (RAF/7/011) — Nigeria 60,000 km2 of the system, ~34% of its population, substantial abstraction in the Sokoto area. https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/raf7011_iullemeden_basin.pdf
notes: No contradiction. Nigeria's 3,074 ha with only 26 ha inside 10 km (0.8%) is the opposite of border-concentrated, exactly as the fadama literature would predict.

aquifer_name: Système Aquifère des Iullemmeden / Iullemmeden Aquifer System
claim_tested: Both NER and NGA have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Both sides have documented, spatially distributed groundwater irrigation over the Iullemeden system: Niger's small-scale well and borehole irrigation in Maradi, Tahoua and Zinder, and Nigeria's fadama tubewell irrigation across the Sokoto Basin floodplains. Neither is confined to a 10 km border strip.
sources: [T1] Olayide, O.E., Sangare, S.A., Koo, J. et al. (2020). Targeting Small-Scale Irrigation Investments using Agent-Based Modeling: Case Studies in Mali and Niger.
