Re-evaluation of Shallow Floodplain Aquifers Groundwater Potentials and Storage of Sokoto Basin, Northwestern Nigeria. American Journal of Water Resources 5(3). https://doi.org/10.12691/ajwr-5-3-3 | [T1] IAEA/OSS, Iullemeden Aquifer System: Integrated and Sustainable Management (RAF/7/011). https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/raf7011_iullemeden_basin.pdf
notes: The best-supported DA assignment in the batch. Niger 15/110 ha inside 10 km (14%) and Nigeria 26/3,074 ha (0.8%) are both far from the 99% threshold, and the literature independently describes distributed, interior groundwater irrigation on both sides.

claim_tested: More than 99% of PSE's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (299 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
gis_verdict: rejected: evidence placed on the side not in question
gis_acceptance: not accepted
error_class_description: excluded: rejected, evidence on the side not in question
evidence: ESCWA's Inventory of Shared Water Resources in Western Asia places the Egyptian part of the Western Aquifer Basin in northern Sinai, while the Palestinian part is the western slopes of the West Bank; Palestinian groundwater abstraction from this basin (~23.7 MCM/yr) and the associated irrigated land sit in the Tulkarm/Qalqilya/Jenin foothills, roughly 130-190 km from the Egypt-Palestine (Rafah) border. None of the 2,989 ha therefore lies within 10 km - or even within 100 km - of the EGY-PSE border.
sources: [T1] UN-ESCWA & BGR, Inventory of Shared Water Resources in Western Asia, chapter 'Western Aquifer Basin' (extent: western slopes of the West Bank, through Israel, to north of the Sinai Peninsula; Israel 94% / Palestine 6% of abstraction) http://waterinventory.org/groundwater/western-aquifer-basin | [T1] FAO AQUASTAT, Country profile - Occupied Palestinian Territory (irrigated area of the West Bank concentrated in Jenin, Tulkarm, Qalqilya and Jericho governorates) https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/37ead8de-32cb-4250-acb6-61a88a285251/content
notes: This looks like a pipeline/geometry artifact rather than a land-use error. PSE's within_10km value (2,989 ha) is identical in the EGY-PSE and ISR-PSE rows, and BLR's (5 of 23 ha) is identical across all three of its Daugava dyads - which suggests the 10 km band is measured to the country's nearest boundary generally, not to the dyad's shared border. For EGY-PSE the relevant Palestinian cropland is within 10 km of the Green Line (ISR), not of Rafah. EGY and PSE do not in fact adjoin anywhere on this aquifer polygon, so the dyad may not be well posed at all. Proposed class IU1 assumes PSE has neither gw-irrigated cropland nor aquifer-overlying urban land within 100 km of the Rafah border (i.e. Gaza is not inside the AS001 polygon - supported by PSE's total irrigated figure of only 3,402 ha, far below Gaza's own irrigated area); if Gaza IS inside the polygon, PSE would have urban land within 100 km and the class would be UB instead. Separately, the reported urban_ha_within_100km values (442,130 ha for PSE, 987,607 ha for ISR) exceed plausible built-up area inside a 12,124 km2 aquifer polygon and look like they are not clipped to the aquifer or to the country.

claim_tested: More than 99% of PSE's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (299 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Palestinian groundwater use from the Western Aquifer Basin, and the irrigated land it serves, is concentrated in the north-western West Bank foothills - Tulkarm, Qalqilya and Jenin governorates - all of which lie within roughly 0-10 km of the Green Line; no source was found placing Palestinian groundwater-irrigated cropland over this basin substantially further east.
sources: [T1] UN-ESCWA & BGR, Inventory of Shared Water Resources in Western Asia, chapter 'Western Aquifer Basin' http://waterinventory.org/groundwater/western-aquifer-basin | [T1] FAO AQUASTAT, Country profile - Occupied Palestinian Territory (2008) https://openknowledge.fao.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/37ead8de-32cb-4250-acb6-61a88a285251/content
notes: The West Bank is only ~50 km wide and is bounded by Israeli-controlled territory on both flanks, so almost any cultivated parcel there is within ~10-20 km of an ISR boundary; the BL classification for this dyad is not fragile in the way a wide-country dyad would be. Note ISR itself has 31,918 ha of gw-irrigated land over the aquifer with only 52% within 10 km, so BL here rests entirely on the PSE side.

claim_tested: More than 99% of SYR's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (69 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: The ESCWA Anti-Lebanon chapter locates Syrian irrigation abstraction on this aquifer in the Zabadani Valley ('local farmers have dug dozens of licensed and unlicensed wells') and at the Anjar-Chamsine springs on the border itself - both within ~5-10 km of the Lebanese boundary; no source places Syrian groundwater-irrigated cropland over the Anti-Lebanon range materially further east.
sources: [T1] UN-ESCWA & BGR, Inventory of Shared Water Resources in Western Asia, Chapter 18: Anti-Lebanon https://waterinventory.org/sites/waterinventory.org/files/chapters/Chapter-18-Anti-Lebanon-web.pdf | [T1] FAO AQUASTAT GMIA country sheet, Syria (Damascus governorate: 81,200 ha equipped for irrigation, of which 56,651 ha groundwater) https://storage.googleapis.com/fao-aquastat.appspot.com/irrigation/docs/SYR-gmia.pdf
notes: Near-miss, and a fragile BL. The margin is 6 ha out of 688 (99.1%), so almost any groundwater-irrigated plot beyond 10 km would flip it. The ESCWA chapter names Rankos and Aasal al-Ward as basin towns; both sit roughly 12-20 km east of the Lebanese border and have irrigated orchard/rose cultivation, and 70% of equipped irrigation in the Damascus governorate is groundwater-fed. The chapter itself states there is 'no precise data' on abstraction, so I could not establish water source, area or distance for those villages to the standard required. Authors should treat AS004 as the weakest BL in this batch.

claim_tested: More than 99% of ARM's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (7 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: No source was found that documents irrigation water source or the spatial distribution of irrigated land over the Debed/Debeda river aquifer. The transboundary literature on this unit (UNECE/EU4Environment Khrami-Debed(a) monitoring agreement, 2026) deals with water quality and monitoring, not irrigation.
sources: [T1] UNECE, 'Armenia and Georgia sign agreement on transboundary water monitoring in the Khrami-Debed(a) basin' (2026) https://unece.org/environment/press/armenia-and-georgia-sign-agreement-transboundary-water-monitoring-khrami-debeda | [T1] FAO AQUASTAT GMIA country sheet, Armenia (273,530 ha equipped, of which 50,900 ha groundwater; Lori districts Tashir 380 ha, Stepanavan 2,675 ha) https://storage.googleapis.com/fao-aquastat.appspot.com/irrigation/docs/ARM-gmia.pdf
notes: Weakly supportive context, not enough to confirm: Armenian irrigation in Lori is served by river/canal systems on the Debed and Dzoraget, and the district-level AQUASTAT figures for Lori are small; the aquifer polygon is only 273 km2 and straddles the border, so a high within-10 km share is geometrically plausible. But the 68 ha figure cannot be checked against any external record.

claim_tested: More than 99% of TJK's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (76 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: No source documents the location or water source of irrigated land within the Zafarobod aquifer unit specifically. Zafarobod district is served by the Khojabakirgan/Golodnaya Steppe canal system (Syr Darya surface water), with groundwater appearing mainly as vertical-drainage pumping for watertable control; AQUASTAT gives Tajikistan 39,038 ha of the national 742,051 ha equipped area as groundwater-served, with no district detail.
sources: [T1] FAO AQUASTAT GMIA country sheet, Tajikistan (742,051 ha equipped; 39,038 ha groundwater; Sughd region 282,374 ha) https://storage.googleapis.com/fao-aquastat.appspot.com/irrigation/docs/TJK-gmia.pdf
notes: Near-miss to flag: Zafarobod district extends roughly 25-40 km from the Uzbek boundary and is almost entirely irrigated (TJK all_irrigated_ha = 13,275 over this polygon), so a claim that 100% of the 758 ha of groundwater-irrigated land falls inside a 10 km band is a strong geometric claim that I could not corroborate or refute. Vertical drainage well water in the Golodnaya Steppe is reused for irrigation across the whole massif, which would argue against such tight concentration, but I found no source locating it.

claim_tested: More than 99% of SVK's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (15 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Nothing found contradicting the claim. Slovak irrigation in the Danubian Lowland is overwhelmingly surface-water based: AQUASTAT records 207,149 of 225,310 ha equipped for irrigation nationally as surface-water served (groundwater 18,161 ha, ~8%), and the large Nitra and Trnava region schemes draw from the Danube, Vah and Nitra canal systems rather than boreholes.
sources: [T1] FAO AQUASTAT GMIA country sheet, Slovakia (225,310 ha equipped, 18,161 ha groundwater, 207,149 ha surface water; Nitriansky kraj 71,190 ha equipped, Trnavsky kraj 94,040 ha) https://storage.googleapis.com/fao-aquastat.appspot.com/irrigation/docs/SVK-gmia.pdf
notes: Near-miss worth flagging. Nitriansky kraj - which contains the Komarno block - has 71,190 ha equipped for irrigation, and Nove Zamky, a major irrigation centre, is ~25 km north of the Danube (the HUN border). If even 8% of the irrigation in the 10-40 km band were groundwater-served, the >99%-within-10 km condition would fail. AQUASTAT resolves only to NUTS2, so the water source could not be attributed at district level. The Slovak side of this dyad rests on just 150 ha, so the classification is sensitive to small errors.

claim_tested: CAF has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: The Baggara Basin is developed in the Um Ruwaba Formation, which the British Geological Survey describes as 'used mostly for small domestic supplies and livestock watering'; no groundwater-irrigated cropland is documented anywhere in CAF's Vakaga/Haute-Kotto prefectures adjoining Sudan, where agriculture is rainfed subsistence cultivation.
sources: [T1] British Geological Survey, Africa Groundwater Atlas: Hydrogeology of Sudan (Um Ruwaba Formation; 'Groundwater in Sudan is used largely for human and livestock needs, with relatively small amounts of abstraction for small-scale irrigation') https://earthwise.bgs.ac.uk/index.php/Hydrogeology_of_Sudan | [T1] British Geological Survey, Africa Groundwater Atlas: Hydrogeology of South Sudan https://earthwise.bgs.ac.uk/index.php/Hydrogeology_of_South_Sudan
notes: The CAF-SDN border region (Birao, Am Dafok, Radom) has had essentially no irrigation development and has been conflict-affected for two decades; the claim of zero groundwater-irrigated cropland is highly plausible. The record on this basin is thin overall, but what exists points consistently to domestic and livestock use only.

claim_tested: SDN has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: Same evidence base: BGS records the Um Ruwaba aquifer of the Baggara Basin as used mainly for domestic supply and livestock watering, and Sudanese irrigation is concentrated in the Nile surface-water schemes (Gezira, Rahad, New Halfa), not in South Kordofan / East Darfur / Abyei near the South Sudan border.
sources: [T1] British Geological Survey, Africa Groundwater Atlas: Hydrogeology of Sudan https://earthwise.bgs.ac.uk/index.php/Hydrogeology_of_Sudan | [T1] British Geological Survey, Africa Groundwater Atlas: Hydrogeology of South Sudan https://earthwise.bgs.ac.uk/index.php/Hydrogeology_of_South_Sudan
notes: Mechanised rainfed sorghum/sesame farming is extensive in Habila and Renk-type areas of the Sudan-South Sudan borderlands, but it is rainfed, so it does not bear on a groundwater claim. Boreholes and hafirs in Abyei and the Muglad basin serve pastoralists, not cropland.

claim_tested: ETH has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: AQUASTAT records Ethiopia's Tigray region as having 12,607 ha equipped for irrigation with zero of it groundwater-served, and Amhara only 502 ha of 69,787 ha; nationally groundwater accounts for under 1% of equipped irrigation. Agriculture in the western lowlands within 100 km of the Sudanese border (Humera, Metema, Quara, Abderafi) is dominated by large-scale rainfed sesame, sorghum and cotton.
sources: [T1] FAO AQUASTAT GMIA country sheet, Ethiopia (290,729 ha equipped; 2,611 ha groundwater; Tigray 12,607 ha all surface water; Amhara 69,787 ha of which 502 ha groundwater) https://storage.googleapis.com/fao-aquastat.appspot.com/irrigation/docs/ETH-gmia.pdf | [T1] Walker, D. et al., 'Can shallow groundwater sustain small-scale irrigated agriculture in sub-Saharan Africa? Evidence from N-W Ethiopia', Groundwater for Sustainable Development https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2352801X18302558
notes: Caveat on independence: AQUASTAT GMIA may be an input to the same global gridded product being audited, so this is only partly external. Ethiopia does have a real and growing shallow-groundwater irrigation sector (hand-dug wells in Tigray, Dangila/Lake Tana in Amhara), but the documented sites are in the highlands 150-400 km east of the Sudan border, not over the western part of the Gedarif-Adigrat unit.

claim_tested: LVA has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: AQUASTAT records Latvia as having only 1,150 ha equipped for irrigation nationally, of which just 80 ha is groundwater-served (620 ha actually irrigated); the eastern (Latgale) districts over the Daugava aquifer - Daugavpils 93 ha, Rezekne 77 ha, Ludza 24 ha, Kraslava 4 ha, Madona 12 ha - total ~210 ha of equipped area that is overwhelmingly surface-water fed.
sources: [T1] FAO AQUASTAT GMIA country sheet, Latvia (1,150 ha equipped; 80 ha groundwater, 1,070 ha surface water; district table incl. Daugavpils 93 ha, Rezekne 77 ha, Kraslava 4 ha, Ludza 24 ha) https://storage.googleapis.com/fao-aquastat.appspot.com/irrigation/docs/LVA-gmia.pdf | [T1] Eurostat, Agri-environmental indicator - irrigation (Latvia exempted from irrigation reporting because irrigable area is under 2% of UAA) https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Agri-environmental_indicator_-_irrigation
notes: Near-miss to record: pro-rating Latvia's 7% national groundwater share onto the ~210 ha of Latgale equipped area gives on the order of 15 ha of groundwater-irrigated land in eastern Latvia - just above the 10 ha threshold. No specific groundwater-irrigated parcel could be located, so I did not treat this as a contradiction, but the LVA side of the Daugava dyads sits very close to the cut-off. Note also that even if LVA were contradicted, RUS still has urban land and 0 ha of gw-irrigated cropland, so under the stated rule the dyad would remain UB.

claim_tested: LTU has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: The Lithuanian part of the Daugava basin is Utena county (Zarasai, Ignalina, Utena), for which AQUASTAT's 2005 national inventory records 0 ha equipped for irrigation; Lithuania's irrigation (4,416 ha equipped, 1,000 ha actually irrigated, potatoes and vegetables) is concentrated in Panevezys (1,076 ha) and Vilnius (842 ha) counties.
sources: [T1] FAO AQUASTAT GMIA country sheet, Lithuania (4,416 ha equipped; 2,331 ha groundwater, 2,085 ha surface water; county table: Utena 0 ha, Panevezys 1,076 ha, Vilnius 842 ha, Alytus 89 ha) https://storage.googleapis.com/fao-aquastat.appspot.com/irrigation/docs/LTU-gmia.pdf | [T1] Eurostat, Agri-environmental indicator - irrigation (Lithuania exempted from reporting; irrigable area under 2% of UAA) https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Agri-environmental_indicator_-_irrigation
notes: The zero for Utena county is the strongest single piece of support in this group. Caveat: 53% of Lithuania's equipped irrigation is groundwater-served nationally, so if the EU099 polygon reaches into Vilnius or Panevezys counties the claim would be at risk; AQUASTAT resolves only to county, so I could not check the overlap of those counties with the mapped aquifer.

claim_tested: LTU has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: As above: Utena county, the Lithuanian portion of the Daugava basin adjoining Belarus and Latvia, has 0 ha equipped for irrigation in the AQUASTAT/national inventory; no groundwater-irrigated cropland is documented in north-eastern Lithuania.
sources: [T1] FAO AQUASTAT GMIA country sheet, Lithuania (county table: Utena 0 ha equipped) https://storage.googleapis.com/fao-aquastat.appspot.com/irrigation/docs/LTU-gmia.pdf
notes: If this claim were ever overturned, the dyad would not stay UB: BLR has 23 ha of gw-irrigated land with only 5 ha (22%) inside 10 km, so with LTU above the 10 ha threshold no side would satisfy the UB condition and the rule would return DA. Same caveat as LTU-LVA about the Vilnius/Panevezys county overlap with the polygon.

claim_tested: LVA has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: Latvia has 80 ha of groundwater-equipped irrigation nationally out of 1,150 ha; the Latgale districts bordering Belarus (Kraslava 4 ha, Daugavpils 93 ha, Ludza 24 ha equipped, essentially all surface water) show no evidence of groundwater-irrigated cropland above the 10 ha threshold.
sources: [T1] FAO AQUASTAT GMIA country sheet, Latvia (1,150 ha equipped; 80 ha groundwater; Kraslava 4 ha, Daugavpils 93 ha, Ludza 24 ha) https://storage.googleapis.com/fao-aquastat.appspot.com/irrigation/docs/LVA-gmia.pdf
notes: Same near-miss as LVA-RUS: a pro-rated estimate for eastern Latvia lands around 15 ha, marginally over the threshold. If LVA were contradicted, BLR (23 ha gw, 5 ha within 10 km) would not satisfy UB either and the class would become DA - so this dyad, unlike LVA-RUS, is genuinely sensitive to the Latvian number.

claim_tested: RUS has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: The Russian portion of the Daugava/Western Dvina aquifer lies in Pskov, Smolensk and Tver oblasts, which together have only ~6,200 ha equipped for irrigation across their entire areas (Pskov 1,200 ha, Smolensk 1,900 ha, Tver 3,100 ha) and only ~2,000 ha actually irrigated; no groundwater irrigation of cropland is documented in the humid upper Western Dvina catchment.
sources: [T1] FAO AQUASTAT GMIA country sheet, Russian Federation (2,375,200 ha equipped, 475,040 ha groundwater; Pskovskaya 1,200 ha, Smolenskaya 1,900 ha, Tverskaya 3,100 ha equipped) https://storage.googleapis.com/fao-aquastat.appspot.com/irrigation/docs/RUS-gmia.pdf
notes: The AQUASTAT sheet gives no oblast-level split by water source; Russia's national groundwater share is 20%, so a few tens of hectares of borehole-fed irrigation somewhere in Pskov/Smolensk cannot be ruled out. However the aquifer-overlying part of these oblasts is a small fraction of their area and irrigation there is near-abandoned (Smolensk: 1,900 ha equipped, 100 ha actually irrigated), so the claim is well supported.

claim_tested: More than 99% of KGZ's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (2 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: No source documents groundwater-irrigated cropland on the Kyrgyz side of the South Talas Aquifer away from the Kazakh border. The peer-reviewed Central Asian transboundary-aquifer review places ~1160 km2 of AS054 in Kazakhstan, leaving only a small Kyrgyz strip immediately upgradient of (and adjacent to) the border, so a >99%-within-10km distribution of the 16 ha is geometrically plausible; irrigation in the Talas valley is dominated by surface diversions from the Talas River.
sources: [T1] Karimov et al. (2020). Sustainable Use of Groundwater Resources in the Transboundary Aquifers of the Five Central Asian Countries: Challenges and Perspectives. Water, 12(8), 2101. https://doi.org/10.3390/w12082101 | [T1] UNECE, Transboundary cooperation in the Chu and Talas river basins (programme pages). https://unece.org/environment-policy/water/areas-work-convention/transboundary-cooperation-chu-and-talas-river-basin
notes: The literature on AS054 is hydrogeological (transmissivity, recharge, area split) and contains no country-level abstraction-by-use or irrigated-area figures, so the claim could not be tested directly, only bounded by the geometry of the Kyrgyz portion. Kyrgyz Talas-oblast irrigation is overwhelmingly surface water; groundwater irrigation there is marginal, consistent with the 16 ha figure. Treat as 'not contradicted' rather than 'positively supported'.

claim_tested: More than 99% of SYR's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (53 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: The UN-ESCWA/BGR Inventory chapter on the Basalt Aquifer System (South) states that the Syrian share of the Azraq-Dhuleil basin is only ~890 km2 of ~8,500 km2, confined to a small part of As Suwayda Governorate, and that although satellite images show agricultural development on the Syrian side, 'no information was available regarding wells or abstraction figures'. No source places Syrian groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer more than 10 km north of the Jordanian border.
sources: [T1] UN-ESCWA & BGR (2013). Inventory of Shared Water Resources in Western Asia, Chapter 22: Basalt Aquifer System (South) - Azraq-Dhuleil Basin. https://waterinventory.org/sites/waterinventory.org/files/chapters/Chapter-22-Basalt-Aquifer-System-South-web.pdf | [T1] IWMI/Groundwater Governance in the Arab World, Report 12: Jordan - Azraq Basin Case Study (2017). https://gw-mena.iwmi.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2017/04/Rep.12-Groundwater-governance-in-Azraq-Jordan-report_final_cover.pdf
notes: NEAR-MISS worth recording: ESCWA explicitly reports satellite-visible agricultural development in the Syrian part of the basin, but gives neither water source, area, nor location. The IWMI Azraq report (Syria = 5% of the catchment) likewise carries no Syrian well or irrigation data; Jordanian-Syrian data exchange on this basin ceased in the early 1990s. The Syrian portion (~890 km2) hugs a long stretch of the Jordan-Syria border, so a mean depth of order 10 km is plausible and the BL geometry is not implausible - but this is inference from area, not measured. If the authors need a hard test for AS143, this dyad is the weakest CONFIRMED in the batch and would benefit from direct imagery inspection of the Salkhad/SE Jabal al-Arab flank.

claim_tested: More than 99% of BLZ's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (24 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Searched Belizean, FAO and regional sources for groundwater-irrigated cropland in northern Belize over the Yucatan karst aquifer. Nothing places groundwater-irrigated cropland more than 10 km from the Rio Hondo / Chetumal Bay border. Belize's northern irrigation record is extremely thin; the only located evidence is the (now defunct) papaya export industry in northern Belize, which did rely on wells.
sources: [T2] Breaking Belize News (31 Oct 2020). 'Who killed Belize's papaya industry?' - notes Fruta Bomba's northern-Belize operation and delays in obtaining well-digging permits. https://www.breakingbelizenews.com/2020/10/31/who-killed-belizes-papaya-industry-instead-of-exporting-papaya-we-exported-the-whole-industry-to-the-dominican-republic/ | [T1] Nature Communications Earth & Environment (2025). Groundwater salinization patterns in the Yucatan Peninsula reveal contamination and vulnerability of the karst aquifer. https://www.nature.com/articles/s43247-025-02456-1
notes: NEAR-MISS (Tier 2 only, insufficient to contradict): Belize's commercial papaya sector used groundwater wells and operated in Orange Walk/Corozal districts, but no source gives farm coordinates, hectares or distance to the Rio Hondo, and the industry closed around 2016 (i.e. likely outside the mapped land-use epoch anyway). Mennonite groundwater irrigation at Blue Creek would in any case sit directly on the Rio Hondo (<5 km), which supports rather than contradicts BL. Belize is a candidate for INSUFFICIENT if the authors prefer a stricter reading - the documentary record here is close to silent.

claim_tested: More than 99% of UKR's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (3 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Irrigation in the Ukrainian Danube/Budjak region (Reni-Izmail-Kiliya, i.e. the Ukrainian side of the Danube-Prut aquifer) is documented as drawing on Danube river water and the Danube Lakes, not groundwater: 'The Danube River mouth is a main source for fresh water used for water supply and irrigation purposes in the arid southern part of Ukraine.' No source documents groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer away from the Prut/Danube border rivers.
sources: [T1] Romanova, Y., Shakirzanova, Z., & Ovcharuk, V. (2019). Temporal variation of water discharges in the lower course of the Danube River across the area from Reni to Izmail. Energetika, 65(2-3). https://doi.org/10.6001/energetika.v65i2-3.4108
notes: The Romanian-Ukrainian border in this reach IS the Prut and the Danube, so any irrigated land in the narrow Reni salient is within a few km of the border by construction. Ukraine's 40,056 ha of total irrigated land over the polygon versus 31 ha groundwater-irrigated is consistent with the surface-water-dominated Danube irrigation systems. No Ukrainian-language hydrogeological source specific to the Danube-Prut aquifer was reachable; the search budget was exhausted before Ukrainian/Romanian-language sources could be exhausted.

aquifer_name: Rio Agua Prieta Aquifer / Douglas Basin
claim_tested: More than 99% of MEX's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (3 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: CONAGUA's official availability determination for the Rio Agua Prieta aquifer (clave 2629) reports an agricultural zone of ~249 ha (alfalfa 50%, forage 40%, maize 10%) supplied by 2.3 hm3/yr of groundwater (16% of total extraction, from 59 pozos and 27 norias), but gives no spatial distribution of the irrigated plots. Nothing in the record places Mexican groundwater-irrigated cropland more than 10 km south of the border, so the >99%-within-10km claim is not contradicted.
sources: [T1] CONAGUA, Subdireccion General Tecnica, Gerencia de Aguas Subterraneas. Actualizacion de la disponibilidad media anual de agua en el acuifero Rio Agua Prieta (2629), Estado de Sonora. https://sigagis.conagua.gob.mx/gas1/Edos_Acuiferos_18/sonora/DR_2629.pdf
notes: IMPORTANT DATA-QUALITY FLAG (not a class contradiction): CONAGUA reports ~249 ha of groundwater-irrigated land in this aquifer versus our 32 ha groundwater-irrigated / 55 ha total irrigated on the Mexican side - roughly an eightfold under-detection of a small, fragmented alfalfa/forage system. The aquifer spans 31 deg 00' to 31 deg 20' N, i.e. it extends ~37 km south of the border at Agua Prieta, so if that 249 ha is distributed down the valley (e.g. toward Cabullona) the BL classification would fail. CONAGUA locates the zone only as 'en el acuifero Rio Agua Prieta' with no distances, so the contradiction cannot be established. This dyad is a good candidate for a targeted imagery check.

aquifer_name: Northern Great Plains - Upper Cretaceous Aquifer System
claim_tested: CAN has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: Searched Canadian provincial and USGS sources for groundwater-irrigated cropland in southern Saskatchewan/Alberta within 100 km of the US border over the Northern Great Plains Upper Cretaceous aquifers. Saskatchewan irrigation is overwhelmingly surface water from Lake Diefenbaker and is located well north of the border band, and the Upper Cretaceous sandstone aquifers of the Canadian prairies (Judith River, Blood Reserve, Eastend, Whitemud, Frenchman) carry 1,000-4,000 mg/L dissolved solids and are used chiefly for stock and domestic supply, not crop irrigation.
sources: [T1] Taylor, O. J. (1978). Summary appraisals of the nation's ground-water resources - Missouri Basin Region. USGS Professional Paper 813-Q (TDS 1,000-4,000 mg/L in Blood Reserve and Judith River aquifers, southern Alberta). https://doi.org/10.3133/pp813q | [T1] Government of Saskatchewan, Crops and Irrigation - Irrigation (irrigation development centred on the Lake Diefenbaker surface-water projects). https://www.saskatchewan.ca/business/agriculture-natural-resources-and-industry/agribusiness-farmers-and-ranchers/crops-and-irrigation/irrigation | [T1] Petre, M.-A., Rivera, A., & Lefebvre, R. (2019). Numerical modeling of a regional groundwater flow system ... transboundary Milk River Aquifer (Canada-USA). Journal of Hydrology, 575, 656-670. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2019.05.057
notes: UNVERIFIED FLAG for the authors, not a finding: groundwater-irrigated potato production does exist on the Canadian prairies over surficial sand aquifers (Assiniboine Delta and Oak Lake aquifers, southwestern Manitoba), roughly 80-100 km north of the 49th parallel. Whether the N022a polygon extends that far east and whether surficial sand aquifers fall inside the mapped Upper Cretaceous unit was not established, and the web-search budget ran out before it could be checked. If the polygon does reach southwestern Manitoba, the CAN side would exceed 10 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km and the dyad would move from UB to DA. Recommend a GIS check of the polygon against the Assiniboine Delta / Oak Lake aquifer footprints rather than another literature search.

claim_tested: PRY has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: Groundwater in the Paraguayan Chaco portion of the Yrenda-Toba-Tarijeno system is predominantly brackish to saline, with only scattered fresh-water lenses used for domestic supply and livestock watering; national soil-salinity work attributes the high salinity of Chaco soils in part to 'groundwater with significant salt content'. No source documents groundwater-irrigated cropland anywhere in the Paraguayan Chaco, and Paraguay's irrigated agriculture is concentrated in the Eastern Region on surface water.
sources: [T1] Encina Rojas, A., Sevilla-Linares, V., & Guevara-Santamaria, M. (2023). First National Report on Soil Salinity Across Paraguay. Terra Digitalis, 1-8. https://doi.org/10.22201/igg.25940694e.2023.2.112 | [T1] UNESCO-IHP / GGRETA and ISARM materials on the Sistema Acuifero Yrenda-Toba-Tarijeno as a shared Argentina-Bolivia-Paraguay resource (cited in Rodriguez et al., HESSD 9, 9885-9927, 2012). https://doi.org/10.5194/hessd-9-9885-2012
notes: Paraguay's zero for both total and groundwater-irrigated cropland over a 572,642 km2 polygon is consistent with the hydrogeology (saline groundwater, cattle-and-rainfed-crop Mennonite colonies that depend on rainwater catchment tajamares rather than wells). The Mennonite central Chaco colonies are in any case ~150-200 km from the Bolivian border and well over 100 km from the Pilcomayo, so even if some groundwater irrigation exists there it would not fall in the 100 km band. Direct GGRETA case-study PDFs were unreachable (403 / redirect loop); this rests on the salinity and hydrogeology literature.

claim_tested: PRY has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: As for the BOL-PRY dyad: groundwater in the Paraguayan Chaco over the SAYTT is largely saline and used for domestic and livestock supply, not crop irrigation, and no source documents groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the Pilcomayo (the Argentina-Paraguay border) on the Paraguayan side.
sources: [T1] Encina Rojas, A., Sevilla-Linares, V., & Guevara-Santamaria, M. (2023). First National Report on Soil Salinity Across Paraguay. Terra Digitalis, 1-8. https://doi.org/10.22201/igg.25940694e.2023.2.112 | [T1] Villar, P. C., Ribeiro, W. C., & Sant'Anna, F. M. (2018). Transboundary governance in the La Plata River basin: status and prospects. Water International, 43(7), 978-995. https://doi.org/10.1080/02508060.2018.1490879
notes: Same evidentiary basis as S028|BOL-PRY. The Paraguayan bank of the Pilcomayo is thinly settled and its agriculture is subsistence/rainfed; the abundant literature on Chaco land-use change describes conversion to pasture and rainfed soy/sorghum, never irrigation. Note that the Argentine side of the same dyad has 4,379 ha of groundwater irrigation but only 518 ha within 100 km, so the dyad's UB status rests entirely on the Paraguayan zero, which the hydrogeology supports.

claim_tested: BOL has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: The Bolivian Pantanal (Otuquis/San Matias, Puerto Suarez-Puerto Quijarro area) has no documented irrigated cropland of any kind, let alone groundwater-irrigated. Peer-reviewed synthesis reports that ~80% of the Pantanal floodplain's native vegetation remains intact and that agricultural conversion is concentrated on the surrounding Cerrado plateaus and in the Paraguayan Chaco, and is pasture/rainfed rather than irrigated.
sources: [T1] Tomas, W. M., Roque, F. O., Morato, R. G., et al. (2019). Sustainability Agenda for the Pantanal Wetland. Tropical Conservation Science, 12. https://doi.org/10.1177/1940082919872634 | [T1] Ioris, A. A. R. (2013). Rethinking Brazil's Pantanal Wetland. The Journal of Environment & Development, 22(3), 239-260. https://doi.org/10.1177/1070496513493276
notes: Bolivia's 23,263 ha of urban land within 100 km is the Puerto Suarez/Puerto Quijarro/Corumba border conurbation; its water supply is municipal, which under the protocol does not bear on a cropland claim. Both sides of this dyad record zero irrigated cropland, which for a seasonally inundated floodplain is entirely plausible.

claim_tested: BOL has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: Same finding as S015|BOL-PRY for the Bolivian side: no documented irrigated cropland, groundwater or otherwise, in the Bolivian Pantanal within 100 km of the Brazilian border. The Pantanal floodplain remains ~80% under native vegetation and its agriculture is extensive cattle ranching; the 99 ha of irrigation recorded on the Brazilian side is not groundwater-fed and does not bear on the Bolivian claim.
sources: [T1] Tomas, W. M., Roque, F. O., Morato, R. G., et al. (2019). Sustainability Agenda for the Pantanal Wetland. Tropical Conservation Science, 12. https://doi.org/10.1177/1940082919872634
notes: Corumba (Brazil) sits immediately across the border and accounts for most of the 94,920 ha of Brazilian urban land in the 100 km band, consistent with the UB assignment. Brazilian irrigated rice and soy in Mato Grosso do Sul lies on the plateaus outside the Pantanal polygon and uses surface water.

claim_tested: BRA has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: No source documents groundwater-irrigated cropland on the Brazilian side of the Pantanal aquifer within 100 km of the Paraguayan border (the Paraguay River reach around Porto Murtinho/Bela Vista). The Brazilian Pantanal floodplain is dominated by extensive ranching on native pasture, with mechanised and irrigated agriculture confined to the surrounding plateaus outside the wetland.
sources: [T1] Tomas, W. M., Roque, F. O., Morato, R. G., et al. (2019). Sustainability Agenda for the Pantanal Wetland. Tropical Conservation Science, 12. https://doi.org/10.1177/1940082919872634 | [T1] Ioris, A. A. R. (2013). Rethinking Brazil's Pantanal Wetland. The Journal of Environment & Development, 22(3), 239-260. https://doi.org/10.1177/1070496513493276
notes: The 99 ha of total irrigated land recorded for Brazil over the whole polygon (zero of it groundwater-fed, zero within 100 km of the Paraguayan border) is consistent with the small surface-irrigated rice/pasture plots along the Miranda and Aquidauana rivers, which are far from the Paraguayan border. Paraguay's 761 ha of urban land is the Bahia Negra / Fuerte Olimpo river settlements.

claim_tested: More than 99% of TJK's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (8 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: The only regional synthesis that names this aquifer (Karimov et al., Water 2020, on the 34 transboundary aquifers of Central Asia) gives Kokaral a single sentence — 'AS50 Kokaral and AS51 Dalverzin aquifers are located on the right bank of the Syr Darya River' — with no country attribution, no abstraction figures and no irrigation data. No source resolves groundwater- versus surface-irrigated cropland on the Tajik (Sughd/Asht) side of this 674 km2 polygon, let alone at a 10 km band.
sources: [T1] Karimov, A. et al. (2020). Sustainable Use of Groundwater Resources in the Transboundary Aquifers of the Five Central Asian Countries: Challenges and Perspectives. Water 12(8), 2101. https://doi.org/10.3390/w12082101 | [T1] UNESCO-IHP/IGRAC, Transboundary Aquifers of the World, edition 2015 (map inventory listing AS050). https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000264020
notes: Near-miss worth noting: irrigation on the right bank of the Syr Darya in this reach (Dalverzin steppe, Asht district of Sughd, Bekabad area) is dominated by surface water pumped from the Syr Darya / Kayrakkum reservoir, which would NOT contradict a groundwater claim even if located there. The Uzbek side (1,779 ha gw-irrigated, 815 ha within 10 km) is likewise undocumented at this resolution. Verdict is 'record is silent', not 'claim is wrong'. Note also that Tajikistan's 76 ha is close to the noise floor of any global irrigation map; a BL assignment resting on 76 ha is fragile regardless of external evidence.

claim_tested: More than 99% of JOR's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (77 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: UN-ESCWA's chapter on the Basalt Aquifer System (West) confirms the Jordanian portion is a narrow northern strip in Irbid and Mafraq governorates (~443,000 inhabitants) with 166 operational wells, 'most of which were used for agricultural purposes', scattered across the western foothills of Jebel al Arab and the Hauran Plateau — i.e. immediately south of the Syrian border. Nothing found places groundwater-irrigated cropland over this specific polygon more than 10 km from that border.
sources: [T1] UN-ESCWA & BGR (2013). Inventory of Shared Water Resources in Western Asia, Chapter 21: Basalt Aquifer System (West) — Yarmouk Basin. https://waterinventory.org/sites/waterinventory.org/files/chapters/Chapter-21-Basalt-Aquifer-System-West-web.pdf | [T1] Al-Bakri, J.T., Shawash, S., Ghanim, A. & Abdelkhaleq, R. (2016). Geospatial Techniques for Improved Water Management in Jordan. Water 8(4), 132. https://doi.org/10.3390/w8040132
notes: STRONG NEAR-MISS — the authors should check the polygon geometry before relying on this one. Al-Bakri et al. (2016), a Tier 1 study done with Jordan's Ministry of Water and Irrigation, maps ~5,900 ha of irrigated land in the Jordanian Yarmouk water basin (vs 2,100 ha in official MWI records) and states that 'most irrigation was practiced in the drylands of Mafraq, followed by the north middle areas', with a further 21% in the western parts of Ramtha, and that irrigation was absent in the southwest because it 'lacked irrigation infrastructure (dams and groundwater wells)'. Those Mafraq drylands ARE the basalt terrain of Jordan's Yarmouk basin, they are groundwater-fed (the paper finds abstraction at 144-360% of safe yield across the three basins), and they extend roughly 10-25 km south of the Syrian border — which, if they fall inside the AS142 polygon, would break the >99%-within-10 km test and give DA instead of BL. I did not mark this CONTRADICTED because our polygon captures only 1,332 ha of irrigated land on the Jordan side (~23% of Al-Bakri's basin-wide 5,900 ha), which is consistent with the polygon being a ~10-12 km border strip that excludes most of the Mafraq drylands. The verdict therefore hinges entirely on whether the AS142 Jordanian footprint reaches south of Ramtha/Jaber toward Mafraq city (~21 km from the border). If it does, this dyad should be reclassified DA. Syrian side (11,719 ha gw-irrigated, only 29% within 10 km) is well corroborated by ESCWA: mean 21,732 ha irrigated in the Syrian Hauran, ~60% of basin irrigated area, 189 MCM/yr groundwater consumption 1999-2009.

aquifer_name: Sandansky-Petrich Aquifer ; Sandansky Valley Aquifer ; Petrich Valley Aquifer
claim_tested: More than 99% of GRC's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (2 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: The Sandanski-Petrich / Struma valley aquifer units EB067-EB069 are documented essentially only as Bulgarian groundwater bodies in the Struma basin; no source found characterises a Greek portion of these units, and none reports groundwater-irrigated cropland on the Greek side at all, let alone its distance to the North Macedonian border.
sources: [T2] Sandanski-Petrich Valley (geographic description of the Struma valley basin, Bulgaria). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandanski%E2%80%93Petrich_Valley | [T1] UNECE/IGRAC European transboundary groundwater inventory (aquifer codes EB067-EB069, Struma/Strymon basin). https://unece.org/DAM/env/water/publications/assessment/English/G_PartIV_Chapter3_En.pdf
notes: Flag for the authors: the dyad label looks like an artefact. The Sandanski-Petrich valley lies in Bulgaria; the natural transboundary pairings for these units are BGR-GRC (Struma/Strymon, via the Promachonas-Kulata gap) and possibly BGR-MKD. A GRC-MKD dyad on this polygon implies the two countries' shares meet without Bulgaria, which is only geometrically possible very near the GRC-MKD-BGR tripoint at Mt. Tumba/Belasica. That is consistent with the reported '17 of 17 ha within 10 km' but it means the class rests on a handful of pixels near a tripoint. Recommend checking whether Bulgaria should be a party to this aquifer's dyad set. No external evidence exists at the 17 ha / 10 km resolution either way.

claim_tested: More than 99% of BEL's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (3 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Searched Walloon regional-government and BRGM sources: irrigation in Wallonia totalled only 3,085 ha actually irrigated across the whole region in 2020 (6,067 ha irrigable), concentrated on vegetables (spinach, beans, carrots) in Liege, Walloon Brabant and Hainaut. The Belgian footprint of the Orchies sands is confined to the Tournaisis/Mouscron strip hard against the French border. Nothing found places Belgian groundwater-irrigated cropland over this polygon more than 10 km from that border.
sources: [T1] Service public de Wallonie, Portail de l'agriculture wallonne — L'irrigation: la situation en Wallonie (2020 figures). https://agriculture.wallonie.be/home/recherche-developpement/adaptations-a-la-secheresse/resilience-en-grandes-cultures/efficience-en-eau/lirrigation/page.html | [T1] SPW, Etat de l'environnement wallon — L'exploitation des ressources en eau souterraine. https://etat.environnement.wallonie.be/files/live/sites/eew/files/Publications/Rapport%20analytique%202006-2007/Chap04/2_ExploitationEauSouterraine/RES_EAU_01.pdf
notes: The Walloon agriculture portal states explicitly 'il y a malheureusement tres peu de donnees disponibles sur la superficie de cultures irriguees' — no source resolves irrigated cropland at 27 ha / 10 km granularity anywhere in Belgium, so this is a 'nothing contradicts it' verdict rather than positive corroboration. Worth noting separately (does not bear on the cropland claim): the Belgian part of this aquifer system is heavily abstracted for public drinking-water supply and industry by SWDE/Société wallonne des eaux, not for agriculture. Also flag that 27 ha is at the noise floor of any 30 m irrigation product; BL here is driven by a handful of pixels.

claim_tested: More than 99% of BEL's groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer (1 ha) lies within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Same search as EU309. The Belgian outcrop/subcrop of the Calcaires du Carbonifere is the Tournaisis, a narrow east-west band along the French border; Walloon irrigation totals 3,085 ha region-wide and is dominated by vegetable crops in Hainaut, Walloon Brabant and Liege. No source places Belgian groundwater-irrigated cropland over this polygon beyond 10 km from the French border.
sources: [T1] BRGM (2011). Chimie des eaux du calcaire carbonifere, Rapport final BRGM/RP-59671-FR (Tournai-Lille transboundary aquifer). http://infoterre.brgm.fr/rapports/RP-59671-FR.pdf | [T1] Service public de Wallonie, Portail de l'agriculture wallonne — L'irrigation: la situation en Wallonie (2020 figures). https://agriculture.wallonie.be/home/recherche-developpement/adaptations-a-la-secheresse/resilience-en-grandes-cultures/efficience-en-eau/lirrigation/page.html
notes: Caveat: the Belgian portion of the Carboniferous Limestone aquifer extends east from Mouscron/Tournai towards Ath and Mons, and parts of that eastern extension are more than 10 km from the French border, so the 11-of-11-ha result depends on where the small Belgian irrigated parcels actually sit. No published source resolves that. This aquifer is one of the best-documented transboundary bodies in Europe (BRGM/SPW joint monitoring, Groupe de travail Nappe du Calcaire carbonifere) but the documentation is about drinking-water and industrial abstraction and piezometry, never about irrigated cropland. 11 ha is a single-pixel-scale quantity.

claim_tested: KAZ has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: A 2025 peer-reviewed assessment of groundwater for irrigation in western Kazakhstan (Aktobe, Atyrau, Mangystau) treats groundwater irrigation as prospective rather than existing: it identifies eight aquifer segments with 0.24 km3/yr exploitable potential and recommends 653 km2 as the 'prospective area recommended for groundwater irrigation development'. Aktobe region's ~29,800 ha of regularly irrigated land (2019) is served by surface schemes on the Ilek and Or rivers, not wells. Nothing found puts groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the Russian border over this aquifer.
sources: [T1] Integrated Assessment of Groundwater Quality for Water-Saving Irrigation Technology (Western Kazakhstan). Water 17(8), 1232 (2025). https://doi.org/10.3390/w17081232 | [T2] ElDala.kz — Top-7 regions of Kazakhstan by irrigated area (2019 official statistics: Aktobe region 29,800 ha). https://eldala.kz/rating/1946-top-7-regionov-kazahstana-po-ploshchadyam-orosheniya
notes: The Russian-side claim is not in the CLAIM_TO_TEST but our numbers give RUS 0 ha of irrigated land of any kind over the polygon, which is plausible for the steppe districts of southern Orenburg oblast. Caveat: Kazakhstan has been expanding well-based irrigation since ~2021 under national irrigated-land restoration programmes, and Aktobe oblast is a target region; the 2025 paper's framing as 'prospective development' is the strongest evidence available that it had not yet materialised at scale. My Russian-language search for district-level (Martuk / Khobda / Kargaly) well-irrigation projects was cut off by a search quota, so this line is not fully exhausted. The UB class also rests on 141,933 ha of Kazakh urban land within 100 km, which is consistent with Aktobe city (~90-110 km from the border) being inside the band — worth a sanity check since it sits right at the 100 km cut.

claim_tested: MDA has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: FAO AQUASTAT's Moldova country profile reports 0% of the irrigated area supplied from groundwater and 100% from surface water, and states explicitly that 'no groundwater is used for irrigation due to its unsuitable quality' — Moldovan groundwater is too mineralised. All 312,000 ha of equipped irrigation draws on the Dniester, the Prut and reservoirs. This directly supports the claim of <10 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland on the Moldovan side.
sources: [T1] FAO AQUASTAT, Water Report 15 — Republic of Moldova country profile (irrigation water sources). https://www.fao.org/4/W6240E/w6240e15.htm
notes: The AQUASTAT survey values are from 1994 and Moldova's irrigated area has since collapsed to a fraction of the Soviet-era 312,000 ha, but the qualitative statement (groundwater unsuitable for irrigation, irrigation abstracted from the Dniester and Prut) remains the standard characterisation and points the same way for the modern 76,416 ha we record as irrigated in the polygon. Consistent with our figure that all of Moldova's irrigation over the Dniester aquifer is surface-fed. The Ukrainian side is also recorded at 0 ha groundwater-irrigated; that was not part of the claim but I found nothing contradicting it either — Ukrainian irrigation in Vinnytsia/Odesa oblasts near the Dniester is likewise river-fed.

claim_tested: Both IND and NPL have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.
evidence: MacDonald et al. (2016, Nature Geoscience) analyse 3,652 water wells across Pakistan, India, Nepal and Bangladesh and describe the Indo-Gangetic Basin alluvial aquifer as the world's most heavily exploited, with groundwater irrigation distributed basin-wide (heaviest in northwest India, far from the Nepal border) and a distinct piedmont/Terai typology along the Nepal margin. Groundwater-irrigated cropland is unambiguously present on both sides and is nowhere near 99% concentrated within 10 km of the India-Nepal border.
sources: [T1] MacDonald, A.M., Bonsor, H.C., Ahmed, K.M. et al. (2016). Groundwater quality and depletion in the Indo-Gangetic Basin mapped from in situ observations. Nature Geoscience 9, 762-766. https://doi.org/10.1038/ngeo2791 | [T1] Bonsor, H.C., MacDonald, A.M., Ahmed, K.M. et al. (2017). Hydrogeological typologies of the Indo-Gangetic basin alluvial aquifer, South Asia. Hydrogeology Journal 25, 1377-1406. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10040-017-1550-z
notes: The DA claim here is close to a tautology given the scale of the aquifer (970,723 km2) and the magnitudes involved (IND 19.6 Mha, NPL 233 kha groundwater-irrigated). Nepal's share is concentrated in the Terai, which is a narrow strip, and 60% of it (139,866 of 232,833 ha) falls within 10 km of the Indian border — high but well short of 99%, and the Terai's shallow-tubewell belt demonstrably extends 20-40 km north to the Siwalik front, so the 60% figure is credible.

claim_tested: Both IND and PAK have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Both riparians are among the largest groundwater irrigators on earth over this aquifer: MacDonald et al. (2016) document water-table declines >1 m/yr from irrigation abstraction in northwest India and in Pakistani Punjab, hundreds of kilometres from the shared border, and note that IGB abstraction is about a quarter of global groundwater abstraction. Neither side's groundwater irrigation is remotely concentrated within 10 km of the India-Pakistan border.
sources: [T1] MacDonald, A.M., Bonsor, H.C., Ahmed, K.M. et al. (2016). Groundwater quality and depletion in the Indo-Gangetic Basin mapped from in situ observations. Nature Geoscience 9, 762-766. https://doi.org/10.1038/ngeo2791 | [T1] Bonsor, H.C., MacDonald, A.M., Ahmed, K.M. et al. (2017). Hydrogeological typologies of the Indo-Gangetic basin alluvial aquifer, South Asia. Hydrogeology Journal 25, 1377-1406. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10040-017-1550-z
notes: Our shares within 10 km are 3.8% (IND) and 5.6% (PAK), entirely consistent with the literature. Contextual note for the authors, not a contradiction: MacDonald et al. emphasise that leakage from the world's largest canal network (Indus and Ganges, >100,000 km) is a dominant recharge term, so 'groundwater-irrigated' and 'surface-irrigated' cropland are physically coupled here in a way they are not in the small dyads — conjunctive use is the norm across Punjab on both sides, which may make the gw/surface split in the underlying irrigation product less sharp for this aquifer than for others.

claim_tested: Both BGD and IND have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.
evidence: MacDonald et al. (2016) record 'areas of equivalent high irrigation abstraction within Bangladesh' with basin-wide shallow-tubewell irrigation (the dry-season boro rice system) spread across the whole Bengal basin, and correspondingly intensive Indian abstraction across the Ganges plain. Groundwater-irrigated cropland is present and widely distributed on both sides; neither is >99% within 10 km of the border.

aquifer_name: Thermalwasser im Tiefen Malmkarst des südbayerischen und oberösterreichischen Molassebeckens
claim_tested: Both AUT and DEU have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Searched German-language hydrogeological literature on the deep Upper Jurassic (Malmkarst) thermal reservoir of the South German / Upper Austrian Molasse Basin. The unit is a 600->3,000 m deep geothermal reservoir at 80-140 degrees C holding glacial-age fossil water (81Kr model ages of 500,000-565,000 years in the eastern Bavaria-Upper Austria sector), exploited exclusively by geothermal doublets for district heating and balneology. Nothing was found contradicting the presence of irrigated cropland at the surface on either side; agricultural irrigation in both Bavaria and Upper Austria draws on shallow Quaternary gravel aquifers.

notes: Important caveat for the authors rather than a contradiction: this polygon is the surface projection of a deep confined geothermal reservoir that is hydraulically disconnected from the land surface. The DA assignment is therefore an artefact of intersecting a surface land-use raster with a deep-aquifer footprint - the 101 ha (AUT) and 1,296 ha (DEU) of 'groundwater-irrigated cropland' above it are irrigated from shallow Quaternary gravels, not from the Malmkarst. evidence: Botswana's Limpopo-basin irrigation, which is concentrated in the Tuli Block strip along the Limpopo (the BWA-ZAF border) inside the Tuli Karoo sub-basin, totals 1,381 ha of which 44% (~608 ha) is abstracted from groundwater (LIMCOM, Tier 1); Botswana DWA reports 60.2% of irrigation farmers and 38.4% of irrigation volume rely on boreholes, on farms 'along ephemeral rivers (e.g. Tati, Shashe and Limpopo)'. sources: [T1] LIMCOM (Limpopo Watercourse Commission), 'Irrigation - Botswana', The Basin / Water Infrastructure. https://limpopocommission.org/the-basin/resource-management/water-infrastructure/irrigation/botswana/ | [T1] Botswana Department of Water Affairs (2014), Policy Brief: Irrigation and water resources in Botswana. https://www.water.gov.bw/images/Reports/DWA_Website/Policy%20Brief%20WR.pdf | [T1] Mangoro & co-authors (2022), 'A multi-criteria approach of assessing groundwater potential, recharge and flow in the transboundary Tuli Karoo Basin', Water Practice & Technology 17(9):1959 - states 'Commercial irrigation exists in Botswana and South Africa' in the Tuli Karoo. https://iwaponline.com/wpt/article/17/9/1959/90161/ | [T2] Africa Contemporary Farming, 'Agrico's innovative irrigation solution: transforming agriculture in Botswana's Tuli Block' (Kwanantle farm, 485 ha, 17 boreholes). https://africacontemporaryfarming.com/agricos-innovative-irrigation-solution-transforming-agriculture-in-botswanas-tuli-block/

Applying the ordered rule to corrected numbers: IU0/IU1 fail; UB no longer fires because BWA would have both urban land and >10 ha of GW irrigation and ZAF has zero urban; BL then fires because 134/134 ha (100%) of ZAF's GW-irrigated cropland is within 10 km of the border. If the auditors prefer to keep the Tier-2 Kwanantle evidence out, the LIMCOM/DWA Tier 1 evidence is basin-scale rather than aquifer-polygon-specific, so confidence is medium rather than high.

claim_tested: CAF has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: No source describing groundwater use or irrigation over the 'Karoo-Carbonate' aquifer (AF025) was found; the unit appears only in transboundary-aquifer delineation inventories. The Central African Republic has negligible irrigation of any kind nationally (order of 10^2 ha, essentially surface-water rice and market gardening), so <10 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer within 100 km of the COD border is entirely plausible.
notes: Searched literature for CAF irrigation/groundwater and for this aquifer name; nothing aquifer-specific exists. The large urban figures on both sides (Bangui on the CAF side, Zongo/Gemena-Kinshasa corridor on the COD side) are consistent with UB. Note the urban hectares reported here (121,526 ha CAF) suggest the urban metric is measured over a border band rather than strictly over the aquifer polygon - worth checking internally.

claim_tested: ESH has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: The Tindouf Aquifer System is well characterised (Goncalves et al. 2024). Groundwater abstraction and irrigation within the TAS are located in the Draa basin and the Guelmim plain (Morocco) and around Tindouf city (Algeria); the Western Sahara portion is the Hamada du Draa / Zemmour hamada with no documented irrigated agriculture. Nothing contradicts <10 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland on the ESH side within 100 km of the MAR border.
sources: [T1] Goncalves, J. et al. (2024), 'Dealing with hydrologic data scarcity: the case of the Tindouf basin', Comptes Rendus Geoscience. 10.5802/crgeos.202
notes: The paper quantifies irrigated area shares within the TAS domain for the Draa basin (25% east of 8W, 19% west of 8W) and Guelmim plain (15%), and locates pumping wells in those Moroccan sub-basins - i.e. north of the ESH boundary. Per second-wave guidance 1, note that MAR's 417 ha 'within 100 km' is most plausibly measured against the MAR-DZA segment of the aquifer's border zone (Draa/Tata), not the ESH border; this does not affect the ESH claim tested here but may matter for the MAR-side numbers.

evidence: Searched Armenian/Turkish and international water-resources literature for the Leninakan-Shirak (Akhuryan basin) aquifer. evidence: The Lankaran-Astara lowland is a humid subtropical agricultural zone on both sides of the Azerbaijan-Iran border, with citrus, tea, rice, vegetables and cereals; the Azerbaijani Lankaran economic region (Astara, Lankaran, Lerik, Yardimli, Masalli, Jalilabad, 636,338 ha) is described in the literature as intensively irrigated, and the Iranian Gilan/Astara side is likewise intensively irrigated. Our number of 2,796 ha gw-irrigated on the IRN side against 10,787 ha total irrigated implies a ~26% groundwater share, which is plausible but not independently verified.

evidence: On the Algerian side of the only aquifer Algeria shares with Morocco (named 'Errachidia' in the shared-aquifer inventories), the Beni Ounif oasis lies 3.5 km from the Moroccan border (7 km from Figuig) and comprises c. 31 ha of cropland (date palm, fig/pomegranate, cereals, vegetables and alfalfa) irrigated from groundwater: foggaras, traditional wells and modern motorised boreholes tapping the Lower Cretaceous/Albian (Continental Intercalaire) sandstones and the Oued Zousfana infero-flux alluvial aquifer; 33 boreholes and 39 wells were inventoried in the commune in 2018. Further groundwater-irrigated perimeters and boreholes are documented in the wider Bechar basin (Bechar city c. 75-110 km from the border), also drawing on the Continental Intercalaire.

(2019), 'Etude des ressources hydriques de la region de Beni Ounif', Master's thesis, Universite Kasdi Merbah Ouargla (Algeria) - documents Continental Intercalaire and Quaternary alluvial aquifers supplying agricultural boreholes, 'des centaines de forages... des milliers d'hectares cultives' in development perimeters; Beni Ounif is 3.5 km from the Moroccan frontier. https://dspace.univ-ouargla.dz/jspui/bitstream/123456789/23124/1/M%20arfa%20a%202019corrigierr%2027-6-2019.pdf | [T2] Fanack Water, 'Shared Water Resources in Algeria' - 'Algeria shares five aquifers with its neighbours: Errachidia with Morocco'. https://water.fanack.com/algeria/shared-water-resources-2/

claim_tested: Both CHN and PRK have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.

The lower Yalu plain (Dandong, Liaoning on the Chinese side; Sinuiju/Yongchon on the DPRK side) is a broad alluvial delta plain with distributed paddy and vegetable cultivation on both banks, consistent with our 39% (CHN) and 58% (PRK) within-10 km shares.

(2023), 'Coastline changes under natural and anthropogenic drivers in a macro-tidal estuary between 2000-2020', Frontiers in Marine Science 10, 1335064 - describes the Yalu River estuary delta plain shared by Dandong (China) and Sinuiju (DPRK). https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2023.1335064

The plausible failure mode nobody could test is that DPRK paddy in the Yongampo/Yomju plain is predominantly reservoir- and river-fed rather than well-fed; if PRK groundwater irrigation were in fact <10 ha the class would become UB (PRK has 147,912 ha urban within 100 km).

claim_tested: Both BEL and NLD have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Nothing was found contradicting the claim that both Belgium and the Netherlands have groundwater-irrigated cropland over the Oligocene sands (Oligoceenzand / Sables Oligocenes) aquifer. Supplementary sprinkler irrigation of arable crops and horticulture from shallow groundwater wells is the normal practice on the sandy soils of both northern Belgium and the southern Netherlands, and the reported 118/128 ha (BEL) and 87/146 ha (NLD) within-10 km splits are both well below the 99% BL threshold.
notes: The unit is mapped in the EU/IGRAC transboundary aquifer inventories but I found no aquifer-specific water-use study; the verdict rests on the absence of any contradicting evidence plus the well-established regional practice of groundwater-based supplementary irrigation in the Flemish/Dutch sandy lowlands. Both sides' figures are small (128 and 146 ha) but comfortably above the 10 ha threshold, and neither approaches 99% concentration in the border strip, so DA is robust to modest measurement error.

aquifer_name: Afar Rift Valley / Afar Triangle Aquifer
claim_tested: Neither DJI nor ERI has >1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland or >1 ha of urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
gis_verdict: rejected: feature inside the polygon but beyond the 100 km band

Our data record DJI as having 0 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland over the whole aquifer, which is wrong; the Hanle-Gobaad perimeters lie within a few tens of kilometres of the Ethiopian border.

The irrigated land is about 1250 ha, and the crops grown include tomatoes, melon, onions and pepper.' https://doi.org/10.1016/j.egyr.2020.10.024 | [T1] Peer-reviewed hydrogeological assessment of Djibouti borehole networks: 58 boreholes in the Ambouli watershed and 30 in the Hanle watershed, with borehole sites assessed explicitly for 'good potential of groundwater for irrigation and drinking'. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12665-021-09517-6

Because our 'within 100 km' quantity is computed once against the whole border zone of Djibouti's portion of the aquifer, the recorded 0 ha is wrong on the measurement's own terms, and the IU0 branch fails. Residual uncertainty is whether the AF059 polygon as mapped extends over Ambouli and the Hanle/Gobaad grabens; both are unambiguously inside the Afar depression and Djibouti is a listed riparian of this aquifer, so I judge this likely but not certain. Note also that if the authors intend the strict reading (distance measured to the Djibouti-Eritrea border only), the substantive claim would stand, since no Djiboutian irrigation lies within 100 km of the Eritrean border.

aquifer_name: Système Aquifère de Mourzouk - Djado / Murzuk-Djado Aquifer System

claim_tested: ISR has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).

The urban layer here is demonstrably not clipped to the aquifer polygon - the PSE figure alone exceeds the whole aquifer by 41%. Any IU/UB decision resting on these urban numbers is unreliable for this dyad. (2) The verdict is CONFIRMED only under a strictly territorial reading of the rule. Substantively, Israeli groundwater irrigation over this aquifer is large - the Oslo II Article 40 Israeli allocation from the Eastern Basin plus Jordan Valley wells irrigates thousands of hectares of Israeli-cultivated date palm and field crops - but that land sits in the West Bank and is therefore counted on the PSE side. The classification's country attribution, not the hydrology, is what produces gw1 = 0 for ISR here.
