claim_tested: Neither MOZ nor MWI has >1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland or >1 ha of urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
evidence: The 'Mwanza grits and shales' unit appears only in Malawi's national border-based transboundary-aquifer delineation exercise; the BGS Hydrogeology of Malawi compilation does not list it, and no source describes its extent, groundwater use or the land use over it. Nothing was found that either confirms or contradicts the claim as written.
sources: [T1] Rivett, M.O. et al., 'A national border-based assessment of Malawi's transboundary aquifer units: towards achieving SDG 6.5.2', Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies / Water International 45(7-8):865-883 (2020) https://ideas.repec.org/a/taf/rwinxx/v45y2020i7-8p865-883.html | [T1] BGS Earthwise, Hydrogeology of Malawi (does not include a Mwanza unit; notes growing smallholder groundwater irrigation nationally) https://earthwise.bgs.ac.uk/index.php/Hydrogeology_of_Malawi | [T1] National Statistical Office of Malawi, 2018 Population and Housing Census - Mwanza town population 18,039 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mwanza,_Malawi
notes: STRONG near-miss the authors should resolve directly from the polygon, because it would flip the class. Mwanza town, the Mwanza district seat, had 18,039 inhabitants at the 2018 Malawi census and sits at 15.5986S, 34.5178E, roughly 8 km east of the Mozambican border at the Mwanza/Zobue crossing - well inside the 100 km band and in the immediate area the unit is named after. The unit's polygon is only 11.3 km2, so whether the town falls inside it is a matter of a few kilometres and I could not verify it from any published map. If Mwanza town (or the built-up strip along the M6 at the border post) intersects the polygon, the MWI urban limb of the IU0 claim fails; with no groundwater-irrigated cropland found on either side, the rule would then produce UB rather than IU0. This is a one-line GIS check for the authors and is the single highest-value follow-up in this batch. Note also that ur1 = ur2 = 0.0 and area = 11.3 km2 are mutually consistent here, so this is not an input-implausibility case - it is a resolution case.

claim_tested: GTM has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: Searched Guatemalan and Mexican sources for groundwater-irrigated cropland in Petén over the Boca del Cerro-San Pedro unit (Usumacinta/San Pedro lowlands). Guatemala's irrigated area is overwhelmingly on the Pacific piedmont and in the Motagua valley; the Petén lowlands have essentially no formal irrigation districts and no documented well-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the Mexican border. Nothing found that contradicts the <10 ha claim for GTM.
sources: [T1] US Army Corps of Engineers / IGRAC, Evaluación de Recursos de Agua de Guatemala; IGRAC Guatemala country profile (groundwater use and irrigation distribution) https://www.un-igrac.org/es/data/country-profiles/guatemala/
notes: record-only near-miss: Petén does have expanding oil-palm and banana agriculture along the Usumacinta/San Pedro, but published accounts describe it as rainfed or river-fed, not well-irrigated. Input plausibility: ur1 = 32,336 ha of urban land on the Guatemalan side over a 21,279 km2 polygon (1.5%) is high for the very sparsely urbanised Petén and is worth checking against the urban layer's clipping; it does not affect the verdict because the UB claim concerns cropland only.

aquifer_name: Valle de Mexicali - San Luis Rio Colorado Aquifer / Yuma - Imperial Valley
claim_tested: Both MEX and USA have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Both the Mexicali/San Luis Río Colorado valley and the Yuma-Imperial area are documented as having substantial pumped-groundwater irrigation in addition to Colorado River deliveries, distributed across the valleys rather than concentrated in a 10 km border strip (Mexicali Valley well fields, Yuma Mesa and Yuma County groundwater units, San Luis Mesa). The claim as written is supported.
sources: [T1] IBWC/CILA Minute 242 and successor minutes on groundwater pumping within 5 miles of the Arizona-Sonora boundary; USGS/Arizona Department of Water Resources Yuma AMA groundwater assessments; CONAGUA aquifer availability determinations for Valle de Mexicali and San Luis Río Colorado https://www.ibwc.gov/treaties-minutes/
notes: Caveat for the authors rather than a contradiction: in both valleys the dominant irrigation water source is Colorado River surface delivery, and the groundwater-irrigated hectare figures (46,240 ha MEX / 55,688 ha USA) probably reflect conjunctive-use fields that the GW-irrigation raster attributes wholly to groundwater. This inflates gw magnitude but does not change the DA classification, which only needs both sides non-zero and neither >99% within 10 km (MEX 18.3%, USA 22.0%).

aquifer_name: Sistema Aquífero / Sistema Acuífero Arapey / Serra Geral
claim_tested: Both BRA and PRY have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.
evidence: The Serra Geral fractured basalt aquifer (confining/overlying unit of the Guarani system) is documented as a heavily used irrigation and supply source in western Paraná/Mato Grosso do Sul (Brazil) and, at lower intensity, in Alto Paraná, Canindeyú and Itapúa (Paraguay), with wells distributed across the basalt plateau rather than concentrated at the Paraná river border. Nothing contradicts the claim.
sources: [T1] BGR/SEAM Paraguay, Caracterización hidrogeológica e hidrogeoquímica del Sistema Acuífero Guaraní en Paraguay (proceedings) https://www.bgr.bund.de/EN/Themen/Grundwasser/Projekte/Versorgungssicherheit/TZ_Paraguay/sag-py_proceedings_cuiaba_pdf.pdf | [T1] GWP/World Bank, Transboundary groundwater management issues for the Guarani Aquifer (case study) https://www.gwp.org/globalassets/global/toolbox/case-studies/americas-and-caribbean/transboundary.-groundwater-management-issues-for-guarani-aquifer-368-english.pdf
notes: The polygon name mixes 'Arapey' (the Uruguayan name for the same basalt unit) with 'Serra Geral', so the mapped extent is very large (343,218 km2) and spans several dyads; the BRA-PRY segment measured here is only part of it. Brazil's gw within 100 km (8,490 ha) is only 14% of its total gw over the polygon (60,159 ha), consistent with a distributed, non-border-concentrated pattern.

claim_tested: BRN has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: Peer-reviewed work on Brunei states that surface water accounts for more than 99.5% of the country's freshwater supply and groundwater for less than 1%, and that groundwater at the national agricultural development areas (including the rice schemes) is still at the exploration stage, with only two test wells drilled and weak-to-moderate yields. There is therefore no established groundwater-irrigated cropland on the Brunei side of the Limbang aquifer.
sources: [T1] Soil and Groundwater Investigation for Sustainable Agricultural Development: A Case Study from Brunei Darussalam. Sustainability, 14(3), 1388 (2022) https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/14/3/1388 | [T1] Electrical resistivity tomography and induced polarization study for groundwater exploration in the agricultural development areas of Brunei Darussalam. Environmental Earth Sciences (2022) https://doi.org/10.1007/s12665-022-10284-1
notes: Near-miss worth recording: Brunei is actively drilling exploratory production wells at eight agricultural development sites for paddy irrigation, so this claim could become false within a few years. Brunei's total rice area is only ~852 ha nationally, concentrated in Brunei-Muara, and the schemes are surface-irrigated (Imang/Benutan reservoirs). Input plausibility: ur1 = 30,286 ha of urban land attributed to Brunei over this 6,268 km2 polygon looks high given that the Brunei portion adjacent to Limbang is mostly Temburong district (~10,000 people) plus forest; check whether the urban layer is clipped to the polygon.

claim_tested: KGZ has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: Searched in Russian and English for the Nanay (Нанай) groundwater deposit on the Kyrgyz-Uzbek boundary in the Fergana foothills. Only generic Kyrgyz and Central Asian transboundary-groundwater inventories (UNECE, CAWater-Info) surfaced; no source describes this unit, its abstraction, or any well-irrigated cropland on the Kyrgyz side. The record is silent, so the claim can be neither confirmed nor contradicted from external evidence.
sources: [T1] UNECE, Управление подземными водами и трансграничные подземные воды в Республике Кыргызстан (Tolstikhin & Sakhvaeva) - Kyrgyz transboundary groundwater inventory; PDF fetch blocked by the proxy, listed here as the search target https://www.unece.org/fileadmin/DAM/env/water/cwc/groundwater/ | [T2] CAWater-Info, Запасы и ресурсы подземных вод, типы месторождений (Central Asian groundwater deposit inventory) https://www.cawater-info.net/bk/1-2-3.htm
notes: Context that cuts against a contradiction: irrigation in this part of the Fergana valley is overwhelmingly canal-fed surface water, and the Kyrgyz side records only 31.3 ha of irrigated cropland of any kind over the polygon, so a >10 ha groundwater figure is unlikely on priors. INTERNALLY IMPOSSIBLE INPUT: the polygon area is 47.75 km2 = 4,775 ha, but ur2 (Uzbek urban land) is reported as 12,530 ha - 2.6 times the entire aquifer polygon. The urban layer is clearly not clipped to the polygon for this unit, which also means the UB assignment and the clsF=BL disagreement here rest on unreliable urban numbers. This is the strongest instance of the guidance-5 problem in this batch.

claim_tested: BIH has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: The Tara massif is a high, forested Dinaric karst plateau (Tara National Park on the Serbian side, the Foca/Drina canyon uplands on the Bosnian side) with thin soils, deep karst drainage and no irrigation agriculture; the hydrogeological literature treats it as a protected recharge/spring-water area, not an abstraction-for-irrigation area. Nothing found contradicting the BIH cropland claim.
sources: [T1] Karst Geoheritage of Tara National Park (Serbia) and Its Geotouristic Potential. Geoheritage (2021) https://doi.org/10.1007/s12371-021-00612-5 | [T1] UNESCO/GEF DIKTAS, Improving Groundwater Governance and Sustainability of the Dinaric Karst Aquifer System https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/improving-groundwater-governance-and-sustainability-dinaric-karst-aquifer-system | [T1] FAO AQUASTAT, Bosnia and Herzegovina irrigation country profile (irrigation concentrated in the Sava lowlands and Neretva valley, not the eastern karst uplands) https://www.fao.org/aquastat/en/geospatial-information/global-maps-irrigated-areas/irrigation-by-country/country/BIH/index.html
notes: Input plausibility: ur1 = 4,517 ha of urban land on the Bosnian side over a 1,240 km2 polygon (3.6%) is high for a near-uninhabited karst massif unless the polygon reaches down into Foca or Visegrad; worth checking the polygon-urban intersection. Does not affect the verdict, since the UB claim is about cropland only.

claim_tested: Both BGR and ROU have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.
evidence: The Dobrudja Neogene/Sarmatian aquifer is a documented transboundary unit with abstraction on both the Bulgarian (Dobrich) and Romanian (Constanta) sides, including agricultural wells; on the Bulgarian side 70.7 of 93.4 ha (75.7%) of groundwater-irrigated cropland lies within 10 km, well short of the >99% BL threshold. Nothing contradicts the claim that both sides have groundwater-irrigated cropland and neither is >99% border-concentrated.
sources: [T1] Hydrogeological Settings in Dobrudja Area and Groundwater Monitoring Networks in Transboundary Aquifers. In: Climate Change and the Sustainable Use of Water Resources / NATO Science Series, Springer https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4020-6985-7_6 | [T1] Groundwater Exploration in Carbonate Reservoirs Using Borehole Investigations: A Case Study from South Dobrogea, Romania. Energies 17(2), 426 https://doi.org/10.3390/en17020426
notes: Caveat: large-area irrigation in Romanian Dobrogea is historically Danube-fed surface water (Carasu/Danube-Black Sea canal system), so part of the 2,939 ha attributed to groundwater on the Romanian side may be surface-irrigated. That would reduce gw2 but not below 10 ha, so DA still holds. ur2 = 95,018 ha urban on the Romanian side (17.5% of the polygon) is high even allowing for Constanta and is worth a clipping check.

claim_tested: Both AUT and SVK have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.
evidence: The Austrian Marchfeld, immediately west of the March/Morava border river, is Austria's most intensively irrigated arable region and irrigates predominantly from groundwater wells (several thousand irrigation wells, supported since the 1990s by Marchfeldkanal recharge); the Slovak Zahorie/Danubian lowland side likewise has well irrigation distributed across the lowland. Neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km (AUT 88.9%, SVK 18.6%). Nothing contradicts the claim.
sources: [T1] Betriebsgesellschaft Marchfeldkanal (public operating company), Landwirtschaft / Grundwasser pages on groundwater irrigation and artificial recharge in the Marchfeld https://marchfeldkanal.at/wasserwirtschaft/grundwasser/ | [T1] Bundesamt fuer Wasserwirtschaft (BAW), Die Qualitaet des Bodenwassers im Marchfeld https://www.baw.at/wasser-boden/projekte/qualitaet_bodenwasser_marchfeld.html
notes: Methodological flag for the authors: this polygon is the deep 'Upper Pannonian Thermal Aquifer', whereas Marchfeld and Zahorie irrigation wells tap the shallow Quaternary gravels above it. The classification is intersecting a surface irrigation raster with a deep geothermal-aquifer footprint, so the 'groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer' quantity is a vertical mismatch. The DA verdict on the claim as written still stands. Input plausibility: ur2 = 289,227 ha of Slovak urban land is 38.9% of the 7,435 km2 polygon and far exceeds the built-up area of Bratislava plus its hinterland - very likely an unclipped urban layer.

claim_tested: MRT has >1 ha of neither groundwater-irrigated cropland nor urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
evidence: Checked both limbs. The Mauritanian sector within 100 km of the Algerian border is the Erg Chech / El Hank hamada in northeastern Tiris Zemmour, with no permanent settlement and no cultivation. The only Mauritanian places anywhere near the frontier are Chegga (an abandoned French Foreign Legion fort and caravan/military post, not a town, with no census population) and Ain Ben Tili and Bir Moghrein, both roughly 170 km and >300 km west of the Algerian border respectively. No urban land and no groundwater-irrigated cropland within the band.
sources: [T1] Frontiere entre l'Algerie et la Mauritanie (border description; first official crossing opened 2018 at the Chegga sector, previously no crossing point) https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fronti%C3%A8re_entre_l%27Alg%C3%A9rie_et_la_Mauritanie | [T2] Jeune Afrique, Algerie-Mauritanie: ouverture du premier passage frontalier (2018); Hespress, fermeture d'une zone frontaliere sensible pres de Tindouf (2025) - both describe the zone as uninhabited desert military area https://www.jeuneafrique.com/617403/politique/algerie-mauritanie-ouverture-du-premier-passage-frontalier/
notes: Near-miss recorded per guidance 4: Chegga is the only built structure in the band, but it is a fort and mosque plus an artisanal gold-mining camp opened after 2019, nowhere near 10 ha of urban land, so the IU1 assignment survives on the urban limb as well as the cropland limb. The Tindouf system's Mauritanian extension (El Hank) is described only in delineation/geological terms (OSS, geologie de la Mauritanie); no aquifer-specific use record was found for the Mauritanian portion.

claim_tested: MOZ has >1 ha of neither groundwater-irrigated cropland nor urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
gis_acceptance: accepted: feature strictly inside the polygon and band
error_class_description: applied: settlement above the threshold yet recorded zero over the whole polygon
evidence: The Mozambican side of Coastal Sedimentary Basin VI (the Maputaland coastal plain) is Matutuine district, whose entire territory lies on the coastal sedimentary aquifer and within 100 km of the South African border. It contains the district seat Bela Vista and the towns of Ponta do Ouro (about 15 km from the South African border), Zitundo and Catuane, with a district population of roughly 37,000-40,000 recorded by Mozambique's National Institute of Statistics; the built-up footprint of these settlements is far more than 10 ha. The urban limb of the IU1 claim is therefore false for MOZ.
sources: [T1] Instituto Nacional de Estatistica (INE) Mozambique, Censo 2017 - population of Matutuine district and its administrative posts (Bela Vista/Missevene, Zitundo, Catuane, Machangulo) https://mozambique.opendataforafrica.org/gfnke/popula%C3%A7%C3%A3o-maputo-2017 | [T1] Hydrogeochemical aquifer characterization and its implication for groundwater development in the Maputo district, Mozambique (peer-reviewed; establishes the Mozambican coastal sedimentary aquifer as the relevant unit) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/333896498 | [T2] Ponta do Ouro (town in extreme south of Mozambique, about 15 km from the South African border) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ponta_do_Ouro
notes: Contradicted on the urban limb alone. I found no evidence of groundwater-irrigated cropland on the Mozambican side - Matutuine farming is about 7,000 smallholdings averaging 0.9 ha of rainfed maize, cassava, cowpea, groundnut and sweet potato - so applying the ordered rule to corrected numbers gives UB, not DA: both sides have urban land within 100 km, neither has >10 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland. Also flag for the authors: ur2 = 53,147 ha of South African urban land (6.3% of the 8,443 km2 polygon) is plausible only if dispersed rural KwaZulu-Natal settlement is being counted as urban - the same layer records exactly 0 ha for the Mozambican side, which is the asymmetry that produced the IU1 label.

claim_tested: RWA has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: Searched Rwandan government and media sources for groundwater-irrigated cropland in the eastern districts (Kirehe, Nyagatare, Kayonza) that lie on the Kagera aquifer within 100 km of Tanzania. Rwanda's large eastern schemes near the border - Nasho/Mpanga and Kagitumba - are solar-pumped surface water from lakes and the Akagera river, not groundwater; the Kirehe 'Akagera aquifer' boreholes supply domestic water, and the Rwanda Water Board describes small-scale irrigation from the mapped groundwater sites as future potential (about 100 ha at eight high-potential sites), not existing hectares. Nothing contradicts the <10 ha claim for RWA.
sources: [T1] Rwanda Water Board (RWB), mapping groundwater sources in Eastern and Southern Provinces; borehole installation for drought resilience https://www.rwb.rw/actualites/info-details/rwb-kicks-off-mapping-groundwater-sources-in-eastern-and-southern-provinces-to-improve-water-security | [T1] Government of Rwanda, Rwanda Irrigation Master Plan (FAOLEX) https://faolex.fao.org/docs/pdf/rwa174262.pdf | [T2] InfoNile / New Times, 'How Groundwater Drilling Transformed Livelihoods in Kirehe' (2024) - boreholes for domestic supply, irrigation described as potential https://allafrica.com/stories/202412020095.html
notes: This is the closest CONFIRMED in the batch to flipping. Rwanda is actively drilling in exactly the right place (Kirehe and Nyagatare sit on the Kagera aquifer directly on the Tanzanian border), and RWB's own projection of about 100 ha of borehole-fed small-scale irrigation would, if realised, exceed the 10 ha threshold and move this dyad to DA - which is what clsF already assumes. As of the sources found, the irrigation is prospective. Input plausibility: ur1 = 29,622 ha (6.1%) and ur2 = 94,746 ha (19.6%) of a 4,824 km2 polygon; the Tanzanian figure is high for rural Kagera region and may reflect dispersed settlement or an unclipped urban layer.

claim_tested: Neither MOZ nor MWI has >1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland or >1 ha of urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
gis_verdict: rejected: feature outside the aquifer polygon
gis_acceptance: not accepted: 45.4 km outside, beyond the tolerance of 5 km + 2 km
error_class_description: excluded: rejected, feature outside the polygon beyond its own uncertainty
evidence: The 'Mwanza grits and shales' unit is one of the Malawi transboundary aquifer units delineated along the Malawi-Mozambique border and is named for, and outcrops at, Mwanza in southern Malawi. Mwanza is the district capital and lies on the border with Mozambique on the M1 to Tete, a few kilometres from the Mwanza/Zobue border post; its population was 18,039 at the 2018 Malawi Population and Housing Census. Its built-up footprint is far more than 10 ha and is within 100 km (indeed within about 5 km) of the border, so the urban limb of the IU0 claim is false for MWI.
sources: [T1] National Statistical Office of Malawi, 2018 Malawi Population and Housing Census - Mwanza town, 18,039 inhabitants http://www.nsomalawi.mw/2018-malawi-population-and-housing-census | [T1] Fraser, C., Kalin, R. M., & Kanjaye, M. (2020). A national border-based assessment of Malawi's transboundary aquifer units: Towards achieving sustainable development goal 6.5.2. Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, 31, 100726 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejrh.2020.100726
notes: Contradicted on the urban limb only. I found no groundwater-irrigated cropland on either side, so applying the ordered rule to corrected numbers gives UB (at least one side has urban land, both sides <10 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland) - not IU1 and not DA. Caveat that keeps confidence at medium rather than high: the polygon is tiny (8.35 km2 = 835 ha), and I could not retrieve the Fraser et al. figure showing its exact outline (ScienceDirect and ResearchGate are both blocked to the fetch tool), so I cannot verify from the source that Mwanza town centre falls inside the 835 ha outcrop rather than just beside it. The unit's name, its position in the border buffer and Mwanza town's location on the border make the overlap likely but not proven. On the Mozambican side the corresponding settlement in the band is Zobue in Moatize district, Tete province.

claim_tested: GTM has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: Searched Spanish-language MAGA (Guatemalan Ministry of Agriculture) irrigation-unit reporting for Huehuetenango and material on Nenton municipality; the documented irrigation units in Huehuetenango are gravity/surface schemes (e.g. Chiantla), and the Nenton karst plateau (Laguna Brava / Yolnajab) is a rainfed subsistence maize-and-bean landscape. No groundwater-irrigated cropland found on the Guatemalan side of this aquifer.

INPUT PLAUSIBILITY FLAG: ur1 = 20,246.6 ha (202 km2) of urban land attributed to the Guatemalan side is not credible for the Nenton/Jacaltenango area, whose municipal seats are villages of a few thousand people; the urban layer looks unclipped or over-dilated. This does not affect the verdict because the claim tested is about cropland only.

claim_tested: USA has >1 ha of neither groundwater-irrigated cropland nor urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
evidence: The La Abra Plain is in Pima County, Arizona (not Texas as the MEX-USA pairing might suggest), immediately west of Lukeville on the Sonora border, and the entire US portion lies inside Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument — federally protected desert with no cropland and no settlement. USGS WRI 95-4295 covers exactly this transboundary area (Quitobaquito Springs and La Abra Plain, Arizona and Sonora) and describes no agricultural groundwater use on the US side. Lukeville, AZ, the only US built structure nearby, is a port of entry with a resident population of roughly 50.
sources: [T1] Carruth, R.L. (1996). Hydrogeology of the Quitobaquito Springs and La Abra Plain area, Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, Arizona, and Sonora, Mexico. USGS Water-Resources Investigations Report 95-4295. https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/wri954295 | [T1] US Geological Survey GNIS / topographic mapping — La Abra Plain, Pima County, Arizona (feature ID 5550834). https://www.geonames.org/5550834/la-abra-plain.html
notes: Locating this unit was the crux: it is an Arizona-Sonora feature at Organ Pipe Cactus NM, not a Texas-Chihuahua one. Its US side being empty of cropland and urban land is essentially guaranteed by National Monument status. INPUT PLAUSIBILITY FLAG: ur1 = 5,870.8 ha (58.7 km2) of urban land on the Mexican side of a 306 km2 polygon means 19% of the whole aquifer would be built up; Sonoyta, Sonora (~15,000 people) has a built-up footprint an order of magnitude smaller. The urban layer looks unclipped or heavily over-dilated here.

claim_tested: BRA has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: Rice irrigation in Santa Vitoria do Palmar and the Chui border strip draws on surface water from Lagoa Mirim and Lagoa Mangueira and associated canals, not on wells. Documented groundwater irrigation from the Rio Grande do Sul Coastal Aquifer System is reported for the northern and central litoral (e.g. the Tapes region and Litoral Norte), 250-400 km north of the Uruguayan border. No groundwater-irrigated cropland was found over this aquifer within 100 km of the BRA-URY border.
sources: [T1] Analise das caracteristicas geoquimicas para irrigacao das aguas subterraneas do Sistema Aquifero Quaternario Costeiro, regiao de Tapes, Rio Grande do Sul. Boletim Geografico do Rio Grande do Sul (state planning secretariat). https://revistas.planejamento.rs.gov.br/index.php/boletim-geografico-rs/article/view/4598 | [T1] Compartimentacao hidroestratigrafica do sistema aquifero costeiro do estado do Rio Grande do Sul. Revista Aguas Subterraneas (ABAS) / CPRM-SGB. https://aguassubterraneas.abas.org/asubterraneas/article/view/30286
notes: Near-miss worth recording: the input assigns BRA 523.2 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland over the polygon but only 3.9 ha within 100 km of the border, which matches the geography — the polygon is a 36,393 km2 coastal strip and the well-irrigated fraction sits far to the north. Santa Vitoria do Palmar is Brazil's largest rice municipality (ir1 = 85,395 ha over the polygon), so if any meaningful share of that were well-supplied the claim would fail; the literature consistently attributes it to the lagoons. Uruguayan horticulture around Chuy/Rocha does use wells, but the claim tested is about Brazil.

claim_tested: BRN has >1 ha of neither groundwater-irrigated cropland nor urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
gis_verdict: rejected: feature outside the aquifer polygon
gis_acceptance: not accepted: 3.5 km outside, beyond the tolerance of 1 km + 2 km
error_class_description: excluded: rejected, feature outside the polygon beyond its own uncertainty
evidence: Brunei side: the Belait District, which is the only Bruneian territory adjoining the Baram basin, had 65,531 inhabitants at the 2021 census, and its two towns — Kuala Belait (town proper 4,544; wider mukim tens of thousands) and Seria, about 20 km further east — sit on the coastal plain roughly 5-25 km from the Sarawak border crossing at Sungai Tujoh, on the Belait/Liang Formation clastic sequence that is the Bruneian continuation of the Baram delta province. evidence: The Sudd Basin / Umm Ruwaba aquifer is described in the hydrogeological record (BGS Earthwise for Sudan and South Sudan; Fanack's shared-water-resources profile, which lists Sudan as sharing the Um Ruwaba aquifer with South Sudan only) as a low-to-moderate-productivity formation used almost entirely for small domestic supplies and livestock watering, with only about 1,524 ha equipped for groundwater irrigation in the whole of South Sudan. I could not establish where the Sudanese portion of the mapped polygon abuts the Ethiopian border, so I cannot test the urban or cropland limb of the claim against a specific location.
sources: [T1] BGS Earthwise, Hydrogeology of South Sudan (Umm Ruwaba Formation; 1,524 ha equipped for irrigation by groundwater, 2011). https://earthwise.bgs.ac.uk/index.php/Hydrogeology_of_South_Sudan | [T1] BGS Earthwise, Hydrogeology of Sudan (Umm Ruwaba / Sudd basin sediments). https://earthwise.bgs.ac.uk/index.php/Hydrogeology_of_Sudan | [T1] Fanack Water, Shared Water Resources in Sudan (Um Ruwaba aquifer shared with South Sudan). https://water.fanack.com/sudan/shared-water-resources-in-sudan/
notes: The blocking ambiguity is the dyad itself. If the polygon and country attribution predate 2011, the relevant border is the Gambella–Upper Nile/Jonglei one, where Akobo town sits literally on the Ethiopian border and Nasir about 60 km from it, both squarely on the Sobat/Pibor Umm Ruwaba plain and both market towns of ten to tens of thousands — that would contradict the claim on the urban limb and give UB. The authors can resolve this cheaply by checking which border segment the SDN portion of AF046 actually touches. Separately, flag for protocol item 5: ur1 = 213,278 ha (2,133 km2) of urban land on the ETHIOPIAN side of a 52,830 km2 polygon is about 4% urban, which is wildly implausible for the Gambella lowlands and is strong evidence that the urban layer is not clipped to the aquifer polygon for this feature. claim_tested: Neither GEO nor RUS has >1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland or >1 ha of urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.

claim_tested: ALB has >1 ha of neither groundwater-irrigated cropland nor urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.

The Albanian portion is the upper Cem catchment in Kelmend (Malesi e Madhe) - an alpine valley of scattered villages (Tamare, Selce, Vukel, Nikc, Lepushe, Vermosh) with no town and no documented irrigation scheme. Nothing found contradicts the claim that ALB has <10 ha of both groundwater-irrigated cropland and urban land over the polygon.

notes: This is a fragile classification and the authors should treat it as such. (1) gw1=8.7 ha is only 1.3 ha below the 10 ha threshold, so any modest revision flips ALB into the 'has groundwater irrigation' category and the dyad out of IU1. (2) On the urban limb, the Kelmend administrative unit (former commune, ~3,000-4,000 residents at the 2011 INSTAT census, centre at Tamare) sits directly on the Albanian part of the basin only a few kilometres from Montenegro; its dispersed built-up footprint could plausibly exceed 10 ha under a fine-resolution built-up layer such as GHSL, even though no single place there qualifies as a town. I found no source establishing this, so I do not record a contradiction, but ur1=0.0 exactly should not be taken at face value. The source paper does not discuss settlement or water use on the Albanian side at all. Note also that clsF=BL while cls=IU1, i.e. the pipeline itself is unstable for this dyad.

aquifer_name: Uschowa / Ol?eva (part of the Karawanken / Karavanke transboundary groundwater body)

claim_tested: Both EGY and ISR have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.

aquifer_name: Nata Karoo Sub-basin / Caprivi Lower Aquifer
claim_tested: AGO has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).

BGS and SADC-region hydrogeological syntheses describe Angolan groundwater use in this region as limited to hand-pumped and small motorised boreholes for domestic and livestock supply; no irrigation schemes of any scale are documented, and the region's small amount of cropland is rainfed on dambos and river margins.

claim_tested: SDN has >1 ha of neither groundwater-irrigated cropland nor urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
evidence: The Sudd Basin / Umm Ruwaba aquifer is documented by BGS for Sudan as an unconsolidated sand-silt-clay system of low to moderate productivity that 'is used mostly for small domestic supplies and livestock watering' rather than for irrigation, so the groundwater-irrigation limb of the SDN claim is supported. On the urban limb, the Sudanese side of this border (southern White Nile State around Joda, and the southern fringes of South Kordofan) has no municipal seat that I could place inside the mapped polygon and inside 100 km.

claim_tested: Both DOM and HTI have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.

claim_tested: GEO has >1 ha of neither groundwater-irrigated cropland nor urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
evidence: No aquifer-specific record found. The UNECE Second Assessment of transboundary waters treats 'Ktsia-Khrami' as a RIVER basin (8,340 km2, shared by Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia), not as an aquifer, and gives no groundwater description; no hydrogeological study, national report or IGRAC/ISARM case study of a Ktsia-Khrami aquifer could be located. Neither limb of the GEO claim could be tested against evidence tied to the mapped polygon.
sources: [T1] UNECE, Second Assessment of Transboundary Rivers, Lakes and Groundwaters, Chapter 4: Drainage basin of the Caspian Sea (Ktsia-Khrami river basin entry) https://unece.org/DAM/env/water/blanks/assessment/caspian.pdf | [T1] IGRAC/UNESCO-IHP, Transboundary Aquifers of the World, edition 2015 (delineation inventory only) https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000264020
notes: NEAR-MISS the authors should resolve by inspecting the polygon: the Khrami/Ktsia valley downstream of the Khrami reservoir (Marneuli and Bolnisi municipalities, Kvemo Kartli) is Georgia's most intensively irrigated agricultural district, with both canal and well irrigation and with towns of >20,000 (Marneuli), all comfortably within 100 km of the Azerbaijani border. If any part of the 24.3 km2 polygon reaches the Marneuli plain, BOTH limbs of the GEO claim fail and the class becomes DA rather than IU1/BL. Conversely if the polygon sits only at the Khrami-Kura confluence on the Azerbaijani side, IU1 may be right. INPUT NOTE: ur1 (AZE) = 429.6 ha is 18% of the whole 2,429 ha polygon, a very high built-up fraction for this rural reach; and cls (IU1) differs from clsF (BL), which is worth checking since the two rules are not adjacent in the ordering.

aquifer_name: Cerknica / Kupa Aquifer; Ko?evje Goteni?ka Gora Aquifer; Radovica-Metlika / Zumberak Aquifer
claim_tested: HRV has >1 ha of neither groundwater-irrigated cropland nor urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
gis_acceptance: accepted: feature strictly inside the polygon and band
error_class_description: excluded: definitional, settlement below the urban-cluster threshold
evidence: Croatia holds roughly 1,000 km2 of the Kupa-catchment transboundary karst aquifer and Biondic et al. (2006) state that 'many settlements and a highly developed wood industry are present' in it. Named Croatian towns on this karst directly at the Slovenian border include the town (grad) of Cabar in the Cabranka-Kupa valley, 3,208 inhabitants at the 2021 census and within ~1-2 km of the border, plus Gerovo, Prezid and Delnice further south. Their built-up footprints are far above 10 ha, so the claim that HRV has <10 ha of urban land within 100 km of the HRV-SVN border over this aquifer is false.
sources: [T1] Biondic, B., Biondic, R., Measki, H. (2006). Karst groundwater protection in the Kupa River catchment area and sustainable development. Environmental Geology 49, 828-839. 10.1007/s00254-006-0178-4 | [T1] Croatian Bureau of Statistics (DZS), Census of Population 2021 - Town of Cabar, Primorje-Gorski Kotar County: 3,208 inhabitants https://mojahrvatska.com.hr/grad/cabar/ | [T1] IGRAC, Transboundary Aquifers of Europe map 2022 (EB010-EB012 delineation) https://un-igrac.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/Transboundary_aquifers_Europe_map_2022-1.pdf
notes: Contradiction is on the URBAN limb only. No groundwater-irrigated cropland was found on the Croatian side: Biondic et al. describe the resource as a drinking-water supply (about 6 m3/s of high-quality spring water for western Croatia) and mention no irrigation, and Gorski Kotar/Zumberak agriculture is rainfed grassland and forest. Applying the ordered rule to corrected numbers: neither side has >10 ha groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km, but both sides now have urban land, so IU0 and IU1 both fail and the rule produces UB. Residual uncertainty is whether the specific EB010/EB011/EB012 polygons include the Cabranka-Kupa valley floor where Cabar sits rather than only the Snieznik/Gorski Kotar uplands; the aquifer is by construction transboundary and its Croatian part is ~1,000 km2, so a zero-urban Croatian segment is not credible either way.

claim_tested: GRC has >1 ha of neither groundwater-irrigated cropland nor urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
gis_acceptance: accepted under the coordinate-uncertainty buffer (2.6 km outside, tolerance 5 km + 2 km)
error_class_description: excluded: definitional, settlement below the urban-cluster threshold
evidence: Doirani is a municipal unit of the Municipality of Kilkis with 1,022 inhabitants at the 2021 Greek census, sitting on the southwestern shore of Lake Doiran directly on the Greek-North Macedonian border and squarely on the mapped Dojran/Doirani lake aquifer. The adjacent Mouries municipal unit (1,846 inhabitants, 2021 census, 138.7 km2, bordering the lake and North Macedonia) adds further built-up land within ~10 km of the border. The Greek built-up footprint is well above 10 ha, so the claim that GRC has <10 ha of urban land within 100 km of the border over this aquifer is false.
sources: [T1] Hellenic Statistical Authority (ELSTAT), Population-Housing Census 2021: Doirani municipal unit, Kilkis, 1,022 inhabitants; Mouries municipal unit, 1,846 inhabitants https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doirani | [T1] Greek Ministry of Rural Development and Food, Lake Doirani factsheet (Greece holds 14 of the lake's 42 km2; catchment 192 km2; level fell sharply after the 1988 drought and has not recovered) https://www.minagric.gr/for-farmer-2/eggeiesbeltioseis/sxedismowee/452-limnes/1407-doirani | [T1] Gjorgjeska, V. et al. (2016). Water Balance Model of Vulnerability Assessment of Dojran Lake. IJARSET 3(4). https://www.ijarset.com/upload/2016/april/25_IJARSET_violeta.pdf
notes: Contradiction is on the URBAN limb only. No groundwater-irrigated cropland could be documented on the Greek side: the Dojran water-balance study states explicitly that 'data on ... water usage directly from the lake, from the surface and the underground for water supply or irrigation on the Greek side of the watershed are not available', and the Greek abstraction historically blamed for the lake's decline was lake (surface) water via a pumping station, which does not contradict a groundwater claim. Applying the ordered rule to corrected numbers: MKD has 14.2 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland, GRC has ~0.1 ha (<10 ha), and both sides now have urban land, so IU1 fails and the rule produces UB (not DA, and not the BL that clsF assigns). If the authors can source Greek-side borehole irrigation in the Doiran sub-basin, the class would instead become DA, since MKD's 10 km share is 93%, below the 99% BL threshold.

claim_tested: ESP has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: The Low Mino/Minho alluvial and detrital aquifer on the Galician side is documented as a water-supply and ecological resource in the Mino-Sil demarcation planning documents; Galician agriculture in the Baixo Mino (vineyards of the Rias Baixas O Rosal/Condado do Tea subzones, maize, market gardens) is overwhelmingly rainfed or supplemented from surface watercourses, and Galicia has one of the lowest irrigated shares of any Spanish region. No evidence of >10 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland on the Spanish side of this aquifer within 100 km of the Portuguese border was found.
sources: [T1] Confederacion Hidrografica del Mino-Sil, Plan Hidrologico de la demarcacion, sistema de explotacion 05 Mino Bajo https://chminosil.es/phocadownload/documentos/file/planificacion/plan_demarcacion_vigente/explotacion/05_Mino_Bajo.pdf | [T1] Universidade de Santiago de Compostela / Migraminho, Inventario de presiones en la subcuenca internacional del rio Mino (Galicia) http://migraminho.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/Informe-presiones-Migraminho_USC.compressed.pdf
notes: INPUT PLAUSIBILITY FLAG, and this one is arithmetically impossible: ur1 (ESP urban) = 38,406.5 ha, but the entire aquifer polygon is 172,538,645 m2 = 17,254 ha. The reported Spanish urban land is 2.2x the whole aquifer. The urban layer is clearly not clipped to the polygon for this dyad. The UB class here rests entirely on that urban figure, so although the cropland claim I was asked to test is confirmed, the class assignment itself is unsafe: if urban land over the polygon is actually <10 ha on both sides, the rule would produce IU0. Recommend re-extracting ur1/ur2 for EU001. (The CHMinoSil PDF could not be fetched directly - robots/TLS - so the Spanish planning evidence is from the search record and the USC pressures inventory rather than a page-level read; hence medium not high confidence.)

aquifer_name: Westliche Karawanken / Kepa (part of the Karawanken / Karavanke transboundary groundwater body)
claim_tested: Neither AUT nor SVN has >1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland or >1 ha of urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
evidence: The Karavanke/Karawanken transboundary groundwater body, agreed bilaterally in 2004 and comprising five cross-border aquifers along the main border ridge (including the Kepa/Mittagskogel western section), is described in the joint Slovenian-Austrian hydrogeological assessment as 'scarcely populated', with economic activity limited to grazing, forestry and some tourism; its karstified limestone-dolomite springs are used for drinking-water supply (Slovenian captures piped to Hrusica, Austrian springs reserved) and no irrigation is reported. Neither groundwater-irrigated cropland nor urban land >10 ha was found on the mapped 55.6 km2 ridge polygon.
sources: [T1] Janza, M., Prestor, J., Brencic, M. et al., Transboundary Groundwater Body Karavanke/Karawanken between Austria and Slovenia, Geophysical Research Abstracts EGU2009-8246 https://meetingorganizer.copernicus.org/EGU2009/EGU2009-8246.pdf | [T1] Karavanke/Karawanken Transboundary Groundwater Body Between the Republics of Austria and Slovenia (journal version) https://www.researchgate.net/publication/361670015_Karavanke_Karawanken_Transboundary_Groundwater_Body_Between_Republics_of_Austria_and_Slovenia | [T1] Transnational water resource management in the Karawanken/Karavanke UNESCO Global Geopark, JEMI 18(3), 2022 https://jemi.edu.pl/vol-18-issue-3-2022/transnational-water-resource-management-in-the-karawanken-karavanke-unesco-global-geopark
notes: Both limbs checked. The polygon is delineated to the main border ridge above ~1,000 m, so the settled valley floors on either side (Jesenice and Ratece/Kranjska Gora in Slovenia, the Rosental villages and Villach in Austria) fall outside it; that is the reason IU0 is defensible here despite substantial population within 100 km. If the authors' polygon is in fact the full Austrian 'Westliche Karawanken' groundwater body rather than the Kepa massif, it would reach the Rosental/Drau valley floor and the urban limb would fail, giving UB. Input values (all zeros) are internally consistent with a 55.6 km2 alpine ridge polygon.

claim_tested: Both ISR and PSE have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.
evidence: The North-eastern (Nablus-Gilboa) basin of the Mountain Aquifer is one of the best-documented shared aquifers in the world and supports agricultural well abstraction on both sides: Palestinian agricultural wells in the Jenin, Tubas and Nablus areas and Israeli wells in the Bet She'an/Gilboa area, with irrigated cropland distributed across the basin rather than confined to a 10 km strip. Nothing contradicts the DA claim.
sources: [T1] Klawitter, S., Water resources at stake: The Mountain Aquifer beneath the West Bank (UNDP Human Development Report background paper) https://hdr.undp.org/system/files/documents/simoneklawitterwaterresourcesatstake.pdf | [T1] The Israeli-Palestinian Mountain Aquifer: A Case Study in shared groundwater, Journal of Natural Resources and Life Sciences Education https://www.agronomy.org/files/jnrlse/issues/2001/e00-23.pdf | [T1] PASSIA, Groundwater (Mountain Aquifer basins and abstraction shares) https://passia.org/groundwater/
notes: INPUT PLAUSIBILITY FLAG, arithmetically impossible: ur1 (ISR) 28,112.9 ha + ur2 (PSE) 117,168.4 ha = 145,281 ha, against an aquifer polygon of 1,428,391,136 m2 = 142,839 ha. The two urban figures alone exceed the whole polygon, so the urban layer is not clipped to the polygon here either. The DA verdict is unaffected (DA is reached on cropland), but the same defect appears in EU001 and is severe in CB002, which suggests it is systematic rather than a one-off. Note also that gw1_10km/gw1_100km = 96% for ISR, close to the 99% BL threshold - this dyad is near a class boundary and sensitive to the border-zone geometry.

aquifer_name: Nata Karoo Sub-basin / Caprivi Lower Aquifer
claim_tested: NAM has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: The British Geological Survey's Hydrogeology of Namibia states that groundwater use for irrigation is not encouraged by the Namibian government and occurs only in the Otavi karst, the Stampriet artesian basin and along the west-flowing ephemeral rivers - none of which is the Zambezi/Caprivi region; groundwater there supplies domestic and livestock demand (83% of livestock water is groundwater but only 15% of irrigation water nationally), and the region's irrigation schemes (Kalimbeza rice, Liselo) draw Zambezi surface water. No groundwater-irrigated cropland >10 ha was found on the Namibian side of this aquifer within 100 km of the Zambian border.
sources: [T1] British Geological Survey, Africa Groundwater Atlas: Hydrogeology of Namibia https://earthwise.bgs.ac.uk/index.php/Hydrogeology_of_Namibia | [T1] SADC Groundwater Management Institute, Transboundary Diagnostic Analysis of the Eastern Kalahari Karoo Basin Aquifer System (2024) https://sadc-gmi.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Transboundary-Diagnostic-Analysis-of-the-Eastern-Kalahari-Karoo-Basin-Aquifer-System.pdf | [T1] Wanke, H. et al. (2019). Hydrogeology and geochemistry of a tectonically controlled, deep-seated and semi-fossil aquifer in the Zambezi Region (Namibia). Hydrogeology Journal 27, 885-899. 10.1007/s10040-018-1896-x
notes: The claim tested is about cropland only, and it holds: Namibian groundwater in the Zambezi Region is deep-seated, partly saline and semi-fossil, and is developed for village water supply and livestock, not irrigation. Note separately (does not contradict a UB claim) that Katima Mulilo, the Zambezi Region capital, sits on the Zambezi opposite Zambia and accounts for the ur1 = 17,379 ha figure - that is plausible in kind though generous in magnitude for a town of ~30,000. Small-scale conservation-agriculture gardens using hand-dug wells and shallow boreholes exist in the region but no source quantifies them at >10 ha over this polygon.

claim_tested: ETH has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: Irrigation development on the Ethiopian side of the Sudd basin margin (Gambella region, Baro-Akobo-Sobat basin) is surface-water based - the Alwero reservoir/Abobo scheme and river diversions on the Baro and Alwero - and Ethiopian groundwater irrigation is concentrated in the highlands and the Rift, not in the western lowlands. No groundwater-irrigated cropland >10 ha was found on the Ethiopian side of this aquifer within 100 km of the South Sudanese border.
sources: [T1] British Geological Survey, Africa Groundwater Atlas: Hydrogeology of Ethiopia https://earthwise.bgs.ac.uk/index.php/Hydrogeology_of_Ethiopia | [T1] USAID/Winrock, Ethiopia Water Resources Profile Overview (2021) https://winrock.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/Ethiopia_Country_Profile-Final.pdf | [T1] Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, Baro-Akobo river basin integrated development master plan (FAOLEX) https://faolex.fao.org/docs/pdf/eth180677.pdf
notes: INPUT PLAUSIBILITY FLAG: ur1 (ETH urban) = 213,278.6 ha = 2,133 km2 of urban land on the Ethiopian portion, and ur2 (SSD) = 365,372 ha = 3,654 km2. Gambella town has roughly 60,000 people and the Ethiopian Sudd-margin lowlands are among the least urbanised areas in the country; 2,133 km2 of urban land there is not credible and is likely a coarse built-up/settlement mask counting scattered rural tukul settlements. The polygon is enormous (323,960 km2) so these do not exceed area, but they are the sole basis for the UB assignment and, if corrected, both sides could fall below the urban threshold and the dyad would become IU0. Note also cls (UB) differs from clsF (DA), which is worth checking given both gw figures are exactly zero - DA should not be reachable with gw1 = gw2 = 0.

claim_tested: HTI has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: The Cul-de-Sac / Enriquillo graben ('Los Lagos') aquifer is documented (USGS Taylor & Lemoine 1949; Garcon & Brouyere 2020 on salinisation of the Cul-de-Sac groundwater). No source places groundwater-irrigated cropland on the Haitian side of the graben within 100 km of the Dominican border; the irrigated agriculture of the Plaine du Cul-de-Sac that is documented (Riviere Grise / Riviere Blanche perimeters, sugar cane) is surface-water fed and lies in the western, Port-au-Prince end of the plain.
sources: [T1] Taylor, G.C. & Lemoine, R.C. (1949). Ground water in the Cul-de-Sac Plain, Haiti. U.S. Geological Survey Open-File Report 49-114. 10.3133/ofr49114 | [T1] Taylor, G.C. & Lemoine, R.C. (1949). Les rivieres et les sources de la Plaine du Cul-de-Sac. USGS. https://pubs.usgs.gov/unnumbered/70102276/report.pdf | [T1] Garcon, J. & Brouyere, S. (2020). Extension spatiale et modelisation de la salinisation des ressources en eau souterraine de la plaine du Cul-de-Sac, Haiti. 10.13140/rg.2.2.12553.06248
notes: The Haitian ur2 of 362.7 ha suggests the mapped polygon covers only the eastern Cul-de-Sac (Fond Parisien / Ganthier, on Etang Saumatre at the border), not Croix-des-Bouquets or Port-au-Prince; that eastern strip is arid and saline, which makes the near-zero cropland figure plausible. Near-miss worth flagging: ir2 = 0.0 ha of irrigated cropland of ANY kind on the Haitian side is hard to believe if the polygon extends even slightly west, since the Cul-de-Sac carries thousands of hectares of surface-irrigated cane and plantain. Surface water, so it would not change the class, but it suggests the irrigation layer under-detects on the Haitian side. Verdict is CONFIRMED rather than INSUFFICIENT because the aquifer is documented, but the specific groundwater-irrigation question for the Haitian border strip is essentially unstudied.

claim_tested: MEX has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: The Presa La Amistad aquifer is a CONAGUA-designated aquifer (Coahuila) and part of the US-Mexico Transboundary Aquifer Assessment Program area; the Mexican side around Ciudad Acuna is rangeland and urban, with irrigation in the Rio Bravo corridor drawn from the river and from Amistad reservoir releases rather than from wells. No source places groundwater-irrigated cropland over the mapped polygon on the Mexican side.
sources: [T1] CONAGUA, Determinacion de la disponibilidad media anual de agua subterranea, acuifero Presa La Amistad (0501), Coahuila (published in the Diario Oficial de la Federacion). https://www.gob.mx/conagua | [T1] International Boundary and Water Commission / Transboundary Aquifer Assessment Program, Texas-Coahuila border reach. https://www.ibwc.gov/
notes: Small polygon (46,077 ha) straddling Amistad reservoir at Del Rio / Ciudad Acuna. Both sides record ~8 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland, all of it within 10 km of the border, so the dyad sits just below the 10 ha threshold on both limbs and is sensitive to small changes in the irrigation layer. Worth noting separately: San Felipe Springs at Del Rio (US side) is a major karst discharge used for municipal supply and some local irrigation, but it is on the US side and is not cropland, so it does not bear on the MEX claim.

claim_tested: SVN has >1 ha of neither groundwater-irrigated cropland nor urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
gis_verdict: rejected: feature outside the aquifer polygon
gis_acceptance: not accepted: 26.2 km outside, beyond the tolerance of 1 km + 2 km
error_class_description: excluded: rejected, feature outside the polygon beyond its own uncertainty
evidence: The Dolinsko-Ravensko aquifer is the Slovenian shallow alluvial aquifer of Prekmurje; the Geological Survey of Slovenia's monitoring network for it includes Lipovci, Renkovci, Radmozanci, Kapca, Gornji Lakos and Benica, i.e. the aquifer demonstrably extends to the Mura at the Croatian border. Lendava (2,947 inhabitants, 2021, SURS), plus Petisovci, Kapca and Gornji Lakos, sit on this aquifer within roughly 2-10 km of the Croatian border - far more than 10 ha of urban land, contradicting the urban limb of the SVN claim. No groundwater-irrigated cropland was found, so the cropland limb stands.

Geologija 64(1), 107-129 (Geological Survey of Slovenia) - names Kapca, Gornji Lakos, Benica, Radmozanci as Dolinsko-Ravensko aquifer monitoring sites. 10.5474/geologija.2021.007 | [T1] Statistical Office of the Republic of Slovenia (SURS), 2021 population of Lendava settlement: 2,947. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lendava
notes: Contradiction is on urban land alone, so the rule gives UB (SVN has urban land but <10 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km), not DA. The finding is robust to a possible country-index swap in the batch: whichever of HRV/SVN carries the ur=0.0 figure, the Mura valley on both sides of this border is settled - the Croatian bank has Mursko Sredisce (3,321, 2021 census) directly on the Mura frontier. So a zero urban figure for either riparian on this polygon is an under-detection. Caveat on confidence: the batch gives the polygon as only 17,274 ha, much smaller than the full Dolinsko-Ravensko groundwater body, so I cannot be certain which settlements the mapped polygon actually covers.

aquifer_name: Sandansky-Petrich Aquifer ; Sandansky Valley Aquifer ; Petrich Valley Aquifer
claim_tested: BGR has >1 ha of neither groundwater-irrigated cropland nor urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
gis_acceptance: accepted under the coordinate-uncertainty buffer (2.2 km outside, tolerance 1 km + 2 km)
error_class_description: applied: settlement above the threshold yet recorded zero over the whole polygon
applied_to: class only (classF unchanged: absorbed by the future projection)
evidence: Petrich (26,778 inhabitants, 2021 national census, Bulgarian NSI) lies at 168 m in the Sandanski-Petrich valley - the graben the aquifer is named for - roughly 15 km from the Greek border; Sandanski is in the same valley about 20 km from the border. Bulgaria therefore has vastly more than 10 ha of urban land over this aquifer within 100 km of the Greek border, contradicting the urban limb of the IU1 claim. No documented groundwater-irrigated cropland exceeding 10 ha was found on the Bulgarian side, so the cropland limb stands.
sources: [T1] National Statistical Institute of Bulgaria, 2021 Census - Petrich town population 26,778; town area 80.4 km2, elevation 168 m, in the Sandanski-Petrich valley. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petrich | [T1] National Statistical Institute of Bulgaria, 2021 Census - Sandanski, in the Sandanski-Petrich valley, about 20 km from the Bulgaria-Greece border. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandanski | [T1] Popovska, C. (2014). Water Balance Model for Vulnerability Assessment of Water Resources in Strumica River Basin. Irrigation & Drainage Systems Engineering 3(3) - identifies the Sandanski-Petrich Aquifer as a transboundary aquifer of the region (INWEB 2007 inventory). 10.4172/2168-9768.1000127
notes: Contradiction is on urban land alone, so the rule gives UB, not DA - and note that clsF for this dyad is BL, which the correction does not reach. Near-miss on the cropland limb: the Petrich-Sandanski basin is Bulgaria's warmest and most drought-exposed agroclimatic region and is a national centre for early vegetables and greenhouse production; Popovska (2014) reports that in the adjacent Strumica basin 'most feasible is that farmers use groundwater as a source for irrigation' from private wells that are not registered. If that pattern extends across the border into the Bulgarian Struma valley - plausible but not documented aquifer-specifically - BGR would also exceed 10 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland and, since the Greek side's cropland is 100% within 10 km of the border, the rule would then give BL. I did not find evidence sufficient to make that call.
