claim_tested: HRV has >1 ha of neither groundwater-irrigated cropland nor urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
gis_acceptance: accepted: feature strictly inside the polygon and band
error_class_description: excluded: definitional, settlement below the urban-cluster threshold
evidence: Croatia is a documented riparian of the Mura-Zala basin (Rman et al. 2011: the basin is 'situated between Slovenia, Austria, Hungary and Croatia'), and the only Croatian territory in that basin is Medimurje County. Mursko Sredisce (3,321 inhabitants, 2021 Croatian census; municipality 5,855) sits directly on the Mura at the Slovenian border, with Cakovec (~15,000) about 10 km further south. Croatia therefore has far more than 10 ha of urban land over this aquifer within 100 km of the Slovenian border, contradicting the urban limb of the HRV claim.
sources: [T1] Rman, N., Lapanje, A. & Prestor, J. (2011). Water Concession Principles for Geothermal Aquifers in the Mura-Zala Basin, NE Slovenia. Water Resources Management 25(13), 3277-3299. 10.1007/s11269-011-9855-5 | [T1] Nador, A., Lapanje, A., Toth, G. et al. (2012). Transboundary geothermal resources of the Mura-Zala basin. Geologija 55(2), 209-224 - delineates the transboundary Mura-Zala groundwater body (4,974 km2). 10.5474/geologija.2012.013 | [T1] Croatian Bureau of Statistics, 2021 Census - Mursko Sredisce town 3,321, municipality 5,855; northernmost town in Croatia, on the Mura which forms the Slovenian border. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mursko_Sredi%C5%A1%C4%87e
notes: Contradiction is on urban land alone, so the rule gives UB (HRV has urban land but <10 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km), not DA. Confidence is medium rather than high because I could not verify the mapped polygon's Croatian extent: the three named components (Goricko, Radgona-Vas, Kot) all lie along Slovenia's Austrian and Hungarian frontiers, and the Croatian share of this dyad may be a small sliver of the Strigova hills rather than the settled Medimurje lowland. The batch records ir1 = 0.0 ha of irrigated cropland of any kind for HRV, consistent with a small or hilly sliver. If the polygon does reach the Mura lowland, ur1 = 0.0 is a clear under-detection. Flagging as a candidate for a direct polygon check rather than a settled reclassification.

aquifer_name: Vellacher Kotschna / Bela (part of the Karawanken / Karavanke transboundary groundwater body)
claim_tested: Neither AUT nor SVN has >1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland or >1 ha of urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
evidence: The Vellacher Kotschna / Bela polygon (1,678 ha) is a high alpine karst cirque in the Karawanken/Karavanke on the Carinthia-Slovenia frontier. It contains no cropland and no settlement: the nearest towns are Bad Eisenkappel (Eisenkappel-Vellach, 2,446 inhabitants) some 8 km down-valley to the north-east, and Zgornje Jezersko on the Slovenian side beyond the Seeberg/Jezerski vrh pass. Nothing found contradicts either limb of the IU0 claim.
sources: [T2] Bad Eisenkappel / Eisenkappel-Vellach, Carinthia - 2,446 inhabitants, in the Vellach valley of the Karawanken, 15 km from the Jezersko pass border crossing. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_Eisenkappel
notes: The Karawanken/Karavanke transboundary groundwater body is recognised in Austrian-Slovenian bilateral water management and in the UNECE transboundary groundwater assessments, so a record exists at the level of the wider body; there is no aquifer-specific literature on the Vellacher Kotschna / Bela segment itself. All eight input figures are exactly zero, which for a 1,678 ha alpine karst polygon is entirely plausible. The 10 ha urban threshold is low enough that scattered alpine farmsteads (Vellacher Kotschna huts, the Jezersko valley floor) could in principle approach it, but nothing in the record supports crossing it.

claim_tested: Both JOR and SAU have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Both riparians irrigate extensively from the Saq-Ram (Disi/Saq) sandstone: Jordan in the Disi-Mudawwara wellfields of the southern desert, Saudi Arabia in the Tabuk and Al-Qurayyat areas. Neither country's groundwater-irrigated cropland is concentrated at the frontier - Jordan's is spread across the Disi basin (only 6.6% within 10 km of the border) and Saudi Arabia's is centred on Tabuk, well back from the boundary. Nothing contradicts the claim.
sources: [T1] UN-ESCWA & BGR (2013). Inventory of Shared Water Resources in Western Asia, Chapter on the Saq-Ram Aquifer System (West). https://www.unescwa.org/publications/inventory-shared-water-resources-western-asia
notes: One of the best-documented transboundary aquifers in the world; the claim is a weak one and is amply satisfied. Separately worth noting for the authors: SAU's gw2_100km (20,988.9 ha) is only 60% of its total gw2 (34,712.2 ha), i.e. a substantial share of Saudi groundwater irrigation on this aquifer lies more than 100 km from the border - consistent with the Tabuk centre of gravity, and a reminder that the 100 km band is doing real work on very large polygons like this one (15.2 Mha).

claim_tested: ZWE has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: No source places groundwater-irrigated cropland on the Zimbabwean side of the Middle Zambezi aquifer within 100 km of the Zambian border. Much of the Zimbabwean middle Zambezi valley is protected area (Mana Pools, Matusadona, Chizarira) or tsetse-constrained communal land, and the irrigation that does exist in the valley (Dande/Mushumbi in Mbire) is river-fed.
sources: [T1] Pavelic, P., Giordano, M., Keraita, B., Ramesh, V. & Rao, T. (eds) (2012). Groundwater availability and use in Sub-Saharan Africa: a review of 15 countries. IWMI - Zimbabwe chapter on alluvial aquifers. 10.5337/2012.213
notes: Genuine near-miss that the authors should see. The IWMI review states that Zimbabwe's alluvial deposits occur 'in the Save valley in south eastern Zimbabwe, along the Runde and Nuanetsi rivers, in the Zambezi basin in the north, and in the Umnyati and Sesami rivers in the Gokwe area', that these alluvial aquifers are high-yielding (up to 60 L/s), and that they are 'used mainly to support both large and small scale commercial irrigation'. Because the ZWE-ZMB border here IS the Zambezi/Lake Kariba, any groundwater irrigation on Zimbabwe's Zambezi alluvium is automatically within 100 km - and typically within 10 km - of the dyad's border. The statement is not specific enough as to which valley the irrigation examples refer to (the named schemes in that literature are Save and Limpopo), so I did not treat it as a contradiction. If a Zimbabwe-side figure above 10 ha were established, the rule would give DA (both sides then have >10 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland, and ZMB is only 71.7% concentrated within 10 km, so BL would not fire). This is the dyad in my batch most likely to flip on a targeted search of Zimbabwe National Water Authority / SADC-GMI material.

claim_tested: BEN has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: The Beninese (north-western) portion of the Volta basin is described in the aquifer-specific literature as a weathered-and-fractured basement plus Pendjari/Buem sedimentary system in which groundwater is used chiefly for domestic supply, tapped by hand-dug village wells that mostly dry up in the dry season - the opposite of the year-round yield that groundwater irrigation requires. No source places >10 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland on the Beninese side within 100 km of the Burkinabe border.
sources: [T1] Sambienou, W.G., Gourcy, L. & Alassane, A. (2018). Flow Pattern and Residence Time of Groundwater within Volta River Basin in Benin (Northwestern Benin). Journal of Water Resource and Protection 10(7), 663-680. 10.4236/jwarp.2018.107038
notes: Consistent with the batch's own ir1 = 4.3 ha of irrigated cropland of ANY kind on the Beninese side - there is essentially no irrigation there to be groundwater-fed. Important for the authors: even if the BEN claim were overturned, the class would NOT change. Burkina Faso still has 21,589 ha of urban land and 0 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km, which triggers UB on its own. The dyad would only leave UB if BFA were also shown to have >10 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland over this polygon - and given that Burkina's Est/Gourma region does practise small-scale dry-season market gardening from boreholes and shallow wells, that is the limb actually worth auditing here. I flag it but did not test it, since it is not the claim I was given.

claim_tested: CAN has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
gis_acceptance: accepted: feature strictly inside the polygon and band
error_class_description: applied: groundwater irrigation absent from the whole polygon
applied_to: class only (classF unchanged: absorbed by the future projection)
evidence: In the south Okanagan valley-bottom aquifer between Vaseux Lake and Osoyoos Lake (the model's southern boundary is Osoyoos Lake, on the international border), Toews & Allen (2009) document production/pumping wells in the Oliver region (named wells include Blacksage and Miller Road, i.e. the Black Sage Bench vineyard area) within the SOLID irrigation districts whose two dominant crops are orchard and vineyard; the paper explicitly discusses groundwater pumping as a substitute for the irrigation canal. Oliver/Black Sage Bench is ~15-25 km north of the CAN-USA border, far inside 100 km, and well over 10 ha of orchard/vineyard is served.
sources: [T1] Toews, M.W. & Allen, D.M. (2009). Simulated response of groundwater to predicted recharge in a semi-arid region using a scenario of modelled climate change. Environmental Research Letters 4(3), 035003. 10.1088/1748-9326/4/3/035003 | [T1] Liggett, J.E. & Allen, D.M. (2010). Evaluating the sensitivity of DRASTIC using different data sources, interpretations and mapping approaches (Greater Oliver area, south-central Okanagan). Environmental Earth Sciences 62(8), 1577-1595. 10.1007/s12665-010-0642-z | [T2] Wikipedia, Osoyoos, British Columbia (town is 3.6 km north of the US border; orchards and vineyards, irrigated since 1927). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osoyoos
notes: Caveat the authors should weigh: Toews & Allen state that Okanagan River is the dominant present-day irrigation source and that well pumping is a small share of the aquifer outflow, so the contradiction rests on the 10 ha threshold being very low rather than on groundwater being a major source. The paper does not separate municipal from agricultural well use, so it is possible (though unlikely given the Blacksage/Miller Road well names on the vineyard bench) that the production wells are domestic only. Reclassification logic: with CAN gw_100km > 10 ha, IU0/IU1 fail; UB fails because the only side with urban land (CAN, 163,582 ha) would now also have >10 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland and the USA side has ur2 = 0; BL fails (USA 10.1/22.1 = 46% within 10 km); hence DA, which matches clsF.

aquifer_name: Baja de Rio Bravo / Gulf Coast Aquifer
claim_tested: Both MEX and USA have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Searched for evidence that either the Mexican (Tamaulipas/Baja Rio Bravo) or the US (Lower Rio Grande / Gulf Coast Aquifer) side lacks groundwater-irrigated cropland, or that either side's groundwater irrigation is confined to a 10 km border strip. Nothing found: groundwater irrigation is documented on both sides of the Gulf Coast Aquifer system and is distributed across the coastal plain rather than hugging the Rio Grande.
sources: [T2] General literature and encyclopaedic coverage of the Gulf Coast Aquifer System and the Baja Rio Bravo irrigation district; no source found restricting groundwater irrigation to one side or to a 10 km band. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Coast_Aquifer
notes: The input ratios are themselves far from the BL threshold (MEX 2196/5242 = 42% within 10 km; USA 2858/12699 = 23%), so the claim is robust to substantial measurement error. Note that in the Lower Rio Grande Valley proper, surface water from the Rio Grande dominates irrigation and much shallow Gulf Coast groundwater is brackish; groundwater irrigation is more important further up the coastal plain. That pattern supports, rather than undermines, the 'distributed, not border-concentrated' part of the claim. Web search budget for this session was exhausted early, so this confirmation rests on fewer independent checks than intended.

claim_tested: RUS has >1 ha of neither groundwater-irrigated cropland nor urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
gis_acceptance: accepted: feature strictly inside the polygon and band
error_class_description: excluded: definitional, settlement below the urban-cluster threshold
evidence: The Russian sector of the Uvs Nuur / Ubsunur Hollow basin covers four districts of the Tuva Republic (Mongun-Tayginsky, Ovyursky, Tes-Khemsky, Erzinsky), each with a populated administrative centre inside the hollow and within a few tens of km of the Mongolian border. Khandagayty, seat of Ovyursky District, had 3,207 inhabitants at the 2010 All-Russian Census and sits roughly 15 km from the border at the Borshoo crossing - a settlement of that size occupies well over 10 ha of built-up land, against a recorded ur2 of 0.0 ha. No groundwater-irrigated cropland was found on the Russian side.
sources: [T1] All-Russian Population Census 2010, Khandagayty (Ovyursky District, Tuva Republic): 3,207 inhabitants (census figure, retrieved via Wikipedia). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khandagayty | [T1] UNESCO World Heritage / Uvs Nuur Basin description: basin of 70,000 km2 straddling the Russian-Mongolian border, with Russian clusters in Mongun-Tayginsky, Ovyursky, Tes-Khemsky and Erzinsky districts of Tuva. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uvs_Nuur_Basin
notes: Residual uncertainty is polygon membership, not the settlement: the mapped aquifer is 1,589,842 ha against a 70,000 km2 basin, so it is presumably the central sedimentary depression, and I could not verify from a map that Khandagayty (or Samagaltay/Erzin) falls inside it. Land use in the Russian sector is nomadic pastoralism, so the groundwater-irrigation limb of the claim is very likely correct; the contradiction is on urban land alone. Reclassification: with RUS urban > 10 ha and RUS gw = 0, IU0/IU1 fail and UB fires (RUS has urban land but <10 ha groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km), so UB, not DA.

claim_tested: GEO has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: Searched Georgian and regional hydrogeological literature on the Alazani-Agrichay artesian basin. The Georgian (Kakheti) side is documented as an artesian basin with productive Quaternary and Alazani-series aquifers, but the irrigation record for the Alazani valley describes river- and canal-fed supply ('the river is mainly used for irrigation and for drinking water'), not groundwater-irrigated cropland. No source was found placing groundwater-irrigated cropland on the Georgian side within 100 km of the AZE-GEO border.
sources: [T1] Gaprindashvili, G. & Gaprindashvili, M. (2014). Fresh Groundwater Resources in Georgia and Management Problems. International Journal of Geosciences 5(9), 877-881 (Alazani-Agrichai artesian basin; groundwater flows from Georgia into Azerbaijan). 10.4236/ijg.2014.59077 | [T1] Vepkhvadze, S., Melikadze, G. & Todadze, M. (2019). Recharge and dynamics of a karst groundwater system in Kakheti (Eastern Georgia). Austrian Journal of Earth Sciences 112(1), 42-49. 10.17738/ajes.2019.0003 | [T1] World Bank (2022). Watershed Management and Landscape Restoration Opportunities Assessment for Sioni Reservoir Watershed System in Georgia (hydrogeological zoning: artesian basin of Alazani). 10.1596/38298
notes: Near-miss worth flagging: the Georgian Alazani valley is a confined/self-flowing artesian basin, and Soviet-era and later hydrogeology describe abundant boreholes in Kakheti. If any material fraction of Kakheti's vineyards or vegetable plots are served by artesian boreholes, the claim would fail - but no source quantifying groundwater-irrigated area on the Georgian side could be found, so I do not record a contradiction. Georgian- and Russian-language sources would be the place to look; the session's web-search budget was exhausted, which limited coverage in those languages.

claim_tested: BIH has >1 ha of neither groundwater-irrigated cropland nor urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
gis_acceptance: accepted: feature strictly inside the polygon and band
error_class_description: excluded: definitional, settlement below the urban-cluster threshold
evidence: The Krka rises at the foot of Dinara immediately next to the Croatia-BiH border, so the BiH share of this 66,861 ha karst groundwater body is the Grahovo/Strmica karst. Bosansko Grahovo, the municipal seat there, lies directly on the Croatian border and recorded 651 inhabitants in the town and 2,970 in the municipality at the 2013 BiH census - a built-up footprint comfortably above 10 ha, against a recorded ur1 of 0.0 ha. No groundwater irrigation was found on either side.
sources: [T1] Agency for Statistics of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Census of Population 2013: Bosansko Grahovo town 651, municipality 2,970 (census figures retrieved via Wikipedia). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosansko_Grahovo | [T2] Wikipedia, Krka (Croatia): source near the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina at the foot of Dinara; basin 2,088 km2. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krka_(Croatia)
notes: Confidence is low because I could not verify that Bosansko Grahovo falls inside the mapped Krka polygon: Grahovsko polje is a sinking karst polje whose waters have been attributed in the tracer literature to both the Krka/Butiznica and the Cetina springs, so the BiH slice of this particular groundwater body may be an unpopulated upland strip nearer Strmica. Treat as a candidate rather than a settled reclassification. If accepted: IU0/IU1 fail, UB fires (both sides then have urban land and <10 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km), giving UB - not the BL that clsF assigns.

aquifer_name: The former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia - Central Serbia
claim_tested: Both MKD and XKX have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.
evidence: Searched for evidence that one side of this North Macedonia-Kosovo aquifer has no groundwater-irrigated cropland or has it concentrated in a 10 km border strip. Nothing found that contradicts the claim; both sides carry small but non-trivial groundwater-irrigated areas distributed through the valley bottoms.
sources: [T2] No aquifer-specific source located for this delineation ('The former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia - Central Serbia'); general regional groundwater and irrigation coverage found nothing contradicting the claim. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irrigation_in_North_Macedonia
notes: The XKX side is close to the BL boundary in the input (gw2_10km/gw2 = 0.5/182.8 = 0.3% within 10 km, i.e. very far from border-concentrated, so the DA classification is safe in that direction), while the MKD side is 4.9/16.8 = 29%. The aquifer itself has essentially no aquifer-specific literature - it appears under a legacy delineation name - so this is closer to 'no record' than to a positive confirmation. Web-search budget for the session was exhausted, limiting Macedonian/Albanian/Serbian-language coverage.

aquifer_name: Gori?ko Aquifer; Mura - Zala Basin / Radgona - Va? Aquifer; Kot Aquifer
claim_tested: HRV has >1 ha of neither groundwater-irrigated cropland nor urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
gis_verdict: rejected: feature outside the aquifer polygon
gis_acceptance: not accepted: 8.6 km outside, beyond the tolerance of 1 km + 2 km
error_class_description: excluded: rejected, feature outside the polygon beyond its own uncertainty
evidence: The Croatian share of the Mura-Zala basin groundwater body is Medimurje County, which borders Hungary directly to the east and had 105,250 inhabitants over roughly 730 km2 at the 2021 Croatian census, with the towns of Cakovec, Prelog and Mursko Sredisce all within a few tens of km of the Hungarian border. Urban land on the Croatian side therefore exceeds 10 ha by orders of magnitude, against a recorded ur1 of 0.0 ha. No groundwater-irrigated cropland was established on the Croatian side.
sources: [T1] Croatian Bureau of Statistics, Census of Population, Households and Dwellings 2021: Medimurje County 105,250 inhabitants; county borders Hungary to the east (census figures retrieved via Wikipedia). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Me%C4%91imurje_County
notes: The one weak link is whether Croatia's slice of this composite polygon (Goricko; Mura-Zala Basin / Radgona-Vas; Kot - a grouping that is primarily Slovenian-Hungarian-Austrian) really is the Medimurje lowland. It must be somewhere on the Croatian side of the Croatia-Hungary boundary in the Mura/Zala lowland, and Medimurje is the only such territory; every point of it is well inside 100 km of Hungary and it is one of Croatia's most densely settled counties, so a recorded urban figure of exactly zero is not credible. Reclassification: IU0/IU1 fail; UB fires (both sides have urban land, neither has >10 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km), giving UB - not the BL that clsF assigns.

aquifer_name: Sliv Kvarnerskog zaljeva / Obmo?je Kvarnerskega zaliva
claim_tested: SVN has >1 ha of neither groundwater-irrigated cropland nor urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
evidence: No source could be found that delineates the Slovenian share of the Kvarner Bay catchment groundwater body or names any settlement or agriculture within it. The Slovenian territory draining to Kvarner is a small karst strip on the Sneznik massif and around Jelsane in Ilirska Bistrica municipality; I could not establish that any named settlement falls inside the mapped polygon.
sources: [T2] General geographic coverage of the Kvarner Gulf and of the Slovenian karst hinterland (Sneznik, Ilirska Bistrica, Jelsane); no aquifer-specific description of the Slovenian share located. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kvarner_Gulf
notes: Near-miss to record: Slovenia is small enough that any Slovenian territory in this polygon is automatically within 100 km of the Croatian border, so the whole claim reduces to whether >10 ha of built-up land sits in the Slovenian slice. The candidate settlements are the Jelsane/Novokracine/Susak villages (a few hundred inhabitants each, each plausibly 15-30 ha of built-up land) and, if the polygon is drawn on the Sneznik karst rather than on surface catchments, Ilirska Bistrica town (~4,300). Either would flip the dyad to UB. A GIS overlay of the polygon against Slovenian settlement boundaries would settle this in minutes and is worth doing rather than searching further. Web-search budget for the session was exhausted, so Slovenian- and Croatian-language sources were not reachable.

claim_tested: IRQ has >1 ha of neither groundwater-irrigated cropland nor urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
evidence: The only substantial Iraqi settlement over this part of the Western Desert is Ar-Rutbah (population 31,011 in 2018), and it lies 110 km from the Iraq-Saudi border and 110 km from the Iraq-Jordan border - just outside the 100 km band. The surrounding Iraqi Widyan desert within 100 km of the Saudi border is essentially unpopulated and uncultivated (rainfall ~117 mm/yr), consistent with the recorded gw1_100km = 0.0 and ur1 = 0.0.
sources: [T2] Wikipedia, Ar-Rutbah: population 31,011 (2018); 'Rutba is 70 miles (110 km) from both the Iraq-Jordan border and the Iraq-Saudi Arabia border'; annual rainfall 117 mm. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutbah
notes: This is a genuine near-miss and the authors should know how tight it is: Rutba is ~10 km outside the 100 km band on the stated figure, so a modest error in either the town's position or the border-zone geometry would flip this dyad to UB (Iraqi urban land, no groundwater irrigation; SAU already has ur2 = 57,324 ha and gw2_100km = 0). Nukhayb, further east in Anbar, is the other candidate and is also roughly 100-115 km from the Saudi border. Note also that gw1 = 0.5 ha exists on the Iraqi segment but entirely outside 100 km, which is internally consistent with a few Western Desert well-irrigated plots well north of the border. Per guidance item 1, the Iraqi segment's border zone may be measured partly against Jordan; Rutba is 110 km from that border too, so the conclusion is unchanged.

claim_tested: ZMB has >1 ha of neither groundwater-irrigated cropland nor urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
gis_acceptance: accepted under the coordinate-uncertainty buffer (2.9 km outside, tolerance 1 km + 2 km)
error_class_description: applied: settlement above the threshold yet recorded zero over the whole polygon
evidence: The Bua rises on the Zambian border in the Mchinji Forest Reserve, so the Zambian share of this 1,881,066 ha polygon is eastern Chipata District. Chipata city had 193,288 inhabitants in 2022 and lies 20 km from the Mwami border crossing with Malawi - built-up land far above 10 ha within 100 km of the border, against a recorded ur2 of 3.8 ha. No groundwater-irrigated cropland was found on the Zambian side; farming there is described as drawing on streams and the Luangwa.
sources: [T1] Zambia Statistics Agency, 2022 Census of Population and Housing: Chipata city 193,288, Chipata District 327,059 (census figures retrieved via Wikipedia); Chipata is 20 km from the Mwami border post with Malawi. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chipata | [T2] Wikipedia, Bua River (Malawi): rises about 80 km west of Lilongwe on the border with Zambia in the Mchinji Forest Reserve. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bua_River_(Malawi)
notes: Uncertainty is whether the mapped polygon extends far enough into Zambia to reach Chipata; it must cross the border to make Zambia a riparian, and Chipata sits only 20 km inside, with dense peri-urban settlement continuous from the border. Even the Zambian border settlements at Mwami exceed 10 ha. Reclassification: IU0/IU1 fail; UB fires (Malawi has large urban land and gw1_100km = 0; Zambia likewise), giving UB, not DA. Separate data-quality flag: ur1 = 1,275,680 ha is 68% of the whole aquifer polygon, which is not credible as Malawian built-up land in this rural catchment even though it does not exceed area_ha - the Malawi urban figure and the Zambian figure of 3.8 ha look like errors in opposite directions on the same layer.

aquifer_name: Afar Rift Valley / Afar Triangle Aquifer
claim_tested: DJI has >1 ha of neither groundwater-irrigated cropland nor urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
gis_acceptance: accepted under the coordinate-uncertainty buffer (6.2 km outside, tolerance 25 km + 2 km)
error_class_description: applied: settlement above the threshold yet recorded zero over the whole polygon
evidence: Dikhil, the capital of Djibouti's Dikhil Region, sits 12 km north of the Ethiopian border with 27,378 inhabitants at the 2024 census, is described as one of Djibouti's main agricultural areas with gardens and fruit trees, and was founded around the well of Harrou; the Dikhil region is supplied by the intensively exploited Dalha basalts aquifer, with wellfield abstraction of 2.34 million m3/yr. Djibouti has no perennial surface water, so this cropland irrigation is necessarily groundwater-fed. Both limbs of the claim (ur1 = 0.0 and gw1_100km = 0.0) therefore fail, at ~12 km from the ETH border.
sources: [T1] Razack, M., Jalludin, M. & Berehanu, B. (2025). Water Resource Assessment and Management in Dalha Basalts Aquifer (SW Djibouti) Using Numerical Modeling. Hydrology 12(4), 73. Dikhil region borders Ethiopia, 7,200 km2, 112,000 inhabitants, city of Dikhil 35,000; arid climate, absence of surface water; wellfield abstraction 2.34e6 m3/yr. 10.3390/hydrology12040073 | [T1] Republic of Djibouti 2024 census: Dikhil town population 27,378; town lies 12 km north of the border with Ethiopia (census figure retrieved via Wikipedia). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dikhil | [T1] Ahmed Kayad Abdourahman et al. / Boschetti, T., Awaleh, M.O. & Barbieri, M. (2018). Waters from the Djiboutian Afar. Water 10(11), 1700 - includes new groundwater data from the Hanle-Gaggade plains, the Djiboutian irrigated lowland adjoining Ethiopia. 10.3390/w10111700
notes: This is the clearest contradiction in the batch and it is a double one: urban land (Dikhil, 27,378 people, 12 km from Ethiopia, plus Ali Sabieh further east) and groundwater-irrigated cropland (the Dikhil/Gobaad and Hanle-Gaggade date-palm and vegetable plots, all borehole-fed because Djibouti has no perennial surface water). The Djibouti-wide irrigated area is only ~1,000 ha, but that is two orders of magnitude above the 10 ha threshold and Dikhil is one of the main centres. The Karatag/North-Surkhandarya aquifer underlies the Tursunzoda-Shahrinav piedmont in Tajikistan and the Sariosiyo-Denov piedmont of Surkhandarya in Uzbekistan, both intensively irrigated piedmont plains where well and kariz abstraction supplements canal supply; the reported split (Tajikistan 1,087 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland with 44% inside 10 km of the border; Uzbekistan 3,797 ha with 18% inside 10 km) is consistent with distributed piedmont irrigation on both sides.
notes: This is a DA claim asserting presence of groundwater irrigation on both sides plus absence of >99% concentration within 10 km - the easiest kind of claim to satisfy and the hardest to contradict, since contradicting it would require showing that one side has essentially no groundwater irrigation or that its irrigation is a border-hugging strip. Neither is plausible here: both riparian provinces carry tens of thousands of hectares of total irrigated land (ir1 19,782 ha, ir2 59,366 ha) spread across the piedmont fans, not along the frontier. record_exists=false only because I could not retrieve an aquifer-specific source under the search constraints described in the N005 note; the region is in fact well documented (Surkhandarya basin and Hisor valley hydrogeology) and a normal search would almost certainly return Tier 1 material.

claim_tested: HRV has <1 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km of the shared border over this aquifer (it does have urban-cluster land).
evidence: The Croatian part of the Trebisnjica karst system is the Dubrovnik littoral, where the system re-emerges at the Ombla spring; the documented Croatian uses are hydropower (two 16 km tunnels delivering water to plants near Cavtat since 1965) and public water supply from Ombla, not well-field irrigation. No source found showing >10 ha of well-abstracted groundwater-irrigated cropland on the Croatian side within 100 km of the BiH border.
sources: [T2] Wikipedia, Trebisnjica - karst aquifer zones near Bileca, Popovo polje, Ombla spring, and the 1965 water-transfer tunnels to Croatian facilities near Cavtat. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trebi%C5%A1njica | [T2] Wikipedia, Konavle - the Konavle field, its Roman-era canal irrigation from the spring at Vodovadja, and 2021 population of about 20,000 across 32 settlements. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konavle
notes: Genuine near-miss worth flagging: the Konavle field southeast of Dubrovnik (a few hundred hectares of irrigated horticulture, roughly 30-45 km from the BiH border and within the Trebisnjica/Ombla karst catchment) is irrigated from karst springs - the historic Vodovadja canal and the modern Ljuta-spring scheme. Karst-spring abstraction is groundwater discharge captured at the surface, so whether it counts as 'groundwater irrigation' is a definitional choice made by the input layer, not a factual dispute. The Croatian figure in the batch, gw2 = 5.6 ha, sits just below the 10 ha threshold, so a slightly different treatment of spring-fed irrigation would flip this dyad from UB to DA or BL. Search constraints as described in the N005 note.

aquifer_name: Tawil Quaternary Aquifer System: Wadi Sirhan Basin
claim_tested: JOR has >1 ha of neither groundwater-irrigated cropland nor urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
evidence: The UN-ESCWA Inventory chapter for the Tawil Quaternary Aquifer System / Wadi Sirhan Basin reports irrigation abstraction for the basin rising 'from about 100 MCM in 1984 to almost 3,500 MCM in 2004', but attributes no irrigation to the Jordanian side and names no Jordanian settlement on the basin other than Al-Jafr, which lies in a different basin to the west. Recharge is given as 0-2 mm/yr. Nothing contradicting the claim was found on either limb.

(2022). Estimation of unrecorded groundwater abstractions in Jordan through regional groundwater modelling. Hydrogeology Journal, 30(6), 1769-1787. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10040-022-02523-3
notes: The ~3,500 MCM of irrigation abstraction is essentially all Saudi - the centre-pivot wheat and fodder complex around Tabarjal/Al-Isawiyah in the Al-Jawf region - and that is exactly what our inputs already capture on the Saudi side (gw2 = 94,962.7 ha, of which gw2_100km = 89,099.3 ha). Jordan's real eastern-desert groundwater irrigation is in the Azraq and Hamad basins to the north-west, i.e. outside this polygon - a PER-SEGMENT/adjacent-basin distinction worth recording so a later searcher does not import it as a contradiction. Consistency check on the Saudi side: gw2_10km = 110.4 ha of gw2_100km = 89,099.3 ha is 0.1%, far below the 0.99 BL threshold, so IU1 rather than BL is right.

Per the correction to item 5 I do not report this as exceeding the polygon and it does not breach area_ha, so it is not internally impossible - but a 55% built-up fraction across the Rift is far above any plausible built-up share for this region even including Goma, Bukavu, Butembo and the Ugandan Rift towns, and the pair is the most extreme in this batch. claim_tested: MWI has >1 ha of neither groundwater-irrigated cropland nor urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
evidence: The BGS Africa Groundwater Atlas (Tier 1) places Malawi's Karoo sedimentary sequence in north-south trending basins and to the southwest of the Shire Valley, describes it as well-cemented with low intergranular permeability and only low-to-moderate productivity, and states that relatively little is known about it; it records no irrigation use. No source could be found that locates this specific 'Lower sandstones' transboundary unit or names settlements on it, so neither limb of the claim could be tested.

notes: NEAR-MISS worth the authors' attention: ur2 = 0.0 ha for the Malawian segment looks like probable under-detection. The Karoo outcrop that BGS places southwest of the Shire Valley runs along the Malawi-Mozambique border through Mwanza, Neno and Chikwawa districts, where district seats - Mwanza town sits at a major border crossing a few km from Mozambique - would fall well inside 100 km of this dyad's own border. Malawi is among the most densely settled countries in the region and a 228,302 ha unit recording exactly zero urban hectares on the Malawian side is hard to credit. If the polygon covers any of those seats the rule would return UB rather than IU1. I could not verify the polygon: the Malawi transboundary-aquifer assessment paper on ScienceDirect (S2214581817303774), which defines these national TBA units, is robots-disallowed to WebFetch, and the Scite quota was exhausted. Recommend a manual overlay of this polygon against Malawi's settlement layer - this is the highest-value unresolved dyad in the batch. Not recorded as a contradiction because the location is unverified.

claim_tested: UZB has >1 ha of neither groundwater-irrigated cropland nor urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.

This is also a textbook case of protocol item 1: on a 16.4 Mha multi-riparian aquifer the measured band for the Uzbek segment may be keyed to a different neighbour's boundary entirely, so a Karakalpak town being 'near a border' would not contradict this dyad's claim. Unresolved because I could not establish whether Qongirot (roughly 100-150 km from the Kazakh border) falls inside the band. No WebSearch allowance remained to pursue it; Central Asia is outside the UN-ESCWA inventory's coverage so there was no guessable Tier 1 URL. record_exists false reflects the segment, not the Amu Darya system, which is well documented.

claim_tested: Both SYR and TUR have groundwater-irrigated cropland over this aquifer, and neither side is >99% concentrated within 10 km of the border.

evidence: CROPLAND LIMB CONTRADICTED ON THE ALGERIAN SIDE. Djanet (24.55N, 9.48E) is a cluster of three oases - Adjahil, El-Mihane and Azellouaz - in the Tassili n'Ajjer, on the Algerian portion of the Murzuq-Djado system and roughly 55-70 km west of the Algeria-Libya border, i.e. inside the 100 km band. Bellal, Hadeid & Ghodbani (2017) classify Djanet explicitly as an oasis irrigated from the phreatic water table ('oasis sur nappe phreatique'). Kouadri et al. (2021) document the Oued Djanet infero-flux alluvial aquifer, 17 km2, exploited by 24 boreholes with 9 boreholes and 1 well in operation and described as the region's largest and formerly only water supply, alongside the Tassili Cambro-Ordovician and the Continental Intercalaire which receives agricultural inputs. The water source is unambiguously groundwater: there is no perennial surface water in the Tassili, so oasis date-palm and market-garden plots there are spring-, water-table- and borehole-fed by definition. Gast & Hachid (1995) record the Djanet daira growing from 5,318 inhabitants (1977) to 10,905 (1993), a population supported by these irrigated oases. The irrigated area is on the order of hundreds of hectares and certainly exceeds 10 ha, against gw1_100km = 0.0 ha in our inputs.

notes: PER-SEGMENT TRAP CHECKED (protocol item 1): Djanet's ~60 km is to the DZA-LBY border specifically. The Algeria-Niger border is more than 400 km south of Djanet, so this is not a case of irrigation sitting near a different neighbour's boundary - the finding bears on the dyad actually being tested. USEFUL INTERNAL CROSS-CHECK: our own inputs record ur1 = 15,251.4 ha of Algerian urban land on this polygon, which in that part of the Sahara can only be Djanet and the Illizi/Bordj El Haouas settlements. The data therefore already places those settlements on the mapped aquifer while recording zero groundwater-irrigated cropland beside them, which is internally hard to reconcile with oasis agriculture that is by definition irrigated. CONFIDENCE CAVEAT: the verdict itself is solid and Tier 1, but I could not obtain a published hectare figure for Djanet's irrigated perimeters within budget, so '>10 ha' rests on the documented existence of three irrigated oases, ten operating abstraction points and a daira population above 10,000 rather than on a mapped area. Hence medium rather than high. PROPOSED CLASS DERIVATION: with DZA gw_100km corrected to >10 ha (order 10^2) and LBY already at gw2_100km = 30.2 ha, both sides exceed the 10 ha floor, so IU0, IU1 and UB all fail. BL fails too: Djanet is ~60 km from the border so the Algerian share within 10 km is nowhere near 99%, and LBY is 3.0/30.2 = 9.9%. Therefore DA. Separately note that LBY has gw2 = 19,135.8 ha over the whole polygon but only 30.2 ha within 100 km of this border - the Murzuq oases proper are far to the east, so the Libyan limb genuinely is border-remote.

notes: CONFIDENCE CAVEAT, PLEASE READ: the contradiction rests on a basin-wide population figure, not on a named settlement with coordinates. The paper does not name any Zimbabwean town - Beitbridge is not mentioned anywhere in it - so I cannot pin a specific built-up polygon inside the band the way EB086 pins Malko Tarnovo. Beitbridge town is the obvious candidate on general grounds (it lies roughly 65-70 km east of the Shashe-Limpopo confluence, hence inside 100 km of the BWA-ZWE border) but I could not confirm within budget that it falls on the mapped Tuli Karoo polygon, and the ~60,000 Zimbabwean residents may partly be dispersed rural homesteads that a land-cover product would not class as urban. The finding is honest but softer than a named-town finding; hence medium. NEAR-MISS NOT RECORDED AS A CONTRADICTION: the cropland limb is also suspect, since irrigation is >80% of water use in this aquifer's basin and Zimbabwe specifically is credited with small-scale irrigation, but I could not separate alluvial-groundwater abstraction from direct Limpopo/Shashe river pumping, and the protocol requires the groundwater source to be established. So no cropland contradiction is recorded. If a source establishes groundwater as the source for >10 ha on the Zimbabwean side, the class becomes DA instead of UB. PROPOSED CLASS DERIVATION: with ZWE urban corrected above 10 ha, IU0 fails (BWA has ur1 = 23,994.1 ha). IU1 fails because neither side now has 'neither' limb - BWA has urban, ZWE has urban. UB then fires: at least one side has urban land and under 10 ha of groundwater-irrigated cropland within 100 km, and in fact both do (BWA 4.8 ha, ZWE 8.4 ha). Therefore UB. Also note the clsF = BL artefact here: BWA gw1_10km/gw1 = 4.8/4.8 = 100%, so a variant without the 10 ha floor classifies this whole dyad as border-localised off 4.8 hectares of cropland.

Separately, the Mura/Drava Quaternary alluvium is a documented strategic groundwater resource and Medjimurje's transboundary aquifers have a dedicated protection literature, so record_exists is true; note that abstraction there is municipal supply, not cropland irrigation, and so does not bear on the cropland limb.

aquifer_name: Système Aquifère de Mourzouk - Djado / Murzuk-Djado Aquifer System
claim_tested: NER has >1 ha of neither groundwater-irrigated cropland nor urban-cluster land within 100 km of the shared border, over this aquifer.
evidence: The BGS Africa Groundwater Atlas page for Niger contains nothing on the Djado plateau, Kaouar or the far northeast, and names no abstraction centre there; the only location it treats in any detail is Niamey. The Nigerien portion of the Murzuk-Djado system is hyperarid, effectively uninhabited Djado plateau and Tenere desert, and no groundwater-irrigated cropland or urban land was found within 100 km of the Libyan border over this aquifer.
sources: [T1] British Geological Survey, Africa Groundwater Atlas: Hydrogeology of Niger (Earthwise mirror). Notes nationally that 'Groundwater is the main source of irrigation water for most small farmer who practise irrigation, mainly abstracted from hand dug wells', with no coverage of the Djado or far northeast. https://earthwise.bgs.ac.uk/index.php/Hydrogeology_of_Niger
notes: NEAR-MISS AND THE ONE ROUTE TO A RECLASSIFICATION HERE: the Djado plateau oases, principally Djado and Chirfa, historically supported date-palm gardens irrigated from wells and springs, and lie roughly 80-150 km from the Libyan border. Most were abandoned decades ago (disease, then insecurity) and the surviving populations are a few hundred people, but 10 ha is a low bar for both limbs and I could not establish either their current cultivated extent or their exact distance from the border within the call ceiling. Madama and Toummo, on or near the border itself, are military posts rather than settlements. If a garden area above 10 ha is confirmed inside the band, the class would move from IU1 to DA, since Libya's side is not >99% concentrated within 10 km (30.2 ha of 19,135.8 ha within 100 km, and 3.0 ha within 10 km). The BGS statement that groundwater is the main irrigation source for Niger's smallholders is Tier 1 and cuts toward that possibility nationally, but it is a national statement with no locational content and so is not decisive, which is why I record CONFIRMED rather than a contradiction. record_exists is false in the strict sense: no source I reached describes the Murzuk-Djado system itself.
